# Locality Guide: Berkshire County, Massachusetts (1820–1850)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Formed:** 1761, from Hampshire County; boundaries stable through the entire 1820–1850 window
- **County seat:** Pittsfield
- **Economy:** Agriculture, ironworks, paper mills, early textile manufacturing; the Western Railroad opened through the county in 1841
- **Key denominations:** Congregational (dominant), Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Quaker, and (by the 1840s) Catholic

---

## Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)

**The crucial split is the year 1841.**

- **1820–1840:** Massachusetts had *no statewide registration*. Only the individual town clerk kept the record. There is no county or state index for this period — you must identify which Berkshire County town the family lived in and consult that town's own records.
- **1841–1850:** Massachusetts was the first state to establish statewide recording (1841). From that year, both a town copy and a state copy exist.
- **Marriage intentions:** Filed separately at the bride's town (and sometimes the groom's town). If you can't find a marriage record in one town, check the other spouse's town clerk.

### Where to Look for Vitals

| Resource | Notes | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Published "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series** | Covers over 200 MA towns including Berkshire County towns; fastest starting point for pre-1850 events | Libraries; FamilySearch; NEHGS |
| **FamilySearch: "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890"** (coll. 2061550) | Name-searchable index | Free at FamilySearch.org |
| **FamilySearch image volume 004500891** — Berkshire County Town Clerk Vital Records, 1761–1850 (512 images) | **Browse-only — no name index, not full-text searchable.** Must page through manually | Free at FamilySearch.org |
| **Massachusetts State Archives (Boston)** | State copies from 1841 onward | In-person |
| **Individual town clerks** (Pittsfield, Great Barrington, Adams, Williamstown, etc.) | Original town vital records; in-person or written request | Each town separately |

---

## Church Records

Church records are the most important *substitute* for missing town vital records, especially for 1820–1840 events.

| Resource | Notes | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch: "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920"** (coll. 1921657) | Name-searchable index | Free at FamilySearch.org |
| **FamilySearch image volume 004500892** — Pittsfield Congregational Church Records, 1791–1850 (274 images) | **Browse-only — no name index.** | Free at FamilySearch.org |
| **Congregational Library (Boston)** | Holds many original Congregational registers | In-person; finding aids via NEHGS |
| **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)** | Finding aids for church collections | In-person; AmericanAncestors.org (subscription) |

---

## Census Records

- **1820, 1830, 1840:** Name only the head of household; all others are tick-marks by age and sex
- **1850:** First census to name every person in the household — a major breakthrough
- **1850 mortality schedule:** Lists everyone who died in the twelve months before the June 1850 enumeration (age, sex, birthplace, cause of death) — often supplies a death date where no town record was filed
- **Access:** FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription) for all four censuses

---

## Other Key Record Types

| Type | Where Held | Online? |
|---|---|---|
| **Probate** (wills, administrations, guardianships from 1761) | Berkshire County Probate Court (Pittsfield) | FamilySearch coll. 1678901 (indexed) |
| **Land/Deeds** | Berkshire County Registry of Deeds (Pittsfield) | Largely not online; some FamilySearch microfilm |
| **Military** (War of 1812 service, pension, bounty land) | NARA; Massachusetts State Archives | Fold3 (subscription); FamilySearch |
| **Newspapers** (Pittsfield Sun from 1800; Berkshire County Eagle) — marriage/death notices, legal ads | Berkshire Athenaeum (Pittsfield); Newspapers.com | Partial via Newspapers.com (subscription) |
| **Naturalization** | County courts; FamilySearch coll. 1459213 | FamilySearch (indexed, free) |
| **Tax/Valuation lists** | Individual town clerks; Massachusetts State Archives | Largely not online |

---

## Searching Across the State Lines

Since the family's town is near both New York and Vermont, plan to check neighboring counties too:

- **New York side:** Columbia County and Rensselaer County (NY). New York statewide vital registration began in **1847** — for 1820–1847 NY events, look to church records and town records, not a state index
- **Vermont side:** Bennington County (VT). Vermont statewide vital registration began in **1857** — for 1820–1857 VT events, same approach: church records and town records

# Locality Guide: Berkshire County, Massachusetts (1820–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** 1761, from Hampshire County
- **County seat:** Pittsfield
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Massachusetts, United States
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the population tool for this query; the 1820–1850 federal censuses are themselves the primary population evidence.
- **Economy:** Agriculture, ironworks, paper mills, and early textile manufacturing; the Housatonic River valley drew industrial development.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Yankee (English-descent) Protestant families in this period, with some Irish immigration appearing by the 1840s.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (dominant), Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, and Quaker congregations are documented in the region; some Catholic presence by the late 1840s.
- **Key historical events:** Post-War of 1812 economic growth; the opening of the Western Railroad through the county in 1841 brought new migration and commerce; the 1837 financial panic affected local business records.

## Boundary changes

- Berkshire County was formed in 1761 and its boundaries were stable through the 1820–1850 period. No subdivision occurred during this window.
- Records before 1761 would fall under Hampshire County.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Town-level recording:** The Massachusetts colonial government ordered towns to record births, marriages, and deaths from **1639**, though compliance varied. Original records remain with each individual town clerk. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records), during 1820–1841 the town clerk was the sole keeper — there was no state copy.
- **State-level registration:** Massachusetts was the first state to establish a statewide recording system, beginning in **1841**. From that year, copies went to both the town and the state. This means for events 1820–1840, only the town's own record survives; for 1841–1850, both town and state copies exist.
- **Marriage intentions:** Commonly recorded in the bride's home town; additional recordings may appear in the groom's town and the couple's current residence — check all three if known (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records).
- **Key published resource:** The "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" printed series covers over 200 Massachusetts towns, including Berkshire County towns, and is often the fastest entry point for events in this period. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial), this series is widely available in libraries and on FamilySearch.
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (collection 2061550, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) — searchable by name online; free at FamilySearch.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Image group 004500891 covers Berkshire County Town Clerk Vital and Town Records, 1761–1850 (512 images). This volume is **browse-only** — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. You must page through images without a name search.
- **Gaps:** Non-compliance before 1841 means some events were never recorded at the town level. Known gaps and destroyed records vary by individual town.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Congregational registers are the most common surviving pre-1841 vital substitute. Methodist, Baptist, and Episcopal records also exist for this period.
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (collection 1921657, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) — searchable by name online.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Image group 004500892 covers Congregational Church Records for Pittsfield, Berkshire County, 1791–1850 (274 images). This volume is **browse-only** — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable.
- **Where held:** Original registers typically remain with the individual congregation or have been deposited at the Congregational Library (Boston) or denominational archives. The New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS) holds finding aids.
- **Language:** English throughout this period.
- **Note:** Church records are especially important for 1820–1841 events, because civil registration existed only at the town level and compliance was uneven.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** 1820, 1830, 1840, and 1850 all fall within or on the boundary of this period. 1820–1840 enumerate heads of household with tick-mark counts by age and sex; **1850 is the first census to name every person in the household**.
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1850 mortality schedule records individuals who died in the year preceding the census (June 1849–June 1850) — useful for death dates where no town record was filed.
- **State census:** Massachusetts did not conduct a formal statewide census in this period, but local town assessors' lists sometimes substituted.
- **Access:** Federal census records for Massachusetts are searchable at FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription). The 1820–1840 censuses are indexed; 1850 is fully indexed with names.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills (testate estates), administrations (intestate estates), inventories, guardianships, and dower releases. A person who died leaving a will is testate — search the will books; a person who died without one is intestate — search the administration files.
- **Holding jurisdiction:** Berkshire County Probate Court (Pittsfield) holds original probate files from county formation in 1761 onward through the target period.
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (collection 1678901, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) — searchable online; covers Berkshire County.
- **Date range:** Continuous from 1761 for Berkshire County.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (New England practice; no rectangular-survey grid).
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, and land releases were recorded at the county level. The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial) notes that Massachusetts land records survive in "remarkably complete runs" from the 1630s at county registries.
- **Where held:** Berkshire County Registry of Deeds (Pittsfield) holds the deed books for the 1820–1850 period. No online full-text index for these specific deed books was returned by the survey tools; assume physical or microfilm access.
- **Tax records:** Town-level assessors' valuation lists ("valuation lists") survive for many Berkshire County towns and can substitute for census gaps.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts in or just before the period:** War of 1812 (ending 1815). No major conflicts for Massachusetts during 1820–1850 itself.
- **Record types:** War of 1812 service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants are at the National Archives (NARA). FamilySearch collection index via https://www.familysearch.org/ and Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/, subscription).
- **State records:** Massachusetts adjutant general records for militia service are at the Massachusetts State Archives (Boston).

### Cemetery records

- **Where held:** Berkshire County has numerous town and church cemeteries. Sexton records and burial registers vary by town.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is the primary online index; BillionGraves is a secondary option. Coverage of rural Berkshire County cemeteries is incomplete — a physical survey or local historical society inquiry may be needed.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Pittsfield Sun (published from 1800) and the Berkshire County Eagle are the principal papers covering this period. They printed marriage notices, death notices, and legal advertisements.
- **Where held:** The Berkshire Athenaeum (Pittsfield Public Library) holds microfilm of local newspapers. Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/, subscription) and the Chronicling America project (Library of Congress, free) may have partial digital coverage.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevance:** Berkshire County, while inland, would generate naturalization records for immigrants who settled here. Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any Massachusetts court of record, including Berkshire County courts.
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906" (collection 1459213, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213) — covers this period.
- **Passenger lists:** The "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" collection (id 1784312) covers Boston-port arrivals. For a family arriving via New York's ports, search NARA passenger lists indexed at Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **Content note:** Passenger manifests list every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When searching for a family, examine the full manifest — not just the head of household.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Town assessors' valuation lists (personal and real property). These exist between census years and can confirm a person's residence and economic status.
- **Where held:** Original lists are with individual town clerks or at the Massachusetts State Archives; some have been microfilmed by FamilySearch.
- **Substitute value:** Valuation lists for years such as 1821, 1831, 1841 can confirm residence between the decennial censuses and may list family members.

## Records NOT online

- **Original town clerk vital records (1820–1840):** For events before the 1841 state system, the original record is with each town clerk and is not uniformly digitized or indexed online. The published "Vital Records to 1850" series is the closest proxy.
- **Town assessors' valuation lists:** Generally not online; held by individual town clerks or the Massachusetts State Archives.
- **Most deed books for Berkshire County:** The county registry holds these; no Berkshire-specific deed index was returned by the survey tools as an online-searchable collection.
- **Non-Congregational church records:** Only the Pittsfield Congregational volume was returned by `volume_search`. Other denominations' registers may be held by individual congregations or denominational archives with no online index.
- **Local court records:** Quarterly court minute books and other Berkshire County court files are held physically at the courthouse and the Massachusetts State Archives.

## Known record losses

No tool result in this survey named a specific record loss for Berkshire County vital, church, or court records in the 1820–1850 period. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Massachusetts church records, land, probate, and census returned only generic content (not Massachusetts-specific pages), so I cannot confirm or rule out losses from those sources. Absence of an online index is a coverage gap — not evidence that records were destroyed. Contact the Berkshire County Probate Court and individual town clerks to confirm the survival of specific series before concluding a record is lost.

## Research tips

1. **Work town by town, not county-wide, for 1820–1840 vitals.** Because statewide registration did not begin until 1841, there is no county or state index for births, marriages, and deaths before that year. You must identify which Berkshire County town(s) the family lived in and then check that town clerk's records directly. The published "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial) is the most efficient starting point.
2. **Marriage intentions are a separate record.** Under Massachusetts practice, couples filed a notice of intention to marry at the bride's town — and sometimes the groom's town as well. If you cannot find a marriage record in one town, check the other spouse's town clerk (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records).
3. **The two browse-only FamilySearch volumes require image-by-image review.** Volumes 004500891 (town clerk vitals, 1761–1850, 512 images) and 004500892 (Pittsfield Congregational church, 1791–1850, 274 images) have no name index and are not full-text searchable. Plan time to browse them manually at FamilySearch.org.
4. **Search across the New York and Vermont lines.** A family whose town was close to both state lines likely generated records on both sides. The wiki_place_page "home" section for Berkshire County returned only generic content, so the Neighboring Counties table did not come back in this survey — the specific adjoining counties were not confirmed from tool results. From geographic context, the New York border is served by Columbia County and Rensselaer County (NY), and the Vermont border by Bennington County (VT); verify these neighbors before routing searches to them. New York vital registration at the state level began in 1847; Vermont's began in 1857 — for 1820–1847 NY and 1820–1857 VT events, look to church records and town records in those states, not a state civil index.
5. **Use the 1850 census mortality schedule for death dates.** The mortality schedule lists everyone who died in the twelve months before the June 1850 enumeration, giving age, sex, occupation, birthplace, and cause of death — it often supplies a death date where no town record was filed.
6. **The FamilySearch Wiki place-specific pages (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned only generic content during this survey.** The Massachusetts-specific research pages may exist but were not retrieved by the tools. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Berkshire_County,_Massachusetts_Genealogy directly before treating any absence noted here as definitive.

# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

> **Tool note:** During this session, FamilySearch's place-resolution tools returned empty results for all Irish places, and most Ireland-specific Wiki pages resolved to a generic fallback. The one confirmed Wiki result is the [Ireland Naming Customs page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Naming_Customs). All record-type and repository information below is well-established knowledge, but specific FamilySearch collection IDs could not be confirmed — verify directly on FamilySearch.org or re-run once tools are restored.

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Place:** Billy civil parish, barony of Dunluce Lower, County Antrim, Province of Ulster, Ireland
- **Nearest town:** Bushmills
- **Period:** 1780–1870 — spans the pre-Famine era, the Famine years, and the first post-Famine generation
- **Governing context:** Under the Irish Parliament until 1801; under the UK Parliament (Westminster) from the Act of Union 1801 onward
- **Religious mix:** Predominantly Presbyterian (Ulster Scots), with Church of Ireland (Anglican) and Roman Catholic communities — this denominational split is the single most important variable in predicting which church record series covers any given family
- **Economy:** Agriculture, linen weaving, fishing along the north Antrim coast
- **Key events affecting records:** 1798 United Irish Rebellion (disruption to record-keeping across Ulster); Act of Union 1801; Great Famine 1845–1852 (massive emigration, especially to North America)

---

## Boundary and Registration Changes

| Date | Change |
|---|---|
| 1801 | Act of Union — Irish Parliament abolished; Westminster takes over, but local record-keeping framework unchanged |
| 1 April 1845 | Civil registration of **non-Catholic marriages** begins nationally |
| 1 January 1864 | Civil registration of **all** births, marriages, and deaths begins nationally |

**Implication:** For events in Billy parish before 1864 (and for Catholics, before 1864 for all events), church registers are the primary source — not the state.

---

## The Two Catastrophic Record Losses

These losses dominate all research in this region and period:

1. **1922 Four Courts fire, Dublin:** Destroyed the Public Record Office of Ireland — including most Church of Ireland registers deposited there, original pre-1858 wills, and surviving 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851 census returns for County Antrim.
2. **Deliberate destruction of 1861 and 1871 census returns:** Ordered to free storage space. These full-population censuses no longer exist.

**Result:** No census returns survive for County Antrim within the target period. Griffith's Valuation and the Tithe Applotment Books are the primary substitutes.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records / Civil Registration

- **Coverage within 1780–1870:** Only the years **1864–1870** are covered (births, marriages, deaths for all denominations). Non-Catholic marriages: **1845–1870**.
- **Held by:** General Register Office for Northern Ireland (GRONI), Belfast
- **Online:** Images and indexes at [IrishGenealogy.ie](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie) (free); Ancestry and FindMyPast (subscription)
- **Gap:** All births and deaths 1780–1863, and all Catholic marriages 1780–1863, require church records instead

### Church Records

- **Denominations:** Presbyterian (dominant), Church of Ireland, Roman Catholic
- **Record types:** Baptism, marriage, and burial registers; Presbyterian session minutes and communicant rolls; confirmation registers
- **Where held:**
  - **PRONI (Belfast):** Holds surviving Church of Ireland and Presbyterian registers for County Antrim
  - **Presbyterian Historical Society, Belfast:** Additional Presbyterian records
  - **National Library of Ireland (NLI), Dublin:** Roman Catholic registers on microfilm
  - **FamilySearch:** Has microfilmed many County Antrim registers (specific collection IDs unavailable this session — search FamilySearch.org directly)
- **Online:** Ancestry and IrishGenealogy.ie hold indexes and images of many surviving Irish church registers
- **Critical note on CoI losses:** Church of Ireland registers that had been deposited in Dublin were destroyed in 1922. Surviving originals are at PRONI; transcripts at the Representative Church Body Library (Dublin)

### Census Substitutes (No Census Returns Survive)

| Record | Dates | Content | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tithe Applotment Books | 1823–1837 | Names every male householder liable to tithe, by townland | IrishGenealogy.ie, AskAboutIreland.ie, Ancestry, FamilySearch |
| Griffith's Primary Valuation | c.1858–1861 for Antrim | Names every household head and land occupier; names their immediate lessor | AskAboutIreland.ie (free), Ancestry, IrishGenealogy.ie |
| Valuation Revision Books | From c.1864 annually | Year-by-year updates to Griffith's, tracking changes of occupancy | PRONI (not comprehensively online) |
| Flax Growers List (1796) | 1796 | Names flax growers by townland for County Antrim | Partial online availability — verify on Ancestry/FamilySearch |
| Poor Law (Ballymoney Union) | From 1839 | Workhouse admissions, outdoor relief registers — names poorest families, especially Famine-era | PRONI |

### Land Records

- **Registry of Deeds (Dublin, from 1708):** Deeds, mortgages, and leases for County Antrim landowners; indexes partially online
- **Estate papers:** Many Billy parish lands were part of large County Antrim estates; rental rolls, lease books, and tenancy records may be at PRONI or the NLI
- **Townland is the key:** All Irish land records are organized by townland — identify the specific townland for each ancestor as early as possible

### Probate Records

- **Before 1858:** Handled by the Diocese of Connor (Church of Ireland Consistorial Court) — surviving records at PRONI
- **After 1858:** Civil probate via the Principal Registry (Dublin) and district registries — surviving calendars (indexes) at National Archives of Ireland and PRONI
- **Loss:** Original pre-1900 wills largely destroyed in 1922; surviving will calendars and Betham's will abstracts (National Archives of Ireland) partially substitute

### Military Records

- **British Army:** Service records, muster rolls, pensions at The National Archives (Kew, UK); some on Ancestry and FindMyPast
- **Royal Irish Constabulary (RIC, from 1836):** Service records at National Archives of Ireland (HO 184 series)
- **County militia/yeomanry:** PRONI holds some County Antrim records

### Cemetery / Burial Records

- **FindAGrave.com:** User-contributed headstone photographs
- **Ulster Historical Foundation and Irish Graveyards:** Indexed some County Antrim burial grounds
- **Physical registers:** Held at individual churches or PRONI; many older burial grounds have no surviving register — the headstone may be the only evidence

### Newspaper Records

| Paper | Period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Belfast Newsletter | From 1737 | British Newspaper Archive (subscription); Linen Hall Library (Belfast) |
| Coleraine Chronicle | From 1844 | British Newspaper Archive (subscription) |

Content value: death notices, marriage announcements, legal advertisements, estate sale notices.

### Emigration Records

- **Context:** North Antrim had very high emigration throughout 1780–1870, spiking during the Famine (1845–1852). Common destinations: eastern Canada (New Brunswick, Ontario), US eastern seaboard
- **Departure ports:** Belfast, Londonderry/Derry, Larne
- **Records:** US passenger lists (NARA; indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch); Canadian arrivals at Quebec (Library and Archives Canada); US naturalization records (NARA and state archives)
- **Research chain:** Griffith's Valuation + Tithe Applotment Books (to fix townland) → passenger lists → destination-country census and naturalization records

### Other Records

- **Ordnance Survey Memoirs (1830s):** Detailed parish-level surveys of County Antrim including population, occupations, and topography — essential social context; published by the Royal Irish Academy and available in major libraries
- **National School registers (from 1831):** Name pupils, parents, and father's occupation; held at PRONI
- **Grand jury/county cess records:** Name local contractors and officeholders; held at PRONI; not online

---

## Repository Quick Reference

| Repository | What's there for Billy parish | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **PRONI, Belfast** | Church registers (CoI, Presbyterian, some RC); estate papers; valuation revision books; poor law union records; school registers; petty sessions; wills (post-1858) | In-person; partial online via nidirect.gov.uk/proni |
| **GRONI, Belfast** | Civil birth/marriage/death registers from 1864 | In-person; images at IrishGenealogy.ie |
| **Presbyterian Historical Society, Belfast** | Presbyterian session records | In-person; appointment recommended |
| **Representative Church Body Library, Dublin** | Surviving CoI register copies/transcripts | In-person |
| **National Archives of Ireland, Dublin** | Probate calendars, RIC records, some estate papers | In-person; partial online |
| **The National Archives (Kew, UK)** | British Army service/pension records | In-person; some on Ancestry/FindMyPast |
| **IrishGenealogy.ie** | Civil registration indexes + images; church record indexes | Free online |
| **AskAboutIreland.ie** | Griffith's Primary Valuation (indexed + images) | Free online |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Microfilmed church registers, civil registration, Griffith's, Tithe | Free online |
| **Ancestry.com** | Church records, Griffith's, Tithe, civil registration, Belfast Newsletter | Subscription |

---

## Naming Conventions

*(Based on the FamilySearch Wiki page confirmed during this session: [Ireland Naming Customs](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Naming_Customs))*

**Traditional naming pattern (a clue, not a rule):**
- 1st son → father's father
- 2nd son → mother's father
- 3rd son → father
- 1st daughter → mother's mother
- 2nd daughter → father's mother
- 3rd daughter → mother

Use this to hypothesize grandparents' names when direct records are missing — but a broken pattern is not evidence of non-identity.

**Surname prefix variation:** The same family may appear as O'Flynn, Flynn, and Flinn across different records. Search all prefix and spelling variants simultaneously. Note that Ulster Scots surnames (common in north Antrim) are Scottish in origin — they carry their own spelling variants but typically do not use O' or Mac.

**General spelling instability:** A single family's surname may be recorded multiple different ways within the same parish. Never restrict a search to one spelling.

---

## Recommended Research Sequence for Billy Parish (1780–1870)

1. **Fix the family in a townland** using Griffith's Primary Valuation (c.1858–1861 for Antrim) at AskAboutIreland.ie
2. **Work backward** with the Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837) for the same townland
3. **Search surviving church registers** for the denomination(s) present in that townland — check PRONI's eCATALOGUE for what survives
4. **Search PRONI estate papers** for the relevant landlord's estate (tenancy lists, rental rolls)
5. **Move forward** using civil registration (from 1864) and valuation revision books
6. **Cross-reference emigrant records** in destination countries for any family members known to have left — the townland identification from steps 1–2 is the anchor for that search
7. **Check adjoining parishes** — Billy borders other civil parishes in County Antrim and approaches County Londonderry. Families near boundaries routinely used churches in neighbouring parishes

**PRONI's eCATALOGUE** (nidirect.gov.uk/proni) is the most reliable way to see exactly which registers and collections survive for Billy parish before making a visit.

---

*Re-running this locality guide once FamilySearch's place-resolution tools are restored will add confirmed collection IDs, volume counts, and direct Wiki citations for record dates and repositories.*

Naturalization records in the US are at NARA and in state archives. Specific FamilySearch collection IDs for Irish emigrant passenger lists could not be retrieved in this session.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. When researching a family's emigration, examine the full manifest for all family members — young children and infants are listed alongside adults. Pre-1820 US passenger lists are sparse; Canadian records of early arrivals are also incomplete.
- **Note for cross-referencing:** Griffith's Valuation and the Tithe Applotment Books, used together with the destination country's naturalization and census records, form the standard chain of evidence for linking an Irish emigrant back to a specific townland.

### Tax records

- **Tithe Applotment Books (1823-1837):** See Land Records above. The most important tax-like name source for the period before Griffith's Valuation.
- **Hearth Money Rolls:** Earlier hearth tax records (17th century) predate the target period but establish family names in townlands before 1780.
- **County cess and grand jury records:** County Antrim grand jury presentments (road and bridge maintenance assessments, county expenditures) survive at PRONI and name local contractors, tenants, and officeholders.
- **Substitute value:** Tithe Applotment Books name every male householder liable to tithes and function as a de facto census substitute for c.1823-1837.

### Other record types

- **Griffith's Valuation (1847-1864):** Already noted under Land and Census; names every household head in each townland, including the name of the person from whom each tenant holds.
- **Ordnance Survey Memoirs (1830s):** Detailed parish-level surveys of County Antrim, including notes on the population, occupations, and social conditions of each townland. Not genealogical in the strict sense but provide the social and topographical context essential for research. Available in published form (Royal Irish Academy) and online.
- **Poor law union records:** Billy parish falls within the Ballymoney Poor Law Union (formed 1839). Board of Guardians minutes, indoor relief registers (workhouse admissions), and outdoor relief records survive at PRONI and name the poorest families in the parish, particularly for the Famine period.
- **School records (National Schools from 1831):** National School registers from 1831 onward name pupils, their parents, and sometimes father's occupation. These are at PRONI for County Antrim schools.
- **Valuation revision books:** Annual manuscript revisions to Griffith's Valuation after c.1864 track changes of occupancy and ownership, year by year. Held at the Valuation Office, Dublin, and at PRONI. Useful for tracking families from the 1860s onward.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Relevance to Billy parish / County Antrim | Access |
|---|---|---|
| IrishGenealogy.ie | Civil registration indexes and images (births from 1864, marriages, deaths); church records indexes | Free |
| AskAboutIreland.ie | Griffith's Primary Valuation (indexed, with images) | Free |
| PRONI (online) | Some estate papers, some church registers, tithe maps | Free (some) |
| Ancestry.com | Irish church records, Griffith's Valuation, Tithe Applotment Books, some civil registration, Belfast Newsletter | Subscription |
| FindMyPast | Irish census fragments, some church records, some military records | Subscription |
| FamilySearch.org | Microfilmed church registers, civil registration, some Griffith's | Free |
| British Newspaper Archive | Coleraine Chronicle, Belfast Newsletter, other Ulster papers | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** `collections_search` and `volume_search` both returned zero results because the `standardPlace` could not be resolved by the tool infrastructure during this session. No FamilySearch collection IDs or volume counts can be cited. The repository table above is based on widely documented knowledge about Irish record repositories; specific collection IDs must be looked up directly on FamilySearch.org or via the wiki pages listed below once tools are available.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI), Belfast | Church registers (CoI, Presbyterian, some RC), estate papers, valuation revision books, poor law union records, school registers, petty sessions records, wills (post-1858 district registry), militia records | In-person; partial online access at nidirect.gov.uk/proni |
| General Register Office for Northern Ireland (GRONI), Belfast | Civil birth, marriage, death registers from 1864 for County Antrim | In-person; many images at IrishGenealogy.ie |
| Presbyterian Historical Society, Belfast | Presbyterian session records, historical registers | In-person; appointment recommended |
| Representative Church Body Library, Dublin | Surviving Church of Ireland registers (some County Antrim copies/transcripts) | In-person |
| National Archives of Ireland, Dublin | Probate calendars, RIC records, some estate papers | In-person; partial online access |
| The National Archives (Kew, UK) | British Army service and pension records, RIC headquarters files | In-person; some records on Ancestry/FindMyPast |
| Linen Hall Library, Belfast | Local newspapers, historical books | In-person |

## Records NOT online

The following record types are known to exist for Billy parish / County Antrim but are not fully available online:

- **Valuation revision books** (post-Griffith's annual updates, from c.1864): held at PRONI; not comprehensively digitized or indexed.
- **Poor law union (Ballymoney) workhouse records**: held at PRONI; not fully online.
- **Grand jury presentments and county cess records**: held at PRONI; not online.
- **Estate papers for private County Antrim landowners**: scattered at PRONI, NLI, and in private hands; not systematically digitized.
- **National School registers**: held at PRONI; not comprehensively online.
- **Pre-1864 RC parish registers** (originals): held at individual RC parishes or on NLI microfilm; some are indexed online but images are not uniformly available.
- **Registry of Deeds (Dublin)**: indexes are partially online but the full register images require an in-person visit or IAPI order.

## Known record losses

Two catastrophic losses shape all research into Billy parish for this period:

1. **1922 Four Courts fire, Dublin:** Destroyed the Public Record Office of Ireland, including most Church of Ireland parish registers that had been deposited there, the original pre-1858 probate wills, and the surviving returns from the 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851 Irish censuses. This is the single largest records loss in Irish genealogy.
2. **Deliberate destruction of 1861 and 1871 census returns:** Ordered by the Irish government to free storage space; these two full-population censuses for County Antrim no longer exist.

These losses are widely documented. They could not be confirmed from a FamilySearch Wiki tool result in this session, but researchers should assume them and plan accordingly.

**Partial substitutes for lost records:**
- For census: Griffith's Valuation (c.1847-1864), Tithe Applotment Books (1823-1837), poor law union records, school registers.
- For Church of Ireland registers: transcript volumes in PRONI, the Representative Church Body Library; the Vestry records of individual parishes (separate from register books, sometimes survived).
- For pre-1858 probate: the Will Calendars (indexes) and extracts survive; the Prerogative Court transcripts compiled by Sir William Betham (National Archives of Ireland) partially reconstruct 17th- and 18th-century wills.

## Research tips

- **Naming conventions (confirmed from FamilySearch Wiki, `https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Naming_Customs`):** A traditional pattern was commonly used — first son named for the father's father; second son for the mother's father; third son for the father; first daughter for the mother's mother; second daughter for the father's mother; third daughter for the mother. Use this as a clue to identify grandparents' names when the grandparents themselves cannot be found in records. The pattern is a clue, not a rule: it was not universally followed, and a broken pattern is not evidence of non-identity.
- **O' and Mac prefix variation (confirmed from `https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Naming_Customs`):** The same family may appear as O'Flynn, Flynn, and Flinn across different records. Search all prefix variants and spelling variants simultaneously. For north Antrim, Ulster Scots surnames (Scottish in origin) do not carry O' or Mac but may have their own spelling variants.
- **Spelling variation (confirmed from `https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Naming_Customs`):** A single family's surname may be recorded several different ways within the same parish. Do not restrict searches to a single spelling.
- **Work at the townland level:** Irish records are organized by townland within civil parish. Identify the specific townland for each ancestor as early as possible — this is the key to linking Griffith's Valuation, Tithe Applotment Books, and church register search areas.
- **Efficient research sequence for Billy parish (1780-1870):** (1) Start with Griffith's Valuation to fix the family in a specific townland. (2) Work backward with the Tithe Applotment Books. (3) Search the surviving church registers for the denominations present in that townland. (4) Search the Registry of Deeds and PRONI estate papers for the relevant landlord's estate. (5) Extend forward using civil registration (from 1864) and valuation revision books. (6) Cross-reference with emigrant records in destination countries for families known to have left.
- **Check PRONI's eCATALOGUE:** PRONI's online catalogue (www.nidirect.gov.uk/proni) allows searching by parish, townland, and family name for what is held in Belfast. This is the most reliable way to identify surviving records for a specific Billy parish townland before visiting in person.
- **Adjoining civil parishes and counties:** Billy parish borders other civil parishes in County Antrim and approaches County Londonderry (Derry) to the west. Families near parish boundaries routinely used churches in neighbouring parishes. The FamilySearch Wiki page for County Antrim (`https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/County_Antrim_Genealogy`) lists neighbouring parishes; that page could not be retrieved during this session. Always search the immediately adjoining parish registers alongside Billy's own.

---

The FamilySearch Wiki place tools and most Ireland-specific wiki pages were unavailable during this survey (returning a generic fallback page or empty place-resolution). The guide above rests on the Ireland Naming Customs page (the one confirmed tool result) and notes explicitly where data could not be retrieved. Re-run this locality guide once the tool infrastructure is restored to get confirmed FamilySearch collection IDs, volume counts, and specific wiki-page citations for record dates and repositories.

---

Records for Billy civil parish, County Antrim, in the years 1780-1870 are shaped above all by two facts: civil registration of births and deaths did not begin in Ireland until 1864, so nearly the entire target period relies on church registers, and the 1922 fire in Dublin destroyed most of the major record sets that had been centrally held — including most census returns and many Church of Ireland registers. The records that do survive and matter most for this parish are church baptism, marriage, and burial registers (held at PRONI in Belfast and on FamilySearch microfilm), the Tithe Applotment Books from the 1820s-30s, Griffith's Primary Valuation from around 1858-1861, and poor law union and estate papers for the Famine period. Researchers should work through PRONI's online catalogue to identify exactly which registers and estate collections survive for the specific townlands of interest.

The next step is to consult the FamilySearch Wiki pages for County Antrim and Ireland directly at familysearch.org, since those pages could not be retrieved by the tools during this session, and then build a research plan using the Griffith's Valuation townland as the anchor point.

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840–1880)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 (place_search dateRange: +1811/); specific parent jurisdictions not returned by place_search_all (empty result)
- **County seat / administrative center:** Not stated in tool results
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** No data returned by the place_population tool for this standardPlace
- **Religious denominations:** Church records volume (007936751) contains both English- and German-language records (1842–1895), indicating German-speaking congregations were present
- **Economy / Ethnic composition / Key events:** Not established from tool results returned in this survey

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Archive split:** County Antrim is one of the six Ulster counties that remained in the United Kingdom after 1922. All records for this area are held primarily at **PRONI (Belfast)**, not the National Archives of Ireland in Dublin.

---

## Available Record Types

### 1. Civil Registration

- **Started:** 1 January 1864, nationwide.

- **1864–1870:** Births, marriages, and deaths registered at the General Register Office Northern Ireland (GRONI), Belfast.
- **Held at:** GRONI, Belfast.

---

### 2. Church Records *(primary source for 1780–1863)*

#### Church of Ireland (Anglican/Episcopalian)

- Records in Ireland began in 1536; **two-thirds were destroyed in the 1922 Dublin Public Record Office fire.** However, County Antrim registers that were held locally or deposited in Belfast (PRONI) were *not* affected by that fire.
- **Does the Billy CoI register survive?** This is the critical open question. It cannot be confirmed from this survey's tool results. The two resources to check are:
  - **PRONI's Guide to Church Records** (free PDF, publicly available via PRONI's website) — the definitive checklist for which Northern Ireland church registers survive, by parish, and where each is held.

- PRONI also publishes a list of digitized church records searchable online: [nidirect.gov.uk/articles/digitised-church-records-available-proni](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/digitised-church-records-available-proni)
- **Marriage License Bonds (confirmed online):** *Ireland, Diocesan and Prerogative Marriage License Bonds Indexes, 1623–1866* — FamilySearch collection 3460239; indexed with images; **free**. A useful proxy marriage index for the pre-1864 period, covering Church of Ireland and some Presbyterian families.
- **Held at:** PRONI (primary for Antrim); RCB Library, Dublin (for any registers not at PRONI).

#### Roman Catholic

- Rural parishes in north Antrim typically did not begin keeping registers until **Catholic Emancipation in 1828**. Pre-1828 Catholic baptisms and marriages for Billy parish may simply not exist.
- **Online (confirmed):**

- **Diocese:** Down & Connor covers this part of Antrim.
- **Held at:** NLI (digitized); local parish or diocesan archive for originals.

#### Presbyterian

- Large Presbyterian presence in County Antrim from the 1605 Ulster Plantation. Some registers date from the 17th century, but the average start date for Presbyterian registers in Ireland is around **1830**.
- **Online (confirmed):**
  - Non-Conformist records (births/baptisms, burials, marriages, congregational) at **FindMyPast** (subscription)

- **Tip:** Some Antrim Presbyterian congregations may have registers predating 1830 given the early plantation settlement — check PRONI and UHF specifically for Bushmills-area congregations.

#### Methodist

- Methodist society began in Dublin 1746; records for County Antrim would be at PRONI or the Methodist Historical Society of Ireland. Specific Billy-area holdings not confirmed by this survey.

### 3. Census Records

The FamilySearch Wiki Ireland Census page returned only generic content; no Ireland-specific census details were confirmed by tool results.

### 5. Probate Records

**Confirmed from tool results:**

The Consistorial Court of Connor (the relevant diocese for most of County Antrim) handled probate before 1858; the Prerogative Court of Armagh handled higher-value estates across all Ireland. # Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

> **Tool availability note:** The FamilySearch Wiki's `wiki_read` tool returned only a generic placeholder for every Ireland-specific URL attempted, `place_search` returned empty results for all Irish places, and as a result `collections_search`, `volume_search`, and `external_links_search` could not be run. The Billy Civil Parish page was confirmed via `wiki_search`. Re-run this guide when the FamilySearch wiki-query-api is reachable to surface indexed collections and digitized volume counts.

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Civil parish:** Billy, County Antrim, Province of Ulster
- **Baronies:** Chiefly Lower Dunluce; partly Carey
- **Poor law union:** Coleraine (from 1838)
- **Post town:** Bushmills (includes a portion of Dunserverick)
- **County administrative centre:** Antrim town (county); Coleraine (poor law union)
- **Population:** Use the 1841/1851 census fragments, Griffiths Valuation (c. 1859–1862), and Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837) to estimate household numbers; no population figure was returned in this session.
- **Economy:** Agricultural; Bushmills licensed distillery from 1784; linen weaving typical of mid-Ulster.
- **Religious composition:** Church of Ireland, Presbyterian, Covenanting/Reformed Presbyterian, Roman Catholic, Wesleyan Methodist — all with documented meeting places in the parish.
- **Key events:** 1798 Rising; Great Famine 1845–1852 (emigration); civil registration begins 1 Jan 1864 (non-Catholic marriages from 1 Apr 1845).

---

## Boundary Changes

- Billy was formerly the **head of an ecclesiastical union** comprising also Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride — early Church of Ireland records for those parishes may appear in Billy's registers. Search all five parishes when one produces no result.
- **RC ecclesiastical jurisdiction:** The civil parish of Billy falls in the RC **district of Coleraine**, Diocese of Down and Connor. Search RC registers under *Coleraine* parish, not a register specifically titled "Billy."
- The Poor Law Union of Coleraine was created by the Poor Law Amendment Act (Ireland) 1838; union-based records before 1838 fall under county administration.
- No boundary split of the civil parish itself is recorded during 1780–1870.

---

## Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
| Period | Coverage | Where held | Online access |
|---|---|---|---|

# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

**Note on tool conditions this session.** The FamilySearch Wiki's `wiki_read` tool returned only a generic placeholder page for every Ireland-specific URL attempted (including `Ireland_Genealogy`, `Ireland_Vital_Records`, and the Billy Civil Parish page itself). The `place_search` tool returned empty results for every Irish place name tried, including "Ireland", "County Antrim", and "Billy". As a result, `collections_search`, `volume_search`, `external_links_search`, and `wiki_place_page` could not be run (they require a valid `standardPlace`). The `wiki_search` tool returned specific content for Billy Civil Parish on the first attempt, and that content is the primary grounded source for this guide. All other sections of the guide flag gaps as such. **Re-run this locality guide before relying on any absence reported here; the FamilySearch wiki-query-api may be the cause of the missing coverage.**

FamilySearch Wiki unreachable during this survey (all four wiki_place_page sections for Ireland and all wiki_read URLs for Ireland); these pages may exist — re-run locality-guide before relying on their absence.

---

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Civil parish:** Billy, County Antrim, province of Ulster, Ireland
- **Baronies:** Chiefly in the barony of Lower Dunluce; partly in the barony of Carey (source: FamilySearch Wiki via wiki_search, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy)
- **Poor law union:** Coleraine (same source)
- **Post town:** Bushmills. The parish also includes a portion of Dunserverick (same source).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** County Antrim was an Irish county under the Parliament of Ireland, then from 1801 under the Parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. In 1921 it became part of Northern Ireland. For the period 1780–1870, it was administered as part of Ireland under Westminster.
- **County town / administrative centre:** Antrim town (county level); the poor law union was administered from Coleraine.
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by any tool in this session. Consult the 1841 and 1851 census returns (where surviving) and Griffiths Valuation (c. 1859–1860) for an approximation of household numbers.
- **Economy:** Predominantly agricultural; Bushmills, the post town, was the site of a licensed whiskey distillery from 1784. Linen weaving was common throughout mid-Ulster, including coastal Antrim, during this period.
- **Ethnic and religious composition:** The area had a mixed population of Church of Ireland (Anglican), Presbyterian (including Covenanting/Reformed Presbyterian), Roman Catholic, and Methodist households, broadly reflecting the Ulster pattern. Meeting houses for Presbyterians, Covenanters, and Wesleyan Methodists are recorded in the parish (source: FamilySearch Wiki, same URL as above).
- **Key historical events:** The 1798 United Irish rising affected Ulster; the Great Famine (1845–1852) caused emigration throughout Antrim; civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths began for all Ireland on 1 January 1864 (non-Catholic marriages recorded from 1 April 1845). These events shaped both record survival and population movement during the target period.

## Boundary changes

- **Ecclesiastical predecessor:** Billy was formerly the head of an ecclesiastical union comprising also the parishes of Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride (source: FamilySearch Wiki, same URL). This means earlier Church of Ireland records for those surrounding parishes may have been registered under Billy.
- **Roman Catholic ecclesiastical jurisdiction:** In the RC divisions, the civil parish of Billy forms part of the district of Coleraine, diocese of Down and Connor (the FamilySearch wiki entry states "district of Coleraine"; the specific diocese is not confirmed by tool output for Billy itself, though Connor covers much of County Antrim).
- **Civil administration:** No boundary split of the civil parish during 1780–1870 is recorded in the tools. The civil parish boundaries were stable; the poor law union of Coleraine was created by the Poor Law Amendment Act (Ireland) 1838, so union-based records predate 1838 under county rather than union administration.
- **Post-1921:** County Antrim became part of Northern Ireland, so all modern repositories for this area are in Belfast (PRONI) and London, not Dublin, for records created after partition. For 1780–1870, the originating repositories are shared-Ireland archives.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki Vital Records page for Ireland could not be fetched in this session (wiki_read returned generic content). Based on the general Ireland context: non-Catholic marriages were registered from 1 April 1845; all births, marriages, and deaths were registered at civil superintendent registrar's districts from 1 January 1864. The FamilySearch wiki's Ireland Vital Records page should be consulted directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Vital_Records to confirm these dates and their levels.
- **Where held (civil records from 1864 onward):** The General Register Office (GRO) for Ireland, now split: births, marriages, and deaths for the Republic of Ireland held by the GRO Dublin (Werburgh Street, Dublin 2; https://www.gov.ie/en/organisation/general-register-office/); records for Northern Ireland from 1922 onward at the GRO Northern Ireland (Colby House, Stranmillis Road, Belfast BT9 5RR; https://geni.nidirect.gov.uk/).
- **Access online (civil records):** Births, marriages, and deaths from 1864 onward are indexed and partially imaged on IrishGenealogy.ie (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie) — a free government portal. For births 1864–1922, marriages 1845–1944, and deaths 1864–1966 the images are viewable.
- **Gaps before 1864:** No civil registration. Church records are the primary source. See Church records section below.

### Church records

The FamilySearch wiki page for Billy Civil Parish (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy) lists section headers for Catholic, Church of Ireland, Presbyterian, Methodist, Society of Friends, and Others, but returned **no specific register start dates or holding details** for Billy parish in this session's wiki_search results. The parish wiki page directs researchers to the general Ireland Church Records page: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records.

The denominations with known meeting places in the civil parish, from the FamilySearch wiki history section, are:

- **Presbyterians** (meeting house in the parish)
- **Covenanters** (Reformed Presbyterians; meeting house in the parish)
- **Wesleyan Methodists** (meeting house in the parish)
- **Church of Ireland** (Billy was formerly the head of an ecclesiastical union; Dunluce is the historic CoI parish name associated with this area)
- **Roman Catholics** (part of the RC district of Coleraine)

**Where to find church register details and holdings:**

The Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI) holds microfilm and, increasingly, digital images of the major church registers for County Antrim. PRONI's eCatalogue is searchable at https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/proni. Physical address: 2 Titanic Boulevard, Belfast BT3 9HQ. Microfilm references for County Antrim parishes follow the MIC 1P/ series for Presbyterian registers. A neighboring Antrim civil parish (Ballylinny) returned PRONI microfilm number MIC 1P/327 for its Presbyterian registers; similar references exist for Billy parish registers but were not returned in this session.

The Church of Ireland Register project at the Representative Church Body (RCB) Library, Braemor Park, Churchtown, Dublin 14 (https://www.ireland.anglican.org/about/rcb-library) holds surviving Church of Ireland parish registers for Billy/Dunluce that were not transferred to PRONI. The RCB holds records online via the Irish Church Records portal at https://www.irishchurchrecords.ie.

The Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland, Church House, Fisherwick Place, Belfast BT1 6DW (https://presbyterianhistoryireland.com) holds registers and transcripts not at PRONI.

The Roman Catholic parish registers for Coleraine (the RC district covering Billy) are held at the local parish and are indexed and partially digitized on the Irish Genealogy portal: https://www.irishgenealogy.ie (search under "Church Records" for Coleraine).

**Language:** Church records in this parish are in English. Latin appears occasionally in Roman Catholic registers.

### Census records

- **1901 and 1911 censuses (Ireland):** Both survive in full and are fully indexed and free online at the National Archives of Ireland: https://www.census.nationalarchives.ie. These postdate the target window but provide family reconstruction backward in time.
- **1841 and 1851 censuses:** Almost entirely destroyed — the 1861, 1871, 1881, and 1891 censuses were also destroyed. Fragments of 1841 and 1851 survive for some areas (old age pension claims in the early 20th century used them). No tool in this session confirmed survival for Billy specifically.
- **Substitutes for missing census years:** Griffiths Primary Valuation (conducted for County Antrim c. 1859–1862) lists every household and landholding in each townland; the original books are at the Valuation Office, Irish Life Centre, Abbey Street Lower, Dublin 1 (https://www.valoff.ie), and images are online at https://www.askaboutireland.ie and https://www.irishgenealogy.ie. The Tithe Applotment Books (c. 1823–1837) predate Griffiths and name tithe-paying landholders; digitized at https://www.titheapplotmentbooks.nationalarchives.ie.
- **No specific indexed record counts were returned by volume_search or collections_search** because place_search could not resolve County Antrim in this session.

### Probate and court records

- **Probate before 1858:** Ecclesiastical courts (the Prerogative Court and the Consistorial Court of Connor, which covered County Antrim) held probate jurisdiction. Their records were largely destroyed in the 1922 Four Courts fire. Abstracts and transcripts survive in the Betham Abstracts and other collections at the National Archives of Ireland, Bishop Street, Dublin 8 (https://www.nationalarchives.ie).
- **Probate from 1858 onward:** The Probate Act 1857 established district probate registries; wills and administrations from 1 January 1858 are at PRONI (for Northern Ireland) and at the National Archives of Ireland. Many are digitized and indexed at https://www.willcalendars.nationalarchives.ie.
- **Court records:** Quarter Sessions and Assizes records for County Antrim are held at PRONI.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds; Irish townland system.
- **Tithe Applotment Books (c. 1823–1837):** Name tithe-paying occupiers by townland. Digitized free at https://www.titheapplotmentbooks.nationalarchives.ie. Billy civil parish townlands should be searchable directly.
- **Griffiths Primary Valuation (c. 1859–1862 for County Antrim):** Full household listing by townland. Free online at https://www.askaboutireland.ie and https://www.irishgenealogy.ie.
- **Registry of Deeds:** Memorials of deeds, conveyances, and mortgages registered from 1708 onward at the Registry of Deeds, Henrietta Street, Dublin 1 (https://www.landregistry.ie/registry-of-deeds). An index is searchable online.
- **Estate papers:** Large landowners in the Lower Dunluce barony held significant estates. Their papers (tenancy lists, rental rolls) are held at PRONI and, for some estates, at the National Library of Ireland (Kildare Street, Dublin 2; https://www.nli.ie).

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** 1798 Rising, Napoleonic Wars (1803–1815), Crimean War (1853–1856).
- **British Army service records:** The National Archives (UK), Kew, Richmond, Surrey TW9 4DU (https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk) holds service records, muster rolls, and pension records for soldiers from Ireland who served in the British Army. Many are indexed on FindMyPast (https://www.findmypast.co.uk) and Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com).
- **Militia records:** County Antrim Militia records are at PRONI.
- **Pension records:** Army pension records are at the National Archives (UK); some are digitized on FindMyPast.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** No cemetery list for Billy civil parish was returned by any tool in this session. The parish wiki page on FamilySearch does not detail cemeteries in the content retrieved. The Church of Ireland parish of Dunluce has a historic graveyard at Dunluce, and there are churchyard burials at Bushmills.
- **Online coverage:** Burial records and gravestone inscriptions for County Antrim are indexed by the Ulster Historical Foundation (https://www.ancestryireland.com) and some are on FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com). The Irish Genealogical Research Society also holds transcripts.
- **Physical records:** Church vestry burial registers (where they survive) are held at the RCB Library (Church of Ireland) and PRONI (other denominations).

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The *Coleraine Chronicle* (est. 1844) and *Northern Constitution* covered the Bushmills and Coleraine district. The *Belfast Newsletter* (est. 1737) is the major Ulster-wide paper.
- **Where held:** The British Newspaper Archive (https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk) holds many Ulster titles; subscription required. The Newspaper Library at the British Library, 96 Euston Road, London NW1 2DB also holds physical runs. PRONI holds microfilm copies of many Ulster newspapers.
- **Content value:** Notices of births, marriages, and deaths appeared in local papers; legal notices (land sales, probate) are also useful.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Emigrants from Bushmills and the north Antrim coast departed mainly through Londonderry (Derry) or Belfast. Passenger lists for Liverpool-to-North America sailings also apply for those who crossed to England first.
- **Record types:** Passenger manifests, naturalization petitions, Declaration of Intention records filed in the US courts.
- **Where held:** US passenger arrival records at NARA (https://www.archives.gov); many are on Ancestry and FamilySearch. The Famine Irish emigration project at PRONI documents departures. The Ulster Historical Foundation has an emigration database (https://www.ancestryireland.com).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records

- **Hearth Money Rolls (1660s):** Pre-target window but useful for family reconstruction; published by the Irish Manuscripts Commission.
- **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** See Land records above. These are the most useful tax-type substitute for the early part of the target period.
- **Griffiths Valuation revision books (post-1862):** Annual revisions to Griffiths show when households changed occupancy. Held at the Valuation Office, Dublin; PRONI holds a set for Northern Ireland.

### Other record types

- **School records:** The National School system was introduced in Ireland in 1831. School registers for Antrim national schools are held at PRONI and the National Archives of Ireland. Some are indexed at https://www.irishgenealogy.ie.
- **Ordnance Survey Memoirs (1830s):** The OSI conducted parish-by-parish memoirs covering many social and historical details for Ulster, including County Antrim. The memoirs for Billy parish (if completed) are held at the Royal Irish Academy, 19 Dawson Street, Dublin 2 (https://www.ria.ie) and published by the Institute of Irish Studies, Queen's University Belfast.
- **Poor Law records:** The Coleraine Poor Law Union records are held at PRONI; workhouse admission registers name individuals.

- **1841–1851 census original returns for Billy:** Mostly destroyed; no surviving fragments confirmed by tool output for this parish.
- **Pre-1858 probate original documents:** Destroyed in the 1922 Four Courts fire; abstracts only survive.
- **Estate and landlord records for the Lower Dunluce barony:** Held at PRONI and NLI in manuscript; not digitized.
- **Covenanting (Reformed Presbyterian) registers:** Very few Covenanting congregations have digitized registers; PRONI or the congregation itself.

---

## Known record losses

- **1922 Four Courts fire (Dublin):** Destroyed the Public Record Office of Ireland, which held the original census returns for 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851, the Prerogative Court of Canterbury wills for Ireland, and many Church of Ireland parish registers. This is stated in the general FamilySearch wiki for Ireland (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records is referenced in the Billy Civil Parish wiki), though the specific page could not be fetched in this session. The loss applies to Billy parish records held at Dublin at the time.
- **1861–1891 census returns:** Destroyed by government order during World War I, not in the 1922 fire.
- **Specific losses for Billy civil parish registers:** No tool in this session confirmed or denied the survival of particular Billy parish church registers. That must be verified at PRONI.

---

## Research tips

- **Start with the FamilySearch wiki page for Billy Civil Parish directly.** The page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy was confirmed to exist by wiki_search and carries a history section and church records section. The church records section had no dates filled in as retrieved, but the page may be updated — check it directly.
- **Search Griffiths Valuation and Tithe Applotment together.** Griffiths (c. 1859–1862) and the Tithe Applotment Books (c. 1823–1837) bracket the core of the 1780–1870 window and name householders by townland. Run both at https://www.askaboutireland.ie and https://www.irishgenealogy.ie to establish which families were in which Billy parish townland before and after the Famine.
- **The former ecclesiastical union matters for Church of Ireland searches.** Because Billy was formerly the head of an ecclesiastical union comprising Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride, early Church of Ireland vestry records and burials for those surrounding parishes may appear in Billy's registers. Search all five parishes at the RCB Library and PRONI when one register produces no result (source: FamilySearch wiki via wiki_search, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy).
- **Civil registration of Protestant (non-Catholic) marriages from 1845, not 1864.** The Marriage (Ireland) Act 1844 required civil registration of all non-Catholic marriages from 1 April 1845. For Presbyterian and Church of Ireland families, marriage records begin nearly 20 years before the full civil registration regime.
- **Roman Catholic records run through Coleraine, not a parish covering only Billy.** The FamilySearch wiki states the civil parish of Billy falls in the RC district of Coleraine. Search RC registers under Coleraine parish at IrishGenealogy.ie; do not expect a RC register specifically titled "Billy."
- **Use PRONI's eCatalogue to find MIC 1P/ microfilm numbers for all denominations in Billy.** The MIC 1P/ series is how PRONI holds church register microfilms for County Antrim. For Ballylinny (a neighboring Antrim civil parish), the Presbyterian registers are at PRONI MIC 1P/327 and FamilySearch Library film 973220 — the same pattern applies to Billy's registers once looked up (source: FamilySearch wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ballylinny_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy).

---

## Closing note on FamilySearch tool availability

The FamilySearch Wiki (`wiki_read` and `wiki_place_page`) returned only a generic placeholder for every Ireland URL attempted in this session, and `place_search` returned empty results for all Irish places. This prevented running `volume_search`, `collections_search`, and `external_links_search` for County Antrim. These are tool-availability failures, not evidence of absent FamilySearch holdings. Re-running this guide when the wiki-query-api is reachable will likely add indexed collections, digitized volume counts, and external collection links for County Antrim that this session could not surface.

---

Billy Civil Parish sits in the barony of Lower Dunluce along the north Antrim coast, with its post town at Bushmills. Most records from 1780 to 1864 are church registers held at PRONI in Belfast (on microfilm) and the RCB Library in Dublin (for Church of Ireland originals); there was no civil registration of births or deaths before 1864 and no non-Catholic marriage registration before 1845. The main caution is the 1922 Four Courts fire, which destroyed the Irish census returns before 1901 and many original wills and probate documents, so Griffiths Valuation, Tithe Applotment Books, and surviving church registers carry most of the weight for this period. The FamilySearch tools could not complete a full digital survey in this session, so visiting the PRONI eCatalogue directly at https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/proni and the FamilySearch Catalog at https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog is the recommended next step to find the specific microfilm and digitized holdings for Billy parish.

The next step is to open the PRONI eCatalogue and the FamilySearch Catalog, identify the exact MIC 1P/ film numbers for Billy's Presbyterian, Church of Ireland, Methodist, and Covenanting registers, then use those numbers to determine which registers are already online and which require a PRONI or FamilySearch Library visit.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840s–1860s)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Formed:** 1811
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Religious denominations confirmed:** Lutheran congregations present (digitized church records volume, 1840–1875)

> **Note on FamilySearch Wiki coverage:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Schuylkill County and Pennsylvania returned only generic content during this survey. Visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy for any specific guidance the wiki may provide.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Key gap:** No civil vital registration collection for the 1840s–1860s was found. Pennsylvania did not require statewide vital registration until the early 1900s.
- **Alternative:** Church registers are the primary substitute for this period.

---

### Church Records
- **Denominations confirmed:** Lutheran
- **FamilySearch holding:** Volume **004288771** — 198 images, coverage 1840–1875
- **Digitization level:** Browse-only images — **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.** Must be browsed page by page.
- **Languages:** English and German — both are needed to work through this volume.

---

### Census Records
- **FamilySearch holding:** Volume **007621224** — 412 images, coverage 1850–1860
- **Digitization level:** **96% indexed + images, full-text searchable.** Best starting point in this survey.
- **Ancestry:** Also available at https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/
- **Note:** Mortality schedules (listing deaths in the year preceding the census) exist for 1850 and 1860 — check FamilySearch and Ancestry separately; no specific Schuylkill volume was returned.

---

### Probate Records
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (ID: **1999196**) — 3.2 million images, **browse-only.** Free at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196
- **FamilySearch volume:** **004812990** — 286 images, coverage 1845–1880 — **full-text searchable but only 4% name-indexed.** Use FamilySearch's fulltext search interface; standard name search will miss most records.
- Includes wills, administrations, and inventories.

---

### Military Records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848) and Civil War (1861–1865)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (pre-1906), Civil War draft registrations
- **Where held:** NARA (physical). No Schuylkill County-specific military volume or indexed collection was returned.

---

### Land Records
- No Schuylkill County-specific land records volume or collection for this period was found in online collections.
- Would need to be pursued at the county courthouse or state archives.

---

### Tax Records
- No 1840s–1860s Schuylkill County tax collection found online (available Ancestry collection ends in 1801).

---

### Newspapers
- No digitized newspaper collection for Schuylkill County in this period was returned.
- Research value: obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices. Contact local historical societies or state newspaper archives for print holdings.

---

### Immigration / Naturalization
- **Pre-1906 naturalizations** could be filed in any court of record, including Schuylkill County Common Pleas Court. Do not limit searches to federal courts.
- **Passenger lists** at NARA are not county-specific; examine full manifests for family members.

---

### Cemetery Records
- No FindAGrave or BillionGraves collection for Schuylkill County was returned. Physical sexton records exist but were not identified in tool results.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Collection | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (ID: 1999196) — 3.2M images, browse-only | Free |
| FamilySearch | U.S. Federal Census, Schuylkill Co. 1850–1860 (vol. 007621224) — indexed + images | Free |
| FamilySearch | Probate Records, Schuylkill Co. 1845–1880 (vol. 004812990) — full-text searchable | Free |
| FamilySearch | Lutheran Church Records, Schuylkill Co. 1840–1875 (vol. 004288771) — browse-only | Free |
| Ancestry | 1850 United States Federal Census – Schuylkill County | Subscription |

**Survey completeness:** `volume_search` returned these 3 volumes and confirmed the set is complete for this place and period.

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse | Deed books, court records, probate files |
| Pennsylvania State Archives | State-level records, military records |
| NARA | Military service, pensions, bounty land, passenger lists, pre-1906 naturalizations |
| Local historical/genealogical societies | County histories, compiled records |
| Denominational archives | Church registers beyond FamilySearch holdings |

---

## Records NOT Online
- Vital records (births, marriages, deaths) for the 1840s–1860s — no civil registration collection found
- Tax records for this period
- Newspapers
- Land records (deeds, grants)
- Military records specific to Schuylkill County
- Naturalization records (likely at county courthouse or NARA)

---

## Research Tips

1. **Church records are the essential substitute for absent civil registration.** The Lutheran volume (004288771) is critical, but requires page-by-page browsing in English and German.
2. **Start with the 1850 federal census** — 96% indexed and full-text searchable; use it to establish family composition before moving into less-indexed series.

Here is what the locality-guide found:

---

Around 1800, present-day Alabama was part of the **Mississippi Territory (1798–1817)**, not yet a separate state. This has major implications for where records are held:

**Key archival fact:** Records created around 1800 were made under the Mississippi territorial government and are often indexed under **"Mississippi"** on FamilySearch — not Alabama. You must search both.

**Mobile area (Spanish colonial records)**
Spain administered the Mobile area until 1813, so records for that region — church registers, census returns, land grants — were created under Spanish authority. These are held at the **Archivo General de Indias** in Seville, with copies at the **Library of Congress**.

**Interior settlements — what survives and where**
| Record Type | Coverage | Repository |
|---|---|---|
| Territorial land grants | From 1798, indexed | FamilySearch |
| Territorial tax lists | Primary name lists before 1810 census | — |
| Mississippi Territory censuses | 1801, 1805, 1808, 1810 | Alabama Department of Archives and History (Montgomery); not yet known to be digitized |
| Church records | From 1803 | FamilySearch (indexed) |
| County marriage records | From 1809 | FamilySearch (indexed) |
| Territorial land & court records (image volumes) | 1799–1820 | FamilySearch — digitized but **browse only**, no name search |

**Recommended next step:** Build a research plan that works through the Mississippi territorial collections first, then Alabama collections from 1817 onward, with a parallel track for Spanish colonial records if your ancestor was in or near Mobile.
