entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (ca. 1790–1820, Pre-Statehood)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama admitted as the 22nd state on 14 December 1819. From 1817–1819 it was the Alabama Territory. At 1800, present-day Alabama was the eastern portion of the Mississippi Territory, created 7 April 1798.
- **Administrative center:** Territorial capital of Mississippi Territory was Washington, Mississippi (in present-day Mississippi); the Alabama Territory's capital was St. Stephens, Washington County.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory, United States (1798–1817); Alabama Territory (1817–1819)
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the tools for this place and period.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, early cotton planting (Tennessee Valley); river trade on the Tombigbee and Alabama rivers; Spanish-era fur trade and commerce through Mobile.
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek/Muscogee, Cherokee, Choctaw, and Chickasaw nations held most of the interior; Anglo-American settlers arrived from Georgia and the Carolinas after 1798; French Creole and Spanish colonial populations in the Mobile area; enslaved African Americans present from the colonial period.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist circuit riders and Baptist congregations (interior settlements); Roman Catholic parishes in Mobile (French/Spanish colonial foundation); Presbyterian missionaries active in the region.
- **Key historical events:** Creek War of 1813–1814 disrupted settlement and records for the interior; U.S. seizure of Mobile in 1813 ended Spanish administration; Mississippi Territory established (1798) the first U.S. civil government for the region.

## Boundary changes
- **Before 1798:** Mobile area was French (1702–1763), then British (1763–1780), then Spanish (1780–1813). The interior was nominally British then U.S. territory, but largely controlled by Native nations.
- **1798–1817:** The Mississippi Territory was gradually expanded to include all of present-day Mississippi and Alabama. First Alabama counties: Washington (1800), Madison (1808), Baldwin (1809), Mobile (1812).
- **1817:** Mississippi Territory divided — western half became the state of Mississippi; eastern half became the Alabama Territory.
- **1819:** Alabama admitted as the 22nd state.
- **Critical implication:** Records created ca. 1800 were made under Mississippi territorial authority and many are indexed on FamilySearch under 'Mississippi,' not Alabama. For the Mobile area before 1813, the Spanish colonial record system applies.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration existed during this period. No Alabama-specific registration start date was returned by the tools (the FamilySearch Wiki Alabama pages returned only generic content).
- **What exists:** No civil birth or death registers for this region ca. 1800. County marriage bonds and licenses began in some counties from 1809 — FamilySearch 'Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950' (id 1598408; 612,345 records / 1,224,690 persons; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408) is the earliest indexed collection.
- **Where held:** County probate courts (marriages). No civil birth or death registers for this period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, burials, marriages); territorial census enumerations; probate records; land records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Methodist and Baptist (interior, circuit riders, no fixed parishes at this date); Roman Catholic (Mobile, active since French colonial era, records surviving from colonial period).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch 'Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950' (id 1986396; 156,789 persons; 78,394 images; indexed + images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396) covers from 1803. For Mobile Catholic records predating U.S. control, originals may be at the Diocese of Mobile and the Mobile Municipal Archives (French colonial microfilm). 'Mississippi, Church Records, 1800-1950' (id 2034891; 87,654 persons; 43,827 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2034891) may cover the Alabama portion of the territory.
- **Language:** Mobile Catholic records from the French and Spanish periods will be in French or Spanish.

### Census records
- **Territorial census:** Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 covering present-day Alabama. These are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History, Montgomery (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records).
- **Federal census:** The 1810 federal census was the first to enumerate the Alabama portion of the Mississippi Territory.
- **Census substitutes:** FamilySearch 'Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890' (id 2016756; 287,634 records; index only, no images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756) and 'Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792-1890' (id 1927171; 198,340 records; index only, no images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1927171) both cover the target period and are searchable by name.
- **Access:** Both census substitute indexes are indexed (name-searchable) but have no images attached.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, territorial court proceedings.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch 'Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985' (id 1537764; 438,210 records; 219,105 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764) begins 1809 — just after most of the target period. A browse-only digitized volume for Washington County deed and probate records covers 1803-1820 (imageGroupNumber 004512890; 96 images; 0% indexed; not full-text searchable; must be browsed image-by-image). 'Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799-1920' (id 1855293; 245,670 records; 122,835 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855293) may include records for the Alabama portion of the territory.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (probate court); Alabama Department of Archives and History for territorial-era records.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Alabama is a federal land state — land was distributed by the U.S. federal government after acquisition. Before U.S. control, Spanish and British colonial grants governed the Mobile area.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** U.S. federal land patents (post-1798) are at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov). Spanish colonial land grants are at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Types:** Federal land patents, territorial land grants, county deeds, Spanish crown grants (Mobile area).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch 'Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907' (id 1919694; 312,450 records; 156,225 images; indexed + images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1919694) covers the territorial period and is the primary indexed online source. Two browse-only FamilySearch volumes cover territorial land records: imageGroupNumber 004512889 (territorial court and land records, 1808-1819, Alabama; 214 images; 0% indexed; not full-text) and 004498712 (Mississippi Territory land/court records, 1799-1817; 143 images; 0% indexed; not full-text).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War of 1813–1814; War of 1812 (Gulf Coast theater); American Revolution (some settlers were veterans or received bounty land).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants; territorial militia rolls.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA; https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 digitizes many NARA military records (https://www.fold3.com/). Territorial militia rolls may be at the Alabama Department of Archives and History.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Early cemeteries were private (farm/family) or church-affiliated; larger settlement cemeteries at St. Stephens, Huntsville, and Mobile.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has some coverage; completeness for pre-1820 burials is not confirmed by tool results.
- **Physical records:** Catholic Mobile cemeteries may have burial registers at the Diocese of Mobile; interior settlement burial records are sparse for this period.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Early territorial newspapers (Mobile Gazette; Alabama Republican, Huntsville, beginning 1816). Detailed date ranges were not returned by tools.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/); the Alabama Department of Archives and History and local public libraries hold microfilm.
- **Content value:** Legal notices, land announcements, and early death notices.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile (primary regional port); New Orleans (regional hub).
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (federal requirement began 1820 — pre-1820 lists are sparse); territorial naturalization records in county court files.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); FamilySearch 'Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799-1920' (id 1855293) may contain naturalization proceedings for the Alabama portion of the territory.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and county property tax lists; poll taxes.
- **Date range:** Territorial tax lists exist from the late 1790s onward.
- **Where held:** Alabama Department of Archives and History; FamilySearch 'Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792-1890' (id 1927171) may include territorial tax lists.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the primary substitute for pre-1810 census coverage and for the years between federal enumerations.

### Other record types
- **Spanish colonial records (Mobile area, to 1813):** Census returns, church registers, and land grants for the Mobile District are at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **French colonial records (Mobile area, 1702–1763):** At the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France; microfilm copies at the Mobile Municipal Archives (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (Alabama scope) | Church Records 1803-1950 (156,789 persons); County Marriages 1809-1950 (612,345 records); Probate Records 1809-1985 (438,210 records); Census Substitutes Index 1810-1890 (287,634 records) | Free |
| FamilySearch (Mississippi Territory scope) | Territorial and State Land Records 1798-1907 (312,450 records); County Court Records 1799-1920 (245,670 records); Compiled Census Substitutes 1792-1890 (198,340 records); Church Records 1800-1950 (87,654 records) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military Records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery Records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Free |
| NARA | Passenger lists, naturalization, military (https://www.archives.gov/) | In-person / some online |
| BLM General Land Office | Federal land patents (glorecords.blm.gov) | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume search returned 2 digitized volumes for Alabama, United States (1790-1820) — the complete result set. 1 additional volume was returned for Mississippi Territory (1798-1820) — also the complete result set. All 3 volumes are browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History, Montgomery | Territorial censuses 1801, 1805, 1808, 1810; territorial and state records; militia rolls | In-person; some online finding aids |
| Library of Congress, Washington D.C. | Copies of Spanish colonial records (Mobile District) | In-person; some digitized |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records (Mobile, 1702-1763) | In-person or correspondence |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | Microfilm of French colonial records | In-person |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial land grants, census returns, church registers (Mobile District) | In-person or correspondence |
| County courthouses (Washington, Madison, Baldwin, Mobile counties) | Deed, probate, and marriage records from county formation dates | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 (held at Alabama Department of Archives and History — not known to be digitized based on tool results)
- Spanish colonial records of the Mobile District (Archivo General de Indias; Library of Congress copies — not confirmed digitized online)
- French colonial records (Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer; Mobile Municipal Archives microfilm)
- Territorial militia rolls (Alabama Department of Archives and History)
- Pre-1803 interior Baptist and Methodist church registers (no digitized collection identified by tools)

## Known record losses
No tool result stated that a specific record set for this region and period was destroyed or lost. Sparse online coverage for pre-1819 Alabama is a digitization gap, not necessarily evidence of destruction. Consult the Alabama Department of Archives and History directly to determine the survival status of specific county or territorial record series.

## Research tips
- **Search under Mississippi Territory, not just Alabama.** Around 1800, county records were created under the Mississippi territorial government. FamilySearch's Mississippi-scoped collections — Territorial and State Land Records 1798-1907 (id 1919694) and County Court Records 1799-1920 (id 1855293) — cover the Alabama portion of the territory. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records
- **For the Mobile area before 1813, use the Spanish colonial record system.** Church registers, census returns, and land grants were administered by Spain. The Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and Library of Congress copies are the primary repositories. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records
- **Use territorial tax lists as the primary substitute for pre-1810 census coverage.** Federal census coverage begins with 1810; for 1800 and earlier, territorial tax lists in FamilySearch id 1927171 are the primary name indexes.
- **Land records are the most productive pre-1810 sources for heads of household.** The BLM General Land Office holds federal patents; FamilySearch id 1919694 holds indexed territorial land records from 1798.
- **All 3 browse-only FamilySearch volumes must be browsed image-by-image** — no name index and no full-text search: imageGroupNumber 004512889 (territorial court and land records, 1808-1819, 214 images), 004512890 (Washington County deed/probate, 1803-1820, 96 images), and 004498712 (Mississippi Territory land/court records, 1799-1817, 143 images).
- **The FamilySearch Wiki Alabama-specific pages did not return Alabama-specific content during this survey.** All six page requests returned a generic guide rather than Alabama-specific articles. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy directly in your browser for current Alabama research guidance.

I'm researching an ancestor who lived in the Alabama region around 1800, before statehood. What archives or record repositories will hold for that locality and period?

projectPath: <workspace>

agent_returns.text:
Locality survey written as `loc_001`.

---

Around 1800, present-day Alabama was not yet a state — it was part of the Mississippi Territory (1798-1817), governed from across the territory. The most important thing to know for this period is that records created around 1800 were made under the Mississippi territorial government and are often indexed under "Mississippi" on FamilySearch, not Alabama; you have to search both. The Mobile area adds another layer: Spain administered it until 1813, so records for that corner of the region — church registers, census returns, land grants — were created under Spanish authority and are now held at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress. For the interior settlements, the key surviving records are territorial land grants (indexed on FamilySearch from 1798), territorial tax lists (the only name lists before the 1810 federal census), and the Mississippi Territory censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810, which are held physically at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery and are not yet known to be digitized. Church records from 1803 onward and county marriage records from 1809 are indexed on FamilySearch; three digitized image volumes covering territorial-era land and court records (1799-1820) are on FamilySearch but must be browsed page by page — no name search is available.

The next step would be to build a research plan that routes searches through the Mississippi territorial collections first, then the Alabama collections from 1817 onward, with a parallel track for Spanish colonial records if your ancestor was in or near Mobile.

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (ca. 1790–1820, Pre-Statehood)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama admitted as the 22nd state on 14 December 1819. From 1817–1819 it was the Alabama Territory. At 1800, present-day Alabama was the eastern portion of the Mississippi Territory, created 7 April 1798.
- **Administrative center:** Territorial capital of Mississippi Territory was Washington, Mississippi (in present-day Mississippi); the Alabama Territory's capital was St. Stephens, Washington County.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory, United States (1798–1817); Alabama Territory (1817–1819)
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the tools for this place and period.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, early cotton planting (Tennessee Valley); river trade on the Tombigbee and Alabama rivers; Spanish-era fur trade and commerce through Mobile.
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek/Muscogee, Cherokee, Choctaw, and Chickasaw nations held most of the interior; Anglo-American settlers arrived from Georgia and the Carolinas after 1798; French Creole and Spanish colonial populations in the Mobile area; enslaved African Americans present from the colonial period.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist circuit riders and Baptist congregations (interior settlements); Roman Catholic parishes in Mobile (French/Spanish colonial foundation); Presbyterian missionaries active in the region.
- **Key historical events:** Creek War of 1813–1814 disrupted settlement and records for the interior; U.S. seizure of Mobile in 1813 ended Spanish administration; Mississippi Territory established (1798) the first U.S. civil government for the region.

## Boundary changes
- **Before 1798:** Mobile area was French (1702–1763), then British (1763–1780), then Spanish (1780–1813). The interior was nominally British then U.S. territory, but largely controlled by Native nations.
- **1798–1817:** The Mississippi Territory was gradually expanded to include all of present-day Mississippi and Alabama. First Alabama counties: Washington (1800), Madison (1808), Baldwin (1809), Mobile (1812).
- **1817:** Mississippi Territory divided — western half became the state of Mississippi; eastern half became the Alabama Territory.
- **1819:** Alabama admitted as the 22nd state.
- **Critical implication:** Records created ca. 1800 were made under Mississippi territorial authority and many are indexed on FamilySearch under 'Mississippi,' not Alabama. For the Mobile area before 1813, the Spanish colonial record system applies.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration existed during this period. No Alabama-specific registration start date was returned by the tools (the FamilySearch Wiki Alabama pages returned only generic content).
- **What exists:** No civil birth or death registers for this region ca. 1800. County marriage bonds and licenses began in some counties from 1809 — FamilySearch 'Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950' (id 1598408; 612,345 records / 1,224,690 persons; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408) is the earliest indexed collection.
- **Where held:** County probate courts (marriages). No civil birth or death registers for this period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, burials, marriages); territorial census enumerations; probate records; land records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Methodist and Baptist (interior, circuit riders, no fixed parishes at this date); Roman Catholic (Mobile, active since French colonial era, records surviving from colonial period).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch 'Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950' (id 1986396; 156,789 persons; 78,394 images; indexed + images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396) covers from 1803. For Mobile Catholic records predating U.S. control, originals may be at the Diocese of Mobile and the Mobile Municipal Archives (French colonial microfilm). 'Mississippi, Church Records, 1800-1950' (id 2034891; 87,654 persons; 43,827 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2034891) may cover the Alabama portion of the territory.
- **Language:** Mobile Catholic records from the French and Spanish periods will be in French or Spanish.

### Census records
- **Territorial census:** Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 covering present-day Alabama. These are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History, Montgomery (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records).
- **Federal census:** The 1810 federal census was the first to enumerate the Alabama portion of the Mississippi Territory.
- **Census substitutes:** FamilySearch 'Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890' (id 2016756; 287,634 records; index only, no images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756) and 'Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792-1890' (id 1927171; 198,340 records; index only, no images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1927171) both cover the target period and are searchable by name.
- **Access:** Both census substitute indexes are indexed (name-searchable) but have no images attached.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, territorial court proceedings.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch 'Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985' (id 1537764; 438,210 records; 219,105 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764) begins 1809 — just after most of the target period. A browse-only digitized volume for Washington County deed and probate records covers 1803-1820 (imageGroupNumber 004512890; 96 images; 0% indexed; not full-text searchable; must be browsed image-by-image). 'Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799-1920' (id 1855293; 245,670 records; 122,835 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855293) may include records for the Alabama portion of the territory.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (probate court); Alabama Department of Archives and History for territorial-era records.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Alabama is a federal land state — land was distributed by the U.S. federal government after acquisition. Before U.S. control, Spanish and British colonial grants governed the Mobile area.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** U.S. federal land patents (post-1798) are at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov). Spanish colonial land grants are at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Types:** Federal land patents, territorial land grants, county deeds, Spanish crown grants (Mobile area).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch 'Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907' (id 1919694; 312,450 records; 156,225 images; indexed + images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1919694) covers the territorial period and is the primary indexed online source. Two browse-only FamilySearch volumes cover territorial land records: imageGroupNumber 004512889 (territorial court and land records, 1808-1819, Alabama; 214 images; 0% indexed; not full-text) and 004498712 (Mississippi Territory land/court records, 1799-1817; 143 images; 0% indexed; not full-text).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War of 1813–1814; War of 1812 (Gulf Coast theater); American Revolution (some settlers were veterans or received bounty land).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants; territorial militia rolls.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA; https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 digitizes many NARA military records (https://www.fold3.com/). Territorial militia rolls may be at the Alabama Department of Archives and History.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Early cemeteries were private (farm/family) or church-affiliated; larger settlement cemeteries at St. Stephens, Huntsville, and Mobile.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has some coverage; completeness for pre-1820 burials is not confirmed by tool results.
- **Physical records:** Catholic Mobile cemeteries may have burial registers at the Diocese of Mobile; interior settlement burial records are sparse for this period.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Early territorial newspapers (Mobile Gazette; Alabama Republican, Huntsville, beginning 1816). Detailed date ranges were not returned by tools.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/); the Alabama Department of Archives and History and local public libraries hold microfilm.
- **Content value:** Legal notices, land announcements, and early death notices.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile (primary regional port); New Orleans (regional hub).
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (federal requirement began 1820 — pre-1820 lists are sparse); territorial naturalization records in county court files.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); FamilySearch 'Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799-1920' (id 1855293) may contain naturalization proceedings for the Alabama portion of the territory.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and county property tax lists; poll taxes.
- **Date range:** Territorial tax lists exist from the late 1790s onward.
- **Where held:** Alabama Department of Archives and History; FamilySearch 'Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792-1890' (id 1927171) may include territorial tax lists.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the primary substitute for pre-1810 census coverage and for the years between federal enumerations.

### Other record types
- **Spanish colonial records (Mobile area, to 1813):** Census returns, church registers, and land grants for the Mobile District are at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **French colonial records (Mobile area, 1702–1763):** At the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France; microfilm copies at the Mobile Municipal Archives (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (Alabama scope) | Church Records 1803-1950 (156,789 persons); County Marriages 1809-1950 (612,345 records); Probate Records 1809-1985 (438,210 records); Census Substitutes Index 1810-1890 (287,634 records) | Free |
| FamilySearch (Mississippi Territory scope) | Territorial and State Land Records 1798-1907 (312,450 records); County Court Records 1799-1920 (245,670 records); Compiled Census Substitutes 1792-1890 (198,340 records); Church Records 1800-1950 (87,654 records) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military Records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery Records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Free |
| NARA | Passenger lists, naturalization, military (https://www.archives.gov/) | In-person / some online |
| BLM General Land Office | Federal land patents (glorecords.blm.gov) | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume search returned 2 digitized volumes for Alabama, United States (1790-1820) — the complete result set. 1 additional volume was returned for Mississippi Territory (1798-1820) — also the complete result set. All 3 volumes are browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History, Montgomery | Territorial censuses 1801, 1805, 1808, 1810; territorial and state records; militia rolls | In-person; some online finding aids |
| Library of Congress, Washington D.C. | Copies of Spanish colonial records (Mobile District) | In-person; some digitized |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records (Mobile, 1702-1763) | In-person or correspondence |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | Microfilm of French colonial records | In-person |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial land grants, census returns, church registers (Mobile District) | In-person or correspondence |
| County courthouses (Washington, Madison, Baldwin, Mobile counties) | Deed, probate, and marriage records from county formation dates | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 (held at Alabama Department of Archives and History — not known to be digitized based on tool results)
- Spanish colonial records of the Mobile District (Archivo General de Indias; Library of Congress copies — not confirmed digitized online)
- French colonial records (Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer; Mobile Municipal Archives microfilm)
- Territorial militia rolls (Alabama Department of Archives and History)
- Pre-1803 interior Baptist and Methodist church registers (no digitized collection identified by tools)

## Known record losses
No tool result stated that a specific record set for this region and period was destroyed or lost. Sparse online coverage for pre-1819 Alabama is a digitization gap, not necessarily evidence of destruction. Consult the Alabama Department of Archives and History directly to determine the survival status of specific county or territorial record series.

## Research tips
- **Search under Mississippi Territory, not just Alabama.** Around 1800, county records were created under the Mississippi territorial government. FamilySearch's Mississippi-scoped collections — Territorial and State Land Records 1798-1907 (id 1919694) and County Court Records 1799-1920 (id 1855293) — cover the Alabama portion of the territory. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records
- **For the Mobile area before 1813, use the Spanish colonial record system.** Church registers, census returns, and land grants were administered by Spain. The Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and Library of Congress copies are the primary repositories. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records
- **Use territorial tax lists as the primary substitute for pre-1810 census coverage.** Federal census coverage begins with 1810; for 1800 and earlier, territorial tax lists in FamilySearch id 1927171 are the primary name indexes.
- **Land records are the most productive pre-1810 sources for heads of household.** The BLM General Land Office holds federal patents; FamilySearch id 1919694 holds indexed territorial land records from 1798.
- **All 3 browse-only FamilySearch volumes must be browsed image-by-image** — no name index and no full-text search: imageGroupNumber 004512889 (territorial court and land records, 1808-1819, 214 images), 004512890 (Washington County deed/probate, 1803-1820, 96 images), and 004498712 (Mississippi Territory land/court records, 1799-1817, 143 images).
- **The FamilySearch Wiki Alabama-specific pages did not return Alabama-specific content during this survey.** All six page requests returned a generic guide rather than Alabama-specific articles. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy directly in your browser for current Alabama research guidance.

---

**Locality Guide: Arkansas Region Before 1800 (Spanish Colonial Period)**

Before 1800, what is now Arkansas was part of **Spanish Louisiana**, administered from New Orleans. The only permanent European settlement in the territory was **Arkansas Post**, a small military fort and trading village. There was no civil vital registration — the Catholic Church was the sole keeper of births, marriages, and deaths.

---

- Because Arkansas Post answered administratively to New Orleans, records about it are often filed under **Louisiana** colonial collections, not Arkansas.

# Locality Guide: Arkansas Region — Spanish Colonial Period (1763–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Arkansas Post established 1686 by the French. Transferred to Spanish Louisiana under the Treaty of Paris 1763. Returned to France by the Treaty of San Ildefonso 1800. Acquired by the United States via the Louisiana Purchase 1803. Arkansas Territory created 1813; state of Arkansas admitted 1836.
- **Administrative center:** Arkansas Post (Poste des Arkansas), on the lower Arkansas River — the only significant European settlement in the territory
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Spanish Louisiana (Province of Louisiana and West Florida), administered from New Orleans
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by tools for this period. The European settler community was small — a Spanish garrison, French Creole traders, and scattered frontier families.
- **Economy:** Fur trade, subsistence farming, military garrison
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole settlers, Spanish administrators and soldiers, Quapaw and other Native American peoples
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic only — the sole organized denomination under French and Spanish colonial rule
- **Key historical events:** Treaty of Paris 1763 (France cedes Louisiana to Spain); Treaty of San Ildefonso 1800 (Spain secretly cedes back to France); Louisiana Purchase 1803 (United States acquires the territory)

## Boundary changes
- **1686–1763:** French Louisiana — Arkansas Post operated as a French military fort and trading post.
- **1763–1800:** Spanish Louisiana, District of Arkansas — the Treaty of Paris transferred all French territory west of the Mississippi to Spain. Arkansas Post served as headquarters of the District of Arkansas, a sub-unit of Spanish Louisiana administered from New Orleans.
- **1800:** Treaty of San Ildefonso returns Louisiana to France; effective French administrative control was nominal.
- **1803:** Louisiana Purchase — the United States acquires the territory. Records from this point forward are American.
- **Note:** The "state of Arkansas" did not exist until 1836. No county structure existed before 1813. Records created before 1803 were generated under French or Spanish colonial administration, not under any U.S. or Arkansas jurisdiction.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration of births, deaths, or marriages existed during the Spanish colonial period. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Arkansas Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey and stated no start date specific to Arkansas.
- **What exists:** None for this period. All vital event recording was done by the Catholic Church.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic sacramental registers (see Church Records below) are the only source for births, marriages, and deaths.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only. French Catholic missionaries maintained a presence at Arkansas Post from the early 1700s; the Church continued under Spanish administration.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials — the primary source for vital events for the entire pre-1800 period.
- **Where held:** Surviving registers are held by the Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock and in transcribed form at the Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records)
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** DGS 008814402 — 64 images of Arkansas Post sacramental registers, 1763–1800, in Spanish. Browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. The researcher must read all 64 images by hand.
- **Language:** Spanish (earlier French-era entries may be in French)
- **Gaps:** French-era registers (pre-1763) survival status is unconfirmed from tool results; contact the Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock directly.

### Census records
- **Spanish padrones (colonial censuses):** The Spanish administration periodically took household censuses (padrones) of the District of Arkansas, naming heads of household, family members, and sometimes occupations and origins.
- **Where held:** Surviving padrones are at the Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock, and the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain. Microfilm copies are at the Library of Congress. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Access:** No FamilySearch-indexed collection covers pre-1800 Arkansas census records. The FamilySearch collection Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819–1870 (collection 2085124) begins in 1819 and does not cover this period.
- **Federal census:** The first U.S. federal census covering this territory was 1810; the 1800 census did not include Arkansas (it was not yet U.S. territory for the full census year).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Under Spanish administration, civil matters were handled by the commandant at Arkansas Post. Records include land disputes, estate matters, and civil proceedings.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock, and Archivo General de Indias, Seville. Microfilm at the Library of Congress.
- **Access:** Not available in any online database. Physical or microfilm access required.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Spanish land concessions (concesiones de tierras) — metes and bounds descriptions, often referencing natural features.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The commandant at Arkansas Post issued local concessions; larger grants required approval from the Governor-General in New Orleans. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Arkansas Land and Property returned only generic content during this survey.
- **Types:** Spanish land concessions (1763–1800); U.S. federal land-board confirmation records (post-1803) that reconstruct the pre-1803 grantee chain.
- **Where held:** Original Spanish concession records at the Archivo General de Indias and the Arkansas History Commission. U.S. confirmation records accessible via the BLM General Land Office Records website (glorecords.blm.gov).

### Military records
- **Relevant context:** Arkansas Post maintained a small Spanish garrison throughout this period.
- **Record types:** Spanish military muster rolls (revistas de comisario) and post administrative records for the Arkansas garrison.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias, Seville, and possibly the Archivo General de Simancas. Microfilm at the Library of Congress. Not available online.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** A Catholic burial ground was associated with Arkansas Post. No tool result confirmed surviving physical burial registers or online indexing for this period.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) should be checked but likely has minimal pre-1800 entries for this location.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No newspapers were published in the Arkansas region before 1800. Not applicable for this locality and period.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant context:** Movement into Spanish Louisiana required a royal license or passport. Records of settlers' origins may appear in Spanish colonial correspondence or the registers of the Governor-General's office in New Orleans.
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was the principal entry point for the territory.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias, Seville; Louisiana Historical Center, New Orleans; Louisiana State Archives.
- **Naturalizations:** Not applicable in the modern sense; settlers were subjects of the Spanish Crown.
- **Content note:** Arrival manifests in the modern sense do not exist for this period and this interior location. Look instead for passport applications, settlement permits, and colonial correspondence naming arrivals.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Spanish colonial tax and tribute records may survive at the Archivo General de Indias.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias, Seville. Not available online.
- **Substitute value:** Padrones (census lists) serve a similar substitute function and are more likely to survive.

### Other record types
- **Spanish colonial administrative correspondence:** Letters, reports, and dispatches between the commandant at Arkansas Post and the Governor-General in New Orleans name settlers not found in sacramental registers. Held at the Archivo General de Indias and the Louisiana Historical Center, New Orleans.
- **American land-claim confirmation records (post-1803):** U.S. land boards documented and confirmed or rejected Spanish and French land claims after the Louisiana Purchase. These records often reconstruct the pre-1803 grantee chain and are at the BLM GLO website and NARA.

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | DGS 008814402 — Arkansas Post sacramental registers, 1763–1800 (64 images, browse-only, in Spanish) | Free |
| BLM General Land Office Records (glorecords.blm.gov) | Post-1803 U.S. land patent confirmations documenting pre-existing Spanish grantees | Free |
| Portal de Archivos Españoles — PARES (pares.mcu.es) | Catalogue and partial digitization of Archivo General de Indias holdings, including Louisiana/Arkansas colonial records | Free |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock, AR | Surviving Spanish colonial records (padrones, land records, civil correspondence); transcribed Catholic register records | In-person or written inquiry; arkansashistory.com |

| Library of Congress, Washington DC | Microfilm of Spanish colonial Louisiana records, including some Arkansas Post materials | In-person or via LC online catalogue |
| Louisiana Historical Center, New Orleans, LA | Spanish colonial records for the Province of Louisiana and West Florida; post letters and reports referencing Arkansas Post | In-person |
| NARA, Washington DC | U.S. era confirmation records for Spanish/French land claims (post-1803); earliest U.S. territorial records | In-person or NARA online catalogue |

## Records NOT online
- Spanish padrones (censuses) for the District of Arkansas
- Spanish military muster rolls for Arkansas Post
- Spanish land concessions (originals)
- Spanish civil administrative correspondence for Arkansas Post
- French-era Catholic sacramental registers (pre-1763)
- Probate and estate records from the Spanish commandant's court

The only record set with any online digitized presence is the Arkansas Post sacramental registers 1763–1800 (DGS 008814402 on FamilySearch, browse-only, in Spanish).

No tool result in this survey stated that a specific Arkansas colonial record set was destroyed or lost. The small population and remote location of Arkansas Post during this period means the total surviving documentary record is inherently thin; an empty search result is a coverage gap, not confirmed destruction. Contact the Arkansas History Commission to ask which series are known to be missing.

- **Check Louisiana colonial records for Arkansas context.** Arkansas Post was administered from New Orleans; correspondence, land records, and military reports about the post may be filed under Louisiana colonial collections rather than Arkansas. - **U.S. land confirmation records are a back-door into the Spanish period.** After 1803, federal land boards documented pre-existing Spanish and French grants. Confirmation files often name the original grantee and concession date. Search glorecords.blm.gov under Arkansas.
- **Records will be in Spanish (and earlier ones in French).** The sacramental registers and all administrative documents require reading 18th-century Spanish script. Consider engaging a professional with experience in colonial Louisiana records.

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Arkansas Region — Spanish Colonial Period (1763–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Arkansas Post established 1686 by the French. Transferred to Spanish Louisiana under the Treaty of Paris 1763. Returned to France by the Treaty of San Ildefonso 1800. Acquired by the United States via the Louisiana Purchase 1803. Arkansas Territory created 1813; state of Arkansas admitted 1836.
- **Administrative center:** Arkansas Post (Poste des Arkansas), on the lower Arkansas River — the only significant European settlement in the territory
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Spanish Louisiana (Province of Louisiana and West Florida), administered from New Orleans
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by tools for this period. The European settler community was small — a Spanish garrison, French Creole traders, and scattered frontier families.
- **Economy:** Fur trade, subsistence farming, military garrison
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole settlers, Spanish administrators and soldiers, Quapaw and other Native American peoples
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic only — the sole organized denomination under French and Spanish colonial rule
- **Key historical events:** Treaty of Paris 1763 (France cedes Louisiana to Spain); Treaty of San Ildefonso 1800 (Spain secretly cedes back to France); Louisiana Purchase 1803 (United States acquires the territory)

## Boundary changes
- **1686–1763:** French Louisiana — Arkansas Post operated as a French military fort and trading post.
- **1763–1800:** Spanish Louisiana, District of Arkansas — the Treaty of Paris transferred all French territory west of the Mississippi to Spain. Arkansas Post served as headquarters of the District of Arkansas, a sub-unit of Spanish Louisiana administered from New Orleans.
- **1800:** Treaty of San Ildefonso returns Louisiana to France; effective French administrative control was nominal.
- **1803:** Louisiana Purchase — the United States acquires the territory. Records from this point forward are American.
- **Note:** The state of Arkansas did not exist until 1836. No county structure existed before 1813. Records created before 1803 were generated under French or Spanish colonial administration, not under any U.S. or Arkansas jurisdiction.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration of births, deaths, or marriages existed during the Spanish colonial period. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Arkansas Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey and stated no start date specific to Arkansas.
- **What exists:** None for this period. All vital event recording was done by the Catholic Church.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic sacramental registers (see Church Records below) are the only source for births, marriages, and deaths.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only. French Catholic missionaries maintained a presence at Arkansas Post from the early 1700s; the Church continued under Spanish administration.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials — the primary source for vital events for the entire pre-1800 period.
- **Where held:** Surviving registers are held by the Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock and in transcribed form at the Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records)
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** DGS 008814402 — 64 images of Arkansas Post sacramental registers, 1763–1800, in Spanish. Browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. The researcher must read all 64 images by hand.
- **Language:** Spanish (earlier French-era entries may be in French)
- **Gaps:** French-era registers (pre-1763) survival status is unconfirmed from tool results; contact the Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock directly.

### Census records
- **Spanish padrones (colonial censuses):** The Spanish administration periodically took household censuses (padrones) of the District of Arkansas, naming heads of household, family members, and sometimes occupations and origins.
- **Where held:** Surviving padrones are at the Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock, and the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain. Microfilm copies are at the Library of Congress. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Access:** No FamilySearch-indexed collection covers pre-1800 Arkansas census records. The FamilySearch collection Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819–1870 (collection 2085124) begins in 1819 and does not cover this period.
- **Federal census:** The first U.S. federal census covering this territory was 1810; the 1800 census did not include Arkansas (it was not yet U.S. territory for the full census year).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Under Spanish administration, civil matters were handled by the commandant at Arkansas Post. Records include land disputes, estate matters, and civil proceedings.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock, and Archivo General de Indias, Seville. Microfilm at the Library of Congress.
- **Access:** Not available in any online database. Physical or microfilm access required.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Spanish land concessions (concesiones de tierras) — metes and bounds descriptions, often referencing natural features.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The commandant at Arkansas Post issued local concessions; larger grants required approval from the Governor-General in New Orleans. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Arkansas Land and Property returned only generic content during this survey.
- **Types:** Spanish land concessions (1763–1800); U.S. federal land-board confirmation records (post-1803) that reconstruct the pre-1803 grantee chain.
- **Where held:** Original Spanish concession records at the Archivo General de Indias and the Arkansas History Commission. U.S. confirmation records accessible via the BLM General Land Office Records website (glorecords.blm.gov).

### Military records
- **Relevant context:** Arkansas Post maintained a small Spanish garrison throughout this period.
- **Record types:** Spanish military muster rolls (revistas de comisario) and post administrative records for the Arkansas garrison.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias, Seville, and possibly the Archivo General de Simancas. Microfilm at the Library of Congress. Not available online.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** A Catholic burial ground was associated with Arkansas Post. No tool result confirmed surviving physical burial registers or online indexing for this period.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) should be checked but likely has minimal pre-1800 entries for this location.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No newspapers were published in the Arkansas region before 1800. Not applicable for this locality and period.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant context:** Movement into Spanish Louisiana required a royal license or passport. Records of settlers' origins may appear in Spanish colonial correspondence or the registers of the Governor-General's office in New Orleans.
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was the principal entry point for the territory.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias, Seville; Louisiana Historical Center, New Orleans; Louisiana State Archives.
- **Naturalizations:** Not applicable in the modern sense; settlers were subjects of the Spanish Crown.
- **Content note:** Arrival manifests in the modern sense do not exist for this period. Look instead for passport applications, settlement permits, and colonial correspondence naming arrivals.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Spanish colonial tax and tribute records may survive at the Archivo General de Indias.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias, Seville. Not available online.
- **Substitute value:** Padrones (census lists) serve a similar substitute function and are more likely to survive.

### Other record types
- **Spanish colonial administrative correspondence:** Letters, reports, and dispatches between the commandant at Arkansas Post and the Governor-General in New Orleans name settlers not found in sacramental registers. Held at the Archivo General de Indias and the Louisiana Historical Center, New Orleans.
- **American land-claim confirmation records (post-1803):** U.S. land boards documented and confirmed or rejected Spanish and French land claims after the Louisiana Purchase. These records often reconstruct the pre-1803 grantee chain and are at the BLM GLO website and NARA.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | DGS 008814402 — Arkansas Post sacramental registers, 1763–1800 (64 images, browse-only, in Spanish) | Free |
| BLM General Land Office Records (glorecords.blm.gov) | Post-1803 U.S. land patent confirmations documenting pre-existing Spanish grantees | Free |
| Portal de Archivos Espanoles — PARES (pares.mcu.es) | Catalogue and partial digitization of Archivo General de Indias holdings, including Louisiana/Arkansas colonial records | Free |

The external-links tool returned only generic links (Ancestry.com census, FindAGrave, Fold3, Newspapers.com, NARA, FamilySearch Wiki Vital Records category) with no collections specific to the pre-1800 Arkansas colonial period.

**Coverage of this survey:** 1 digitized volume matches this place and period; the volume above is the complete result set returned by the tools (totalResults: 1).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock, AR | Surviving Spanish colonial records (padrones, land records, civil correspondence); transcribed Catholic register records | In-person or written inquiry; arkansashistory.com |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock | Original surviving French/Spanish sacramental registers | Contact the diocesan archives directly |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial records for Louisiana including Arkansas Post: padrones, land concessions, military muster rolls, administrative correspondence | In-person or via PARES online catalogue (pares.mcu.es); some documents digitized |
| Library of Congress, Washington DC | Microfilm of Spanish colonial Louisiana records, including some Arkansas Post materials | In-person or via LC online catalogue |
| Louisiana Historical Center, New Orleans, LA | Spanish colonial records for the Province of Louisiana and West Florida; post letters and reports referencing Arkansas Post | In-person |
| NARA, Washington DC | U.S. era confirmation records for Spanish/French land claims (post-1803); earliest U.S. territorial records | In-person or NARA online catalogue |

## Records NOT online
- Spanish padrones (censuses) for the District of Arkansas
- Spanish military muster rolls for Arkansas Post
- Spanish land concessions (originals)
- Spanish civil administrative correspondence for Arkansas Post
- French-era Catholic sacramental registers (pre-1763)
- Probate and estate records from the Spanish commandant's court

The only record set with any online digitized presence is the Arkansas Post sacramental registers 1763–1800 (DGS 008814402 on FamilySearch, browse-only, in Spanish).

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that a specific Arkansas colonial record set was destroyed or lost. The small population and remote location of Arkansas Post during this period means the total surviving documentary record is inherently thin; an empty search result is a coverage gap, not confirmed destruction. Contact the Arkansas History Commission to ask which series are known to be missing.

## Research tips
- **Start with FamilySearch volume DGS 008814402.** It is the only digitized pre-1800 Arkansas record set found by this survey. Browse all 64 images — the registers are in Spanish, cover Arkansas Post, and run 1763–1800.
- **Search the Archivo General de Indias via PARES (pares.mcu.es).** Much of the Spanish colonial record for Louisiana is catalogued there, and a portion is digitized. Search under 'Louisiana,' 'Luisiana,' 'Poste des Arkansas,' and 'Arkansas.' This is the single richest repository for Spanish-era Arkansas records. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Contact the Arkansas History Commission before traveling.** It holds transcriptions of the Catholic registers and surviving Spanish colonial records; their finding aids describe what survives. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Check Louisiana colonial records for Arkansas context.** Arkansas Post was administered from New Orleans; correspondence, land records, and military reports about the post may be filed under Louisiana colonial collections rather than Arkansas. Search the Louisiana Historical Center and Louisiana State Archives.
- **U.S. land confirmation records are a back-door into the Spanish period.** After 1803, federal land boards documented pre-existing Spanish and French grants. Confirmation files often name the original grantee and concession date. Search glorecords.blm.gov under Arkansas.
- **Records will be in Spanish (and earlier ones in French).** The sacramental registers and all administrative documents require reading 18th-century Spanish script. Consider engaging a professional with experience in colonial Louisiana records.

---

**Locality Guide — Ohio (Future State), ca. 1790**
*(Written as **loc_001** in the project file)*

### Boundary / Jurisdictional Context

In 1790, Ohio did not yet exist as a state — it was the **Northwest Territory**, organized only two years earlier. Only **two counties** had been formed by that date:

- **Washington County** (est. 1788, seat: Marietta)
- **Hamilton County** (est. 1790, seat: Cincinnati)

Every record created in 1790 Ohio falls under one of those two county names, not any modern Ohio county. This is essential to know before searching; looking under later county names will produce nothing.

---

### Record Availability Despite Early Documentation Gaps

| Record Type | Situation |
|---|---|
| **Civil birth/death registration** | None — did not exist yet. Church records are the only equivalent. |
| **Church records** | Primary substitute for vital records. FamilySearch holds an "Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950" collection with ~678,000 indexed records. |
| **Marriage** | County-level registration began in 1789. There is a digitized collection for this period. |

- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by place_population for this period.
- **Economy:** Frontier settlement; fort-based military garrisons; fur trade; Ohio River transport
- **Ethnic composition:** Euro-American settlers primarily from Virginia, Pennsylvania, and Connecticut; Indigenous peoples — Shawnee, Delaware, Wyandot, Miami (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio)
- **Religious denominations:** Protestant frontier congregations; Methodist, Presbyterian, and Baptist circuit-riders typical of the period

An absence of results in volume_search or collections_search is a coverage gap, not a confirmed loss. For definitive information on what survives, contact the Ohio History Connection.

## Research tips
- **Determine the 1790 county first.** In 1790 there were only two counties in Ohio: Washington County and Hamilton County. Every Ohio event in 1790 occurred in one of these two; identify which one by the ancestor's location before searching any collection. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)
- **Know which land district applies.** The Virginia Military District, the Connecticut Western Reserve, and the Congress Lands each have records in separate repositories. Place the ancestor on a map before deciding which land repository to approach. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)
- **Church records are the primary vital-record source.** No civil birth or death registration existed in 1790 Ohio. The FamilySearch Ohio Church Records collection (1787–1950, 678,234 records) is the nearest equivalent.
- **The 1790 federal census covers the territory.** Ohio settlers appear in the 1790 census under Northwest Territory; search Ancestry.com or FamilySearch.
- **The browse-only territorial land volume must be examined image by image.** The 1 digitized volume of Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records (1788–1799; imageGroup 005112233; 51 images) has 0% name indexing. There is no name search — the researcher must page through every image manually.
- **Expect Virginia and Kentucky origins.** Many early Ohio settlers came from Virginia and Kentucky via the Ohio River. Check Virginia and Kentucky court, land, and church records for family origins before Ohio arrival.

Locality guide written and saved as **loc_001** in your research.json. Here's the summary:

---

## California Gold Rush (1850s) — Research Guide

**Records landscape at a glance:**
California became a state in 1850 and immediately built county-level record keeping — vital records (births, marriages), probate, mining claims, land deeds, and court records all exist from that year. The catch: coverage is uneven for transient mining camps, and most records live at individual county courthouses or physical repositories rather than being searchable online by name.

---

### Key Sources, Most to Least Accessible

| Record Type | Coverage | Online? | Repository |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1852 California State Census** | Statewide; fills 1850 gap | ✅ FamilySearch (88% indexed) | FamilySearch |
| **County births & marriages (1850+)** | County-level | ✅ FamilySearch (partial) | FamilySearch |
| **Great Registers (voter lists, 1866+)** | Statewide; reach back to Gold Rush arrivals | ✅ FamilySearch | FamilySearch |
| **Mining claim registers** | County-level | ❌ Browse-only / physical | County courthouses |
| **Port arrivals at San Francisco/Sacramento** | Incomplete | ❌ Physical or browse-only | NARA Pacific Region (San Bruno, CA) |
| **Overland trail diaries & journals** | Selective | ❌ Physical | Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) |
| **Probate & land deeds** | County-level | ❌ Mostly physical | County courthouses |
| **Naturalization records** | Partial | ❌ Physical / NARA | NARA Pacific Region |

---

### Critical Research Notes

1. **County boundaries shifted frequently** in the Gold Rush region during the 1850s. Always identify the correct county at the *time of the event* before searching — the county a miner lived in could have changed names or boundaries within a few years.

2. **The 1850 federal census for California was partially destroyed** — the 1852 state census is the primary substitute.

3. **The Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley)** is the premier repository for Gold Rush–era personal papers, diaries, letters, and published reminiscences — especially valuable for identifying origins.

4. **California State Library** holds state government records and newspapers from the era.

5. **FamilySearch Wiki caveat:** The California wiki pages returned generic content during this survey. Visit [FamilySearch California Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy) directly before finalizing a plan.

---

### Suggested Next Step

A **research plan** for a specific individual or family would sequence these sources into a concrete search strategy and flag which record type is most likely to document where a miner came from. Just name the person and I can build it out.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California became a U.S. state on September 9, 1850, bypassing territorial status. From 1848 to statehood it was under U.S. military governance following the Mexican–American War.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Sacramento (state capital from 1854); San Francisco as economic center
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mexico (to 1848), then United States
- **Population during period:** Approximately 92,597 enumerated in the 1850 federal census; Wikipedia reports roughly 300,000 migrants arrived 1848–1855
- **Economy:** Gold mining, agriculture, and trade; San Francisco and Sacramento grew rapidly as supply and financial hubs for the mining camps
- **Ethnic composition:** Highly diverse — American-born Anglo migrants, European (especially Irish, German, French), Chinese, Chilean, Mexican, Native Californian, and Australian populations
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (dominant among Spanish/Mexican-era population and many Irish miners); Protestant denominations (Methodist, Episcopal, Presbyterian, Baptist) established by Anglo settlers; Chinese temples in mining towns
- **Key historical events:** Gold discovered at Sutter's Mill, January 24, 1848; California statehood September 9, 1850; rapid county formation across the gold regions throughout the 1850s

## Boundary changes
- California entered the Union in 1850 with 27 original counties; numerous new counties were carved from these during the 1850s as population swelled in the Mother Lode region
- County lines in the gold regions (El Dorado, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Nevada, Placer, Amador) shifted repeatedly; a mining camp on one side of a line one year could fall in a different county the next
- Before statehood (1846–1850), U.S. military governance generated minimal civil records; Spanish/Mexican mission and land-grant records are the earlier administrative layer
- Records created under Mexican authority (land grants, mission registers) required a separate adjudication process under the U.S. Land Commission after 1851

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Civil registration was at the county level in California from statehood (1850). The FamilySearch Wiki pages specific to California returned only generic fallback content during this survey, so the exact statewide registration start date cannot be confirmed from this survey's tools. FamilySearch holds county-level births from 1850 and county marriages from 1850.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch "California, County Births, 1850–1919" (789,456 records, indexed + images); "California, County Marriages, 1850–1952" (567,890 records, indexed + images). No county death collection covering the 1850s was returned by this survey's tools.
- **Where held:** County courthouses; digitized collections on FamilySearch (free)
- **Gaps:** Coverage is uneven for mining camps, which were transient and often unincorporated; many births and deaths went unrecorded
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers, cemetery records, newspaper death and marriage notices, probate records naming next of kin

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mission church network and parishes serving Spanish/Mexican communities); Protestant denominations established during and after the Gold Rush. Specific founding dates in the gold regions were not returned by this survey's tools.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials
- **Where held:** The FamilySearch wiki_search result confirms the California State Library and Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley hold extensive Gold Rush-era manuscript collections including church materials (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records). FamilySearch holds "California, Mission Records, 1769–1850" (98,765 records, indexed + images) — this collection ends at the Gold Rush's start and is background context for Native Californian and Spanish/Mexican ancestors.
- **Language:** Mission records are in Spanish; later records predominantly in English

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The 1850 federal census — California's first — was partially destroyed; some county returns are missing (FamilySearch wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records). The 1860 federal census is the next complete enumeration.
- **State census:** California held a state census in 1852. FamilySearch has a digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 006601001, 522 images, 88% name-indexed, full-text searchable). **This is the most important census source for Gold Rush-era research** — it covers the gap left by the partially destroyed 1850 federal census.
- **Other enumerations:** Tax lists and mining claim registers function as proxy censuses for adult male residents in years between enumerations
- **Access:** 1852 state census — **indexed + images** on FamilySearch; 1850 federal census surviving returns — indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry; 1860 federal census — indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories; court records include naturalizations, mining disputes, civil suits
- **Testate or intestate:** For Gold Rush miners, intestate (no will) estates were common given the transient population — search administration files as well as wills
- **Date range:** From county formation (1850 for original counties)
- **Where held:** County courthouses and California State Archives. No digitized FamilySearch collection for California probate in this period was returned by this survey's tools — treat as physical or microfilm only pending further search.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal public domain (rectangular survey) for post-1848 U.S. grants; Spanish/Mexican-era land grants (ranchos) adjudicated before the U.S. Land Commission under a separate system
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal patents via the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office for post-1848 federal land; California State Archives for Mexican-era grant papers. The wiki_read for California_Land_and_Property returned only generic content — the specific California repository list was not confirmed from that page.
- **Types:** Federal land patents, Spanish/Mexican land grant documents, county deed books, mining claim registers, tax records
- **Date range:** U.S.-era records from 1848; earlier land grants from the Spanish/Mexican period
- **Where held:** BLM GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov) for federal patents (free); county recorders for deeds; California State Archives for Mexican land grants

### Mining claim records
- **A record type unique to Gold Rush research.** County recorders registered mining claims in dedicated registers. The FamilySearch wiki_search confirms these are held at county recorders (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records).
- FamilySearch has one digitized but **browse-only** volume for San Francisco County, 1849–1855 (imageGroupNumber 006601002, 340 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable) — must be browsed image by image with no name search
- Gold-region county recorders (El Dorado, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Nevada, Placer, Amador, Sacramento) hold original registers — largely physical access

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican–American War (ended 1848); Civil War (1861–1865, just after this window but many California residents enlisted)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants, and draft registrations at NARA; state militia records at the California State Archives
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 subscription database (https://www.fold3.com/)

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Mining-era cemeteries scattered across the Mother Lode counties; many are small, informal, and poorly documented
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) holds California cemetery transcriptions
- **Physical records:** Sexton and burial registers are highly incomplete for the 1850s given the transient mining population; many early burials were never formally recorded

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** San Francisco and Sacramento papers were active from 1848; numerous short-lived papers served individual mining camps
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/, subscription) for digitized papers; the California State Library and Bancroft Library hold microfilm of many papers
- **Content value:** Obituaries, death notices, mining news, arrival notices, legal notices (estate and probate), and advertisements that document residents

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** San Francisco (primary sea entry); Sacramento (river port)
- **Record types:** Ship passenger manifests for San Francisco arrivals held at NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno — wiki_search confirms this (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records). FamilySearch has a digitized but **browse-only** volume of Port Arrival Registers for Sacramento, 1849–1858 (imageGroupNumber 006601003, 298 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable)
- Overland trail migrants are documented through diaries, journals, and wagon train rosters at the California State Library and Bancroft Library — no centralized arrival record equivalent to ship manifests
- Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record — search county district court records
- **Content note:** Ship passenger manifests list every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax, poll tax, personal property
- **Date range:** From county formation (1850)
- **Where held:** County courthouses and California State Archives; not confirmed as digitized by this survey's tools
- **Substitute value:** Poll tax lists name adult male residents and can substitute for missing or destroyed census returns

### Great Registers (voter registration)
- **A California-specific record type.** From 1866, California required voters to register in county Great Registers, recording name, age, occupation, physical description, and nativity
- FamilySearch holds "California, Great Registers, 1866–1910" (1,345,678 records) — **indexed + images** (free)
- Though they begin in 1866 (outside this survey's window), they capture men present since the Gold Rush. A man in the 1866 register aged 36 with nativity "Ohio" was born ca. 1830 and likely arrived during the Gold Rush — a critical bridge backward to the 1850s

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County Births 1850–1919 (789,456 records); County Marriages 1850–1952 (567,890 records); Great Registers 1866–1910 (1,345,678 records); Mission Records 1769–1850 (98,765 records); State Census 1850–1852 (indexed + images); Mining Claim Registers 1849–1855 SF (browse-only); Port Arrival Registers 1849–1858 Sacramento (browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census 1850 and 1860 California | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical California newspapers | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | San Francisco ship passenger manifests; federal court records | Free/fee |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** 14 digitized volumes match California for 1848–1860; only the first 3 are detailed above (a `nextPageToken` was returned). The remaining 11 volumes were not examined in this survey and may include additional indexed or browse-only collections.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| California State Archives, Sacramento | State-level records, Mexican land grants, state agency records | In-person / online request |
| NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno | San Francisco ship passenger manifests, federal court records | In-person / appointment |
| California State Library, Sacramento | Manuscripts, Gold Rush diaries, newspapers, local histories | In-person |
| Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley | Extensive Gold Rush manuscript collections, diaries, journals, overland trail records | In-person / online finding aids |
