# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California became a U.S. state on September 9, 1850, bypassing territorial status. From 1848 to statehood it was under U.S. military governance following the Mexican–American War.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Sacramento (state capital from 1854); San Francisco as economic center
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mexico (to 1848), then United States
- **Population during period:** Approximately 92,597 enumerated in the 1850 federal census; Wikipedia reports roughly 300,000 migrants arrived 1848–1855
- **Economy:** Gold mining, agriculture, and trade; San Francisco and Sacramento grew rapidly as supply and financial hubs for the mining camps
- **Ethnic composition:** Highly diverse — American-born Anglo migrants, European (especially Irish, German, French), Chinese, Chilean, Mexican, Native Californian, and Australian populations
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (dominant among Spanish/Mexican-era population and many Irish miners); Protestant denominations (Methodist, Episcopal, Presbyterian, Baptist) established by Anglo settlers; Chinese temples in mining towns
- **Key historical events:** Gold discovered at Sutter's Mill, January 24, 1848; California statehood September 9, 1850; rapid county formation across the gold regions throughout the 1850s

## Boundary changes
- California entered the Union in 1850 with 27 original counties; numerous new counties were carved from these during the 1850s as population swelled in the Mother Lode region
- County lines in the gold regions (El Dorado, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Nevada, Placer, Amador) shifted repeatedly; a mining camp on one side of a line one year could fall in a different county the next
- Before statehood (1846–1850), U.S. military governance generated minimal civil records; Spanish/Mexican mission and land-grant records are the earlier administrative layer
- Records created under Mexican authority (land grants, mission registers) required a separate adjudication process under the U.S. Land Commission after 1851

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Civil registration was at the county level in California from statehood (1850). The FamilySearch Wiki pages specific to California returned only generic fallback content during this survey, so the exact statewide registration start date cannot be confirmed from this survey's tools. FamilySearch holds county-level births from 1850 and county marriages from 1850.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch "California, County Births, 1850–1919" (789,456 records, indexed + images); "California, County Marriages, 1850–1952" (567,890 records, indexed + images). No county death collection covering the 1850s was returned by this survey's tools.
- **Where held:** County courthouses; digitized collections on FamilySearch (free)
- **Gaps:** Coverage is uneven for mining camps, which were transient and often unincorporated; many births and deaths went unrecorded
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers, cemetery records, newspaper death and marriage notices, probate records naming next of kin

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mission church network and parishes serving Spanish/Mexican communities); Protestant denominations established during and after the Gold Rush. Specific founding dates in the gold regions were not returned by this survey's tools.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials
- **Where held:** The FamilySearch wiki_search result confirms the California State Library and Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley hold extensive Gold Rush-era manuscript collections including church materials (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records). FamilySearch holds "California, Mission Records, 1769–1850" (98,765 records, indexed + images) — this collection ends at the Gold Rush's start and is background context for Native Californian and Spanish/Mexican ancestors.
- **Language:** Mission records are in Spanish; later records predominantly in English

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The 1850 federal census — California's first — was partially destroyed; some county returns are missing (FamilySearch wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records). The 1860 federal census is the next complete enumeration.
- **State census:** California held a state census in 1852. FamilySearch has a digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 006601001, 522 images, 88% name-indexed, full-text searchable). **This is the most important census source for Gold Rush-era research** — it covers the gap left by the partially destroyed 1850 federal census.
- **Other enumerations:** Tax lists and mining claim registers function as proxy censuses for adult male residents in years between enumerations
- **Access:** 1852 state census — **indexed + images** on FamilySearch; 1850 federal census surviving returns — indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry; 1860 federal census — indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories; court records include naturalizations, mining disputes, civil suits
- **Testate or intestate:** For Gold Rush miners, intestate (no will) estates were common given the transient population — search administration files as well as wills
- **Date range:** From county formation (1850 for original counties)
- **Where held:** County courthouses and California State Archives. No digitized FamilySearch collection for California probate in this period was returned by this survey's tools — treat as physical or microfilm only pending further search.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal public domain (rectangular survey) for post-1848 U.S. grants; Spanish/Mexican-era land grants (ranchos) adjudicated before the U.S. Land Commission under a separate system
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal patents via the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office for post-1848 federal land; California State Archives for Mexican-era grant papers. The wiki_read for California_Land_and_Property returned only generic content — the specific California repository list was not confirmed from that page.
- **Types:** Federal land patents, Spanish/Mexican land grant documents, county deed books, mining claim registers, tax records
- **Date range:** U.S.-era records from 1848; earlier land grants from the Spanish/Mexican period
- **Where held:** BLM GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov) for federal patents (free); county recorders for deeds; California State Archives for Mexican land grants

### Mining claim records
- **A record type unique to Gold Rush research.** County recorders registered mining claims in dedicated registers. The FamilySearch wiki_search confirms these are held at county recorders (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records).
- FamilySearch has one digitized but **browse-only** volume for San Francisco County, 1849–1855 (imageGroupNumber 006601002, 340 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable) — must be browsed image by image with no name search
- Gold-region county recorders (El Dorado, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Nevada, Placer, Amador, Sacramento) hold original registers — largely physical access

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican–American War (ended 1848); Civil War (1861–1865, just after this window but many California residents enlisted)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants, and draft registrations at NARA; state militia records at the California State Archives
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 subscription database (https://www.fold3.com/)

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Mining-era cemeteries scattered across the Mother Lode counties; many are small, informal, and poorly documented
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) holds California cemetery transcriptions
- **Physical records:** Sexton and burial registers are highly incomplete for the 1850s given the transient mining population; many early burials were never formally recorded

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** San Francisco and Sacramento papers were active from 1848; numerous short-lived papers served individual mining camps
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/, subscription) for digitized papers; the California State Library and Bancroft Library hold microfilm of many papers
- **Content value:** Obituaries, death notices, mining news, arrival notices, legal notices (estate and probate), and advertisements that document residents

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** San Francisco (primary sea entry); Sacramento (river port)
- **Record types:** Ship passenger manifests for San Francisco arrivals held at NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno — wiki_search confirms this (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records). FamilySearch has a digitized but **browse-only** volume of Port Arrival Registers for Sacramento, 1849–1858 (imageGroupNumber 006601003, 298 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable)
- Overland trail migrants are documented through diaries, journals, and wagon train rosters at the California State Library and Bancroft Library — no centralized arrival record equivalent to ship manifests
- Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record — search county district court records
- **Content note:** Ship passenger manifests list every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax, poll tax, personal property
- **Date range:** From county formation (1850)
- **Where held:** County courthouses and California State Archives; not confirmed as digitized by this survey's tools
- **Substitute value:** Poll tax lists name adult male residents and can substitute for missing or destroyed census returns

### Great Registers (voter registration)
- **A California-specific record type.** From 1866, California required voters to register in county Great Registers, recording name, age, occupation, physical description, and nativity
- FamilySearch holds "California, Great Registers, 1866–1910" (1,345,678 records) — **indexed + images** (free)
- Though they begin in 1866 (outside this survey's window), they capture men present since the Gold Rush. A man in the 1866 register aged 36 with nativity "Ohio" was born ca. 1830 and likely arrived during the Gold Rush — a critical bridge backward to the 1850s

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |

| FamilySearch | County Births 1850–1919 (789,456 records); County Marriages 1850–1952 (567,890 records); Great Registers 1866–1910 (1,345,678 records); Mission Records 1769–1850 (98,765 records); State Census 1850–1852 (indexed + images); Mining Claim Registers 1849–1855 SF (browse-only); Port Arrival Registers 1849–1858 Sacramento (browse-only) | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** 14 digitized volumes match California for 1848–1860; only the first 3 are detailed above (a `nextPageToken` was returned). The remaining 11 volumes were not examined in this survey and may include additional indexed or browse-only collections.

# Locality Guide: New York City, New York (1700-1799)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Amsterdam established 1626 by the Dutch West India Company; seized by the English in 1664 and renamed New York City
- **County seat / administrative center:** New York City (Manhattan), seat of New York County
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New York Province (British colony, 1664-1783); State of New York (after 1783)
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this period
- **Economy:** Major commercial port and trade center; maritime trade, merchant shipping, crafts
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Dutch and English, with growing populations of German, French Huguenot, Jewish, Irish, and African (enslaved and free) residents
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (oldest), Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church), Presbyterian, Lutheran, French Reformed (Huguenot), Jewish (Shearith Israel), Baptist, Quaker
- **Key historical events:** British colonial rule throughout the century; American Revolution (1775-1783); British military occupation of NYC (1776-1783)

## Boundary changes
- New York City in the 1700s consisted principally of New York County (Manhattan). The surrounding counties — Kings (Brooklyn), Queens, and Richmond (Staten Island) — were administratively separate. Records for families in those areas are found at those county levels, not under NYC.
- The Bronx area was part of Westchester County during this period and was not part of New York City.
- Researchers uncertain which county an ancestor lived in should search all adjoining counties: Kings, Queens, Richmond, and Westchester. The neighboring counties table on the NYC wiki page was not returned during this survey.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** There was no civil vital registration in New York City or New York Province during the 1700s. The FamilySearch Wiki page on New York Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey and no specific registration start date can be cited.
- **What exists:** No civil birth, marriage, or death registers for 1700-1799.
- **Where held:** N/A — civil registration had not begun.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the only substitute; see Church Records below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Dutch Reformed (records from 1639), Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church, founded 1697), Presbyterian, Lutheran, French Reformed/Huguenot, Jewish (Shearith Israel congregation)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:**
  - FamilySearch collection "New York, Church Records, 1640-1940" (collection 1469062, 2,345,678 records): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062
  - One digitized volume: Dutch Reformed Church Registers, NYC, 1700-1776 (imageGroupNumber 007733180, 211 images) — **browse-only, in Dutch, 0% name-indexed**
  - The New York Genealogical & Biographical Society and the New-York Historical Society hold colonial-era church collections (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Language:** Dutch Reformed registers are in Dutch. Most other denomination records are in English.
- **Access level:** The FamilySearch Dutch Reformed volume is browse-only and in Dutch — no name index; must be read page by page with knowledge of colonial Dutch handwriting.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** No federal census during 1700-1799. The first federal census is 1790 (at the very end of this period) and names heads of household only.
- **Colonial enumerations:** No colonial census data was returned by the tools for NYC in this period.
- **Substitutes:** Tax assessment lists (by ward) and colonial militia rolls survive for some years and can place a person in a specific ward. Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records, militia rolls list men of military age.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianship
- **Key court:** The Prerogative Court of New York handled wills for the entire New York Province — not local courts. Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records, the New-York Historical Society's published Abstracts of Wills series indexes these records.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971" (collection 1542780, 987,654 records): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780
- **Mayor's Court:** Civil suits, guardianships, and other legal matters are in Mayor's Court records (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records), held at the New York State Archives.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (British colonial system)
- **Types:** Land conveyances, patents, grants, deeds; the New York Colonial Manuscripts at the New York State Archives include colonial-era land records
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Land Records, 1630-1975" (collection 2078654, 1,567,890 records): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Crown (via the Governor of New York Province) issued colonial land patents; the New York State Archives holds the Colonial Manuscripts series. Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records, land conveyances are a key source type for this period.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Queen Anne's War (1702-1713), King George's War (1744-1748), French and Indian War (1754-1763), American Revolution (1775-1783)
- **Record types:** Colonial militia rolls (by ward), Revolutionary War service records, pension files
- **Militia rolls:** Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records, colonial militia rolls list men of military age by ward and survive for some years.
- **Revolutionary War:** Service records and pension files are at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); New York State also maintained adjutant general records.
- **British occupation note:** NYC was under British military occupation 1776-1783; record-keeping may have been disrupted during this period.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Trinity Church cemetery (Anglican, one of NYC's oldest), Dutch Reformed churchyards, Shearith Israel burial ground
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers some colonial-era burial sites
- **Physical records:** Sexton and burial registers held at individual churches and the New-York Historical Society

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The New York Gazette (one of the earliest colonial newspapers) published during this period, per Wikipedia search
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/), New-York Historical Society
- **Content value:** Obituaries, legal notices, ship arrivals, runaway servant/slave notices, public announcements

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New York Harbor was a major colonial port of entry
- **Record types:** Ship manifests (colonial era); no systematic passenger lists comparable to post-1820 manifests. Port entry records are fragmentary.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could occur in any court of record including NYC's Mayor's Court or Court of Common Pleas; records held at the New York State Archives and NARA (https://www.archives.gov/).
- **Content note:** Colonial-era ship records are sparse compared to later periods. Church and land records often provide better evidence of immigrant origins.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Tax assessment lists by ward
- **Date range:** Lists survive for some years and wards during the 1700s (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records). The FamilySearch digitized collection begins at 1799.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799-1804" (collection 1678432, 123,456 records): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678432 — starts at the very end of the target period
- **Substitute value:** Can substitute for census coverage; organized by ward, not by name

### Other records
- **New York Colonial Manuscripts:** Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records, this series at the New York State Archives is a key source for British colonial-era administrative, land, and government records.
- **NY Genealogical & Biographical Society:** Holds extensive colonial collections; contact directly for holdings and access.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | New York, Church Records, 1640-1940 (collection 1469062) | Free |
| FamilySearch | New York, Land Records, 1630-1975 (collection 2078654) | Free |
| FamilySearch | New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971 (collection 1542780) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Dutch Reformed Church Registers, NYC, 1700-1776 (vol. 007733180) — browse-only, Dutch | Free |
| FamilySearch | New York, Tax Assessment Rolls, 1799-1804 (collection 1678432) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1790 only overlaps this period) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |
| NARA | National Archives — naturalization, military | Free to search |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for NYC 1700-1799 (totalResults: 1); this is the complete set returned by that query.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New York State Archives (Albany, NY) | New York Colonial Manuscripts, Mayor's Court records, colonial land and government records | In-person; some records online |
| New-York Historical Society (Manhattan) | Church records, Abstracts of Wills, newspapers, colonial-era collections | In-person; contact for holdings |
| NY Genealogical & Biographical Society (Manhattan) | Extensive colonial-era records, church registers, compiled genealogies | In-person or membership |
| Trinity Church Archives (Manhattan) | Anglican church records from 1697 | In-person or contact |
| New York County Clerk (Manhattan) | Deed books, court records | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Colonial militia rolls for most of the 1700s (physical, likely NY State Archives or NY Genealogical & Biographical Society)
- Most Mayor's Court civil records (physical, NY State Archives)
- NYC ward-level tax assessment lists for most of the 1700s (FamilySearch digitized collection starts at 1799)
- Most Anglican, Presbyterian, Lutheran, and Huguenot church records for this period (partially in FamilySearch collection 1469062, but not fully indexed)
- Colonial-era ship manifests and port entry records (fragmentary; physical at NARA or state archives)

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey identified specific record losses for NYC in the 1700s. The Revolutionary War period (1776-1783) and British military occupation of NYC may have caused disruption to record-keeping, but no tool result confirmed the destruction of any specific record series. Consult the New York State Archives and New-York Historical Society directly for information on gaps.

## Research tips
- Church records are the only source for births, marriages, and deaths in NYC during the 1700s — no civil vital registration existed. The Dutch Reformed Church has the oldest continuous register series. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- The Dutch Reformed Church registers on FamilySearch (vol. 007733180, 1700-1776) are in Dutch and browse-only — no name index. A reading knowledge of colonial Dutch handwriting is necessary.
- Wills probated in colonial New York were handled by the Prerogative Court of New York (province-wide, not local). The New-York Historical Society's Abstracts of Wills series indexes these. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- Tax assessment lists and militia rolls survive for some years organized by ward — these can document a person's presence even when no vital record exists. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- If an ancestor cannot be found in New York County records, search adjoining counties: Kings (Brooklyn), Queens, Richmond (Staten Island), and Westchester (the Bronx area). These were separate jurisdictions with their own record series.
- The New York Colonial Manuscripts at the New York State Archives are the primary source for colonial administrative and government records. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for all four wiki_place_page sections during this survey. The New York City Genealogy and New York state wiki pages may contain additional research guidance — visit them directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy

- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could occur in any court of record including NYC's Mayor's Court or Court of Common Pleas; records held at the New York State Archives and NARA (https://www.archives.gov/).
- **Content note:** Colonial-era ship records are sparse compared to later periods. Church and land records often provide better evidence of immigrant origins.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Tax assessment lists by ward
- **Date range:** Lists survive for some years and wards during the 1700s (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records). The FamilySearch digitized collection begins at 1799.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799-1804" (collection 1678432, 123,456 records): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678432 — starts at the very end of the target period
- **Substitute value:** Can substitute for census coverage; organized by ward, not by name

### Other records
- **New York Colonial Manuscripts:** Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records, this series at the New York State Archives is a key source for British colonial-era administrative, land, and government records.
- **NY Genealogical & Biographical Society:** Holds extensive colonial collections; contact directly for holdings and access.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | New York, Church Records, 1640-1940 (collection 1469062) | Free |
| FamilySearch | New York, Land Records, 1630-1975 (collection 2078654) | Free |
| FamilySearch | New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971 (collection 1542780) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Dutch Reformed Church Registers, NYC, 1700-1776 (vol. 007733180) — browse-only, Dutch | Free |
| FamilySearch | New York, Tax Assessment Rolls, 1799-1804 (collection 1678432) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1790 only overlaps this period) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |
| NARA | National Archives — naturalization, military | Free to search |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for NYC 1700-1799 (totalResults: 1); this is the complete set returned by that query.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New York State Archives (Albany, NY) | New York Colonial Manuscripts, Mayor's Court records, colonial land and government records | In-person; some records online |
| New-York Historical Society (Manhattan) | Church records, Abstracts of Wills, newspapers, colonial-era collections | In-person; contact for holdings |
| NY Genealogical & Biographical Society (Manhattan) | Extensive colonial-era records, church registers, compiled genealogies | In-person or membership |
| Trinity Church Archives (Manhattan) | Anglican church records from 1697 | In-person or contact |
| New York County Clerk (Manhattan) | Deed books, court records | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Colonial militia rolls for most of the 1700s (physical, likely NY State Archives or NY Genealogical & Biographical Society)
- Most Mayor's Court civil records (physical, NY State Archives)
- NYC ward-level tax assessment lists for most of the 1700s (FamilySearch digitized collection starts at 1799)
- Most Anglican, Presbyterian, Lutheran, and Huguenot church records for this period (partially in FamilySearch collection 1469062, but not fully indexed)
- Colonial-era ship manifests and port entry records (fragmentary; physical at NARA or state archives)

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey identified specific record losses for NYC in the 1700s. The Revolutionary War period (1776-1783) and British military occupation of NYC may have caused disruption to record-keeping, but no tool result confirmed the destruction of any specific record series. Consult the New York State Archives and New-York Historical Society directly for information on gaps.

## Research tips
- Church records are the only source for births, marriages, and deaths in NYC during the 1700s — no civil vital registration existed. The Dutch Reformed Church has the oldest continuous register series. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- The Dutch Reformed Church registers on FamilySearch (vol. 007733180, 1700-1776) are in Dutch and browse-only — no name index. A reading knowledge of colonial Dutch handwriting is necessary.
- Wills probated in colonial New York were handled by the Prerogative Court of New York (province-wide, not local). The New-York Historical Society's Abstracts of Wills series indexes these. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- Tax assessment lists and militia rolls survive for some years organized by ward — these can document a person's presence even when no vital record exists. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- If an ancestor cannot be found in New York County records, search adjoining counties: Kings (Brooklyn), Queens, Richmond (Staten Island), and Westchester (the Bronx area). These were separate jurisdictions with their own record series.
- The New York Colonial Manuscripts at the New York State Archives are the primary source for colonial administrative and government records. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for all four wiki_place_page sections during this survey. The New York City Genealogy and New York state wiki pages may contain additional research guidance — visit them directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy

Here is the locality guide for **Virginia during the American Revolutionary War (1775–1783)**:

---

## Virginia — American Revolution Research Guide (1775–1783)

### Key Context

This period predates civil registration anywhere in Virginia. Surviving records are mostly **county-level** (marriage bonds, court order books, deed and will books) and **church-level** (Anglican vestry books, Baptist and Presbyterian minute books), plus military-specific series.

**Critical warning:** Virginia's 1790 federal census was destroyed when Washington burned in 1814. The **1782 personal property and land tax lists** are the earliest population substitute and are essential for locating families after the war.

---

### Military Records — What Survives & Where

| Record Type | Repository | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Continental Line service records | NARA, Record Group 93 | Muster rolls, pay vouchers |
| Virginia militia records | Library of Virginia, Richmond | County-level service |
| **Pension files** | NARA, Record Group 15 | Often the richest single source — depositions frequently name the soldier's wife, birthplace, wartime county, and witnesses |
| Land bounty warrants | Library of Virginia / Virginia State Library | Veterans who received land grants in the Virginia Military District of Ohio left warrant records here |

---

### FamilySearch Collections to Search

| Collection | FamilySearch ID | Size | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783" | 1945678 | ~345,000 records | Indexed — best starting point |
| Revolutionary War land bounty warrants | vol. 005301447 | 341 images | Browse-only; no name index |

---

### County & Church Records

- **Deed and will books** often record land transactions made by soldiers before deployment or by widows afterward
- **Court order books** record oaths of loyalty, estates of soldiers who died, and guardian appointments
- **Anglican vestry books** (pre-disestablishment) and **Baptist/Presbyterian minute books** document vital events
- **Marriage bonds** at the county courthouse (or its microfilm equivalent) cover the war years

---

### Repository Summary

- **Library of Virginia (Richmond)** — militia records, land warrants, tax lists, county court records
- **NARA** — Continental service records (RG 93), pension files (RG 15)
- **FamilySearch.org** — five indexed collections for this period; also check the [Virginia Military Records Wiki page](https://familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records) directly
- **Virginia Military District of Ohio** warrant records — for veterans who took land bounties in Ohio

---

### Recommended Starting Strategy

1. Search **pension files** first — they are the most narrative and frequently identify family members and neighbors as witnesses.
2. Pull the **1782 tax lists** to place the family in a specific county.
3. Search the FamilySearch **"Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783"** collection (ID 1945678).
4. Follow up in county deed, will, and court order books at the Library of Virginia.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Virginia was one of the original thirteen colonies; it declared independence in 1776 and became the Commonwealth of Virginia.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Williamsburg (colonial capital); Richmond (state capital from 1780).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of Virginia (British Crown) before 1776; independent Commonwealth after.
- **Population during period:** No population figures returned by tools for 1775–1783.
- **Economy:** Tobacco plantation agriculture in the Tidewater; grain farming in the Piedmont and Valley; frontier settlement in the trans-Allegheny region.
- **Ethnic composition:** English, Scots-Irish, and German settlers; enslaved African Americans; small numbers of recent European immigrants.
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican (Protestant Episcopal after 1785), Baptist, Presbyterian, Quaker (Society of Friends), Methodist.
- **Key historical events:** American Revolution (1775–1783). Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony (Wikipedia); major engagements including Yorktown (1781) were fought on Virginia soil.

## Boundary changes
- Virginia's boundaries were largely stable during 1775–1783; its western frontier was actively contested and settled.
- Kentucky County was carved from Fincastle County in 1776; Kentucky became a separate state in 1792. Families in far-western Virginia may have records under predecessor counties.
- place_search_all returned no additional historical jurisdictions.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Virginia returned only generic content during this survey — no Virginia-specific registration date is available from a tool result. No statewide civil registration existed in 1775–1783.
- **What exists:** County-level marriage bonds and licenses; no statewide birth or death registration for this period.
- **Where held:** County courthouses; Library of Virginia; FamilySearch collection 'Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900' (id: 1734285, ~2,567,890 records).
- **Gaps:** Total absence of statewide vital registration; survival depends on individual county and church records.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; county marriage bonds; Bible records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican (Episcopal), Baptist, Presbyterian, Quaker, Methodist.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, vestry minutes (Anglican), meeting minutes (Quaker), membership rolls.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 'Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929' (id: 1598230, ~1,234,567 records); Library of Virginia; denominational archives.
- **Language:** English.
- **Note:** Anglican vestry books recorded births, marriages, and deaths before civil registration. Quaker meeting records are especially complete for Quaker families.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census was 1790, after the target period. Virginia's 1790 census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands). No federal census exists for 1775–1783.
- **State/provincial census:** None returned by tools for this period.
- **Other enumerations:** Virginia conducted annual personal property and land tax enumerations from 1782; these are the primary substitute for the missing 1790 census.
- **Access:** FamilySearch volume 005301449 (State enumerations/tax lists, 1782–1799, 87 images) is full-text searchable but not name-indexed — must be browsed; classified as full-text searchable, not name-indexed.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, guardianship orders, letters of administration; county court minute books.
- **Date range:** County courts functioned from the colonial period through and beyond the Revolution.
- **Where held:** County courthouses; Library of Virginia (microfilm); FamilySearch collections 1734285 and 2134567 ('Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920', ~1,789,012 records). FamilySearch volume 005301448 (Augusta County court order books, 1775–1795, 158 images) is 61% name-indexed — indexed + images (partially).
- **Note:** County court minute books record road assignments, indigent relief, and local business naming individuals not party to any suit.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Virginia is not a federal land state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages returned only generic content — Virginia-specific land office details cannot be cited from a tool result. The Library of Virginia holds colonial-era and Commonwealth patent records.
- **Types:** Land patents, deeds, grants, tax records, Revolutionary War bounty land warrants. FamilySearch volume 005301447 (Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, 1779–1800, 341 images) is browse-only — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.
- **Post-war bounty:** Virginia granted bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio to veterans. Warrant and survey records at the Virginia State Library connect veterans to land claims (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; county deed books at courthouses; FamilySearch collection 1734285.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolution (1775–1783).
- **Record types:**
  - Continental Line service records and muster rolls: NARA Record Group 93
  - Virginia militia records: Library of Virginia, Richmond
  - Pension and bounty-land warrant application files: NARA Record Group 15
  - Virginia State Navy records: published series
  - (All per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)
- **FamilySearch collection:** 'Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783' (id: 1945678, ~345,678 records).
- **Digitized volume:** FamilySearch 005301447 (Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, 1779–1800, 341 images) — browse-only.
- **Online:** Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) hosts military service and pension files; NARA (https://www.archives.gov/).

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Church graveyards (Anglican/Episcopal, Presbyterian, Baptist, Quaker); plantation family burial grounds.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/).
- **Physical records:** Sexton records vary by congregation; many 18th-century graves are known only from transcription projects or physical inspection.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg) was the principal newspaper during the Revolutionary period.
- **Content value:** Estate notices, military notices, runaway advertisements, marriage announcements.
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; Colonial Williamsburg Foundation; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for some digitized holdings.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Norfolk and Alexandria.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists; for families with Loyalist connections, emigration records to Britain or Canada in British Colonial Office records.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Library of Virginia; The National Archives, UK, for Loyalist records.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard including children traveling with parents. Examine full manifests for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Personal property and land tax lists, conducted annually from 1782.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 1456723 ('Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850', ~456,789 records); volume 005301449 (State enumerations/tax lists, 1782–1799, 87 images, full-text searchable but not name-indexed).
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; county courthouses; FamilySearch collection 1456723.
- **Substitute value:** 1782+ tax lists are the primary substitute for the destroyed 1790 census; they identify heads of household and often note adult male tithables.

### Other record types
- **Loyalist claims:** Families with Loyalist ties may have filed with the British Claims Commission — records at The National Archives, UK. These often document property, relationships, and wartime movements.
- **Vestry records and overseers of the poor:** Anglican vestry books recorded poor relief, naming individuals absent from other series.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Military Records 1775–1783 (id: 1945678); Church Records 1680–1929 (id: 1598230); Land/Marriage/Will Records 1600–1900 (id: 1734285); Tax Records 1782–1850 (id: 1456723); County Court Records 1650–1920 (id: 2134567) | Free |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War service records, pension files, muster rolls | Subscription |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census and other records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including the Virginia Gazette | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | RG 93 (service/muster rolls), RG 15 (pensions/bounty land) | Online request / in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 3 digitized volumes matching Virginia in the 1775–1800 range; totalResults: 3, which is the complete set — no further pages. No summary block was returned by volume_search despite requesting one.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia militia records, county deed/will/order books, church registers on microfilm, tax lists | In-person / online catalog |
| National Archives (NARA) | Continental Line RG 93, pensions and bounty-land RG 15 | In-person (Washington, DC) / online request |
| Virginia county courthouses | Original deed books, will books, court order books, marriage bonds | In-person / mail request |
| Denominational archives | Baptist, Presbyterian, Quaker, Episcopal registers | Contact individual archives |
| The National Archives, UK | Loyalist Claims Commission records, British Colonial Office emigration records | Online / in-person (Kew, London) |

## Records NOT online
- Virginia militia service records (Library of Virginia) are not fully available online.
- Virginia State Navy records exist in published form; originals are at state repositories.
- County marriage bonds for many Virginia counties have not been digitized.
- Loyalist claim files at The National Archives, UK, are not on US genealogy platforms.

# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Virginia was one of the original thirteen colonies; it declared independence in 1776 and became the Commonwealth of Virginia.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Williamsburg (colonial capital); Richmond (state capital from 1780).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of Virginia (British Crown) before 1776; independent Commonwealth after.
- **Population during period:** No population figures returned by tools for 1775–1783.
- **Economy:** Tobacco plantation agriculture in the Tidewater; grain farming in the Piedmont and Valley; frontier settlement in the trans-Allegheny region.
- **Ethnic composition:** English, Scots-Irish, and German settlers; enslaved African Americans; small numbers of recent European immigrants.
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican (Protestant Episcopal after 1785), Baptist, Presbyterian, Quaker (Society of Friends), Methodist.
- **Key historical events:** American Revolution (1775–1783). Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony (Wikipedia); major engagements including Yorktown (1781) were fought on Virginia soil.

## Boundary changes
- Virginia's boundaries were largely stable during 1775–1783; its western frontier was actively contested and settled.
- Kentucky County was carved from Fincastle County in 1776; Kentucky became a separate state in 1792. Families in far-western Virginia may have records under predecessor counties.
- place_search_all returned no additional historical jurisdictions.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Virginia returned only generic content during this survey — no Virginia-specific registration date is available from a tool result. No statewide civil registration existed in 1775–1783.
- **What exists:** County-level marriage bonds and licenses; no statewide birth or death registration for this period.
- **Where held:** County courthouses; Library of Virginia; FamilySearch collection 'Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900' (id: 1734285, ~2,567,890 records).
- **Gaps:** Total absence of statewide vital registration; survival depends on individual county and church records.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; county marriage bonds; Bible records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican (Episcopal), Baptist, Presbyterian, Quaker, Methodist.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, vestry minutes (Anglican), meeting minutes (Quaker), membership rolls.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 'Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929' (id: 1598230, ~1,234,567 records); Library of Virginia; denominational archives.
- **Language:** English.
- **Note:** Anglican vestry books recorded births, marriages, and deaths before civil registration. Quaker meeting records are especially complete for Quaker families.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census was 1790, after the target period. Virginia's 1790 census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands). No federal census exists for 1775–1783.
- **State/provincial census:** None returned by tools for this period.
- **Other enumerations:** Virginia conducted annual personal property and land tax enumerations from 1782; these are the primary substitute for the missing 1790 census.
- **Access:** FamilySearch volume 005301449 (State enumerations/tax lists, 1782–1799, 87 images) is full-text searchable but not name-indexed — must be browsed; classified as full-text searchable, not name-indexed.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, guardianship orders, letters of administration; county court minute books.
- **Date range:** County courts functioned from the colonial period through and beyond the Revolution.
- **Where held:** County courthouses; Library of Virginia (microfilm); FamilySearch collections 1734285 and 2134567 ('Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920', ~1,789,012 records). FamilySearch volume 005301448 (Augusta County court order books, 1775–1795, 158 images) is 61% name-indexed — indexed + images (partially).
- **Note:** County court minute books record road assignments, indigent relief, and local business naming individuals not party to any suit.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Virginia is not a federal land state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages returned only generic content — Virginia-specific land office details cannot be cited from a tool result. The Library of Virginia holds colonial-era and Commonwealth patent records.
- **Types:** Land patents, deeds, grants, tax records, Revolutionary War bounty land warrants. FamilySearch volume 005301447 (Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, 1779–1800, 341 images) is browse-only — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.
- **Post-war bounty:** Virginia granted bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio to veterans. Warrant and survey records at the Virginia State Library connect veterans to land claims (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; county deed books at courthouses; FamilySearch collection 1734285.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolution (1775–1783).
- **Record types:**
  - Continental Line service records and muster rolls: NARA Record Group 93
  - Virginia militia records: Library of Virginia, Richmond
  - Pension and bounty-land warrant application files: NARA Record Group 15
  - Virginia State Navy records: published series
  - (All per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)
- **FamilySearch collection:** 'Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783' (id: 1945678, ~345,678 records).
- **Digitized volume:** FamilySearch 005301447 (Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, 1779–1800, 341 images) — browse-only.
- **Online:** Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) hosts military service and pension files; NARA (https://www.archives.gov/).

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Church graveyards (Anglican/Episcopal, Presbyterian, Baptist, Quaker); plantation family burial grounds.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/).
- **Physical records:** Sexton records vary by congregation; many 18th-century graves are known only from transcription projects or physical inspection.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg) was the principal newspaper during the Revolutionary period.
- **Content value:** Estate notices, military notices, runaway advertisements, marriage announcements.
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; Colonial Williamsburg Foundation; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for some digitized holdings.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Norfolk and Alexandria.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists; for families with Loyalist connections, emigration records to Britain or Canada in British Colonial Office records.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Library of Virginia; The National Archives, UK, for Loyalist records.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard including children traveling with parents. Examine full manifests for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Personal property and land tax lists, conducted annually from 1782.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 1456723 ('Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850', ~456,789 records); volume 005301449 (State enumerations/tax lists, 1782–1799, 87 images, full-text searchable but not name-indexed).
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; county courthouses; FamilySearch collection 1456723.
- **Substitute value:** 1782+ tax lists are the primary substitute for the destroyed 1790 census; they identify heads of household and often note adult male tithables.

### Other record types
- **Loyalist claims:** Families with Loyalist ties may have filed with the British Claims Commission — records at The National Archives, UK. These often document property, relationships, and wartime movements.
- **Vestry records and overseers of the poor:** Anglican vestry books recorded poor relief, naming individuals absent from other series.

Locality guide written as **loc_001**. Here's what it covers:

---

## New Orleans, Early 1800s — Record Survival and Substitutes

**The core disasters:** Two catastrophic fires in 1788 and 1794 destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial-era records. Despite those losses, researchers have three main surviving pillars:

### What Survived

1. **St. Louis Cathedral Sacramental Registers** — Baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1731 (with gaps from the fires). On FamilySearch: *Louisiana Church Records 1718–1925* (~987,654 indexed records with images).

2. **Notarial Acts** — Over 30 million pages dating to 1734, held at the **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center**. One digitized volume on FamilySearch covers 1803–1820, but it must be browsed image-by-image (no name search); it's in French and English. Records outside that window require a visit or mail request to the Notarial Archives.

3. **Cabildo Records** — Spanish colonial government records that also survived both fires.

---

### Where to Look

- **FamilySearch** — *Louisiana Church Records 1718–1925* and *Probate Records 1756–1984* (456,789 indexed records with images) both cover the 1800–1850 window.
- **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** — Essential for property, contracts, manumissions, and other civil-law acts outside the FamilySearch digitized window.

---

### Critical Vocabulary Note

Louisiana used the **Napoleonic Code (civil law)**, not common law. This changes the terminology entirely:
- "Probate" → **successions**
- "Guardianship" → **tutorships**
- "Legal incompetency" → **interdictions**

Searching with common-law terms will return nothing.

---

### Recommended Next Steps

- Consult the FamilySearch Wiki pages directly:

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800-1850)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Orleans was founded in 1718. The Louisiana Purchase (1803) transferred sovereignty to the United States. Orleans Territory was organized in 1804; Louisiana achieved statehood in 1812.
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans is coterminous with Orleans Parish (the Louisiana equivalent of a county). There is no separate county seat.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Orleans Parish, Louisiana. Pre-1812: Orleans Territory. Pre-1803: French and Spanish colonial governance.
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by survey tools.
- **Economy:** One of the largest ports in North America; central to cotton and sugar trade.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creoles, Spanish, free people of color (gens de couleur libres), enslaved Africans, Anglo-Americans arriving after 1803, and immigrants from France, Germany, Ireland, and the Caribbean.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic predominant (St. Louis Cathedral); Protestant denominations established after 1803.
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase 1803; Louisiana statehood 1812; Battle of New Orleans 1815; recurrent yellow fever epidemics throughout the period.

## Boundary changes
- Pre-1803: Spanish then briefly French colonial administration.
- 1803: Louisiana Purchase — New Orleans transferred to the United States.
- 1804: Orleans Territory organized.
- 1812: Louisiana statehood.
- Louisiana's civil-law (Napoleonic Code) system carried over from the French and Spanish colonial periods and remains in effect, making Louisiana's legal records unlike those of any other U.S. state.

## Known record losses and what survived

Two catastrophic fires struck New Orleans in 1788 and 1794 and destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial records. Despite those losses, significant sources survive for the early 1800s (per FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters):

- **St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers** — baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1731, with gaps caused by the fires.
- **Notarial records** — survived the fires and are an exceptionally rich substitute for missing vital and civil records.
- **Cabildo records** — records of the Spanish colonial governing body survived.
- **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734.

No tool result in this survey identified losses specific to a record set within the 1800–1850 period itself. For any series where an online search returns nothing, contact the holding repository — a negative online result is a coverage gap, not proof of destruction.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Louisiana Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey; the specific year Louisiana required civil vital registration at the state level could not be confirmed from tool results.
- **What exists:** Church (sacramental) records are the primary source for births/baptisms, marriages, and burials during 1800–1850. The **Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925** collection on FamilySearch (collection 1612905) contains 987,654 indexed records with 493,827 images and covers the entire target period.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (indexed + images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905. Physical originals at the Archdiocese of New Orleans archives and St. Louis Cathedral.
- **Gaps:** Fires of 1788 and 1794 created gaps in pre-1800 sacramental registers; post-fire registers survive with gaps through the early 1800s.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant — St. Louis Cathedral from the colonial era); Protestant denominations present from 1803 onward.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Catholic registers also sometimes record enslaved persons' baptisms.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch — Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (collection 1612905, 987,654 records, 493,827 images, indexed + images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905. Originals at the Archdiocese of New Orleans archives.
- **Language:** Records from the colonial period and early statehood are frequently in French or Spanish. The researcher must read the original language or obtain a transcription.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Louisiana was enumerated starting with the 1810 federal census (first after the territory's incorporation). The 1820, 1830, 1840, and 1850 censuses cover Orleans Parish. The 1800 census does not cover Louisiana (not yet U.S. territory).
- **Mortality schedules:** Begin with 1850.
- **Access:** FamilySearch and Ancestry hold the federal census enumerations. No specific Louisiana state census collections for 1800–1850 were returned by survey tools.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Louisiana uses civil-law terminology — "successions" (probate of an estate), "tutorships" (guardianship of minors), and "interdictions" (legal incompetency). Search under these terms.
- **Date range:** The **Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984** collection on FamilySearch (collection 2078341) covers the full target period; it contains 456,789 indexed records with 228,394 images (indexed + images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341.
- **Where held:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court; Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge holds territorial and early state records (per FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Louisiana uses the French arpent system for older surveys, and later U.S. rectangular survey for federal land grants.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Notarial acts are the primary vehicle for property transfers in Louisiana's civil-law system.
- **Types:** Notarial acts cover property sales, contracts, wills (successions), and more. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages from 1734.
- **Digitized:** FamilySearch holds 1 digitized volume of Orleans Parish Notarial Acts covering 1803-1820 (image group 004990115, 167 images). This volume is **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) and in French and English. The researcher must browse image by image — there is no name search.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (physical, with some digitized material online). Acts outside the 1803-1820 window require an in-person visit or mail request to the Notarial Archives Research Center.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812; Battle of New Orleans (January 8, 1815).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants at NARA. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) indexes some War of 1812 records online.
- **Where held:** NARA for federal records; Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge for state militia records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (oldest surviving, est. 1789), St. Louis Cemetery No. 2, and others established in the early 19th century.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) indexes many New Orleans burial sites.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at the archdiocese or individual cemetery offices.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** New Orleans had active newspapers in the early 1800s. Specific digitized holdings were not returned by survey tools.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com) for some digitized issues. The Louisiana State Library and Tulane University hold microfilm and physical collections.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, estate notices, and sheriff's sale notices naming debtors are all genealogically significant.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was one of the largest U.S. ports of entry in the early 1800s, receiving immigrants from France, Spain, Germany, Ireland, and the Caribbean.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists and naturalization petitions (declarations of intention filed in any court of record pre-1906). The **Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964** (collection 1543892, 2,345,678 records, index only, no images) may name foreign-born decedents: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1543892.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard including infants and children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest when researching a family.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Orleans Parish tax lists exist for the early 1800s.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives and Orleans Parish Civil District Court. No specific digitized collection for Orleans Parish tax records was returned by survey tools.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for census years and confirm residency.

### Other record types
- **Notarial acts as vital-record substitutes:** Notarial acts record births, marriages, contracts, property sales, and manumissions in one archive — they are the single most important record type for early 19th-century New Orleans when civil vital registration was absent.
- **Enslaved persons:** For enslaved individuals, Catholic baptismal registers, bills of sale, and plantation records within notarial acts may be the only surviving sources.

| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census 1810-1850; Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837-1957 (567,890 records, 283,945 images) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records — War of 1812 | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger lists, naturalization records, federal military records | Free / in-person |

FamilySearch's full holdings for this area and period may be larger — only that volume was returned. Collections_search operates at the Louisiana state level and returned 4 collections overlapping the 1800-1850 period.

### Physical repositories

| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734 | In-person; some digitized |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial and early state records | In-person / online request |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Catholic sacramental records | In-person / by appointment |
| Orleans Parish Civil District Court | Succession (probate) and court records | In-person |
| NARA Southeast Region (Atlanta) | Federal records for Louisiana | In-person / mail request |

## Records NOT online
- Notarial acts 1821-1850 (physical only at New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center)
- Orleans Parish tax lists (no digitized collection returned by survey tools)
- Many newspaper issues from this period (not yet fully digitized)
- Detailed sacramental register images beyond what FamilySearch collection 1612905 provides

**Boston 1840s Immigration Records**

Locality guide written as **loc_001**.

Boston in the 1840s was one of the five major American ports of entry, receiving tens of thousands of Irish Famine immigrants. The most direct records are the **Customs passenger lists** (NARA Record Group 36), which cover the Port of Boston from 1820 to 1891 and are indexed on FamilySearch as *"Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891"* (roughly 1.2 million records) and also on Ancestry. One digitized volume on FamilySearch (389 images, 1840–1850) is full-text searchable but only 3% name-indexed, so searching by name alone will miss most entries — browse the images or use full-text search.

After the passenger list, the key corroborating records are:

- **1850 federal census** — first census to name every household member
- **Naturalization papers** filed in any Massachusetts court before 1906 (FamilySearch collection 1459213, ~346,000 records)
- **Catholic parish registers** held at the Archdiocese of Boston archives
- **Boston Pilot Missing Persons database** (1831–1921) — the single best tool for Irish immigrants who can't be found in a manifest

**Two important warnings:**
1. 1840s passenger lists give only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — no Irish townland or parish is recorded. You'll need church records or a naturalization file to push further back.
2. Massachusetts registered vital events at the **town level**, so search for the specific town of settlement, not just "Boston."

When you're ready, the next step is to build a research plan targeting the specific immigrant ancestor using these source classes.

Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston

Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record in Massachusetts — federal district, state superior, municipal, or local probate courts — not just federal court. Search all courts for the town of settlement, not just one.
