entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Boston, Massachusetts — Port of Entry (1840–1859)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Boston incorporated as a city in 1822 (town from 1630); Suffolk County formed 1643
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston is both city and county seat of Suffolk County
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Suffolk County, Massachusetts
- **Population during period:** Boston's population was approximately 93,000 in 1840 and 136,000 in 1850 (Wikipedia); by 1850 over a quarter of residents were Irish-born
- **Economy:** Maritime trade, textile finishing, manufacturing; the port was a commercial hub and a primary immigrant landing point
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Anglo-American in 1840; massive Irish influx 1845–1852 during the Great Famine; smaller German, Canadian, and British immigrant streams
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist, Unitarian, Episcopal, Roman Catholic (surging Irish arrivals drove rapid Catholic parish growth), Methodist, Baptist, Jewish congregation from 1840s
- **Key historical events:** Irish Great Famine (1845–1852) drove the largest single immigrant surge Boston had seen; the city and surrounding mill towns were transformed; Pilot newspaper began Missing Persons notices 1831

## Boundary changes
- Boston city and Suffolk County boundaries were stable throughout the 1840s and 1850s
- Charlestown, Roxbury, Dorchester, Brighton, and West Roxbury were still independent towns in the 1840s and were annexed only later (Charlestown 1874; Roxbury 1868; etc.); records for those communities during the target period are under their own town records, not Boston's

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Registration level and start:** Massachusetts required towns to register births, marriages, and deaths. The FamilySearch Wiki specific to Massachusetts vital records could not be reached with a specific page during this survey (all attempts returned a generic fallback); consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records directly for the precise statewide registration date and level.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch has the collection 'Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890' (collection 2061550, approximately 3.4 million records) covering births, marriages, and deaths registered at the town level. Boston registrations are within this collection.
- **Where held:** Town clerk records; digitized via FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550). The Massachusetts State Archives holds original registers.
- **Gaps:** Immigrant arrivals in the 1840s were often not registered for births occurring at sea or shortly after landing; the town-level system depended on voluntary compliance in the early years
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary alternative and often predate or substitute for civil records for Irish Catholic immigrants

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Cathedral of the Holy Cross, St. Patrick's Church, and other parishes founded during the famine wave); Congregationalist; Unitarian; Episcopal; Baptist; Methodist; Jewish congregation
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Catholic registers from the 1840s onward are held at the Archdiocese of Boston archives. FamilySearch has 'Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920' (collection 1921657, approximately 988,000 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657). Not all parishes are digitized — check whether the specific parish of interest has been microfilmed. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston
- **Language:** English for most denominations; early Irish Catholic records may include Latin sacramental entries

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1840 (lists head of household only; individuals not named) and 1850 (first census naming all household members, including birthplace and age — critical for 1840s arrivals). Both fall within the target window.
- **State census:** Massachusetts conducted a state census in 1855 and 1865; these can help locate immigrants who do not appear in the 1850 federal census or who moved between 1850 and 1860
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1850 mortality schedule records deaths in the year preceding enumeration (June 1849–June 1850) — useful for immigrants who died shortly after arrival
- **Access:** 1840 and 1850 federal censuses are indexed and free on FamilySearch; also on Ancestry (subscription)

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories
- **Where held:** Suffolk County Probate Court; FamilySearch has 'Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991' (collection 1678901, approximately 568,000 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901)
- **Value for immigrants:** Probate files can name relatives still in Ireland and confirm relationships not documented in passenger lists

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (colonial-era New England system)
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records
- **Where held:** Suffolk County Registry of Deeds. Not substantially digitized for the 1840s on FamilySearch; physical or in-person access required for deed books
- **Substitute value:** Tax records can place an immigrant in a specific ward or address between census years

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846-1848); some Massachusetts immigrants served
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA; Massachusetts adjutant general records at Massachusetts State Archives
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) and Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for federal records; Massachusetts State Archives for state-level service records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Catholic Cemetery Association of the Archdiocese of Boston (Holy Cross Cemetery, Cambridge Cemetery, others); Mount Auburn Cemetery (non-sectarian, Cambridge); Copp's Hill Burying Ground (older, non-Catholic)
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has partial coverage; not all 1840s burials are indexed
- **Physical records:** Sexton and burial registers held by individual cemeteries and the Archdiocese; many have not been digitized

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Boston Pilot (Irish Catholic, published 1838 onward) is the single most important newspaper for this immigrant group — it ran 'Missing Persons' notices from 1831 to 1921 placed by Irish immigrants seeking separated relatives, and published arrival notices. The Boston Daily Atlas, Boston Post, and Boston Herald were also in circulation.
- **Where held:** The Pilot Missing Persons database is searchable online; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and ProQuest Historical Newspapers hold digitized runs; the Boston Public Library holds microfilm
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (naturalization), arrival columns, and missing-persons advertisements are all genealogically critical for this population

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** The Port of Boston was one of five major US ports of entry in the 1840s; customs passenger lists for Boston cover 1820-1891 and are in NARA Record Group 36. The National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA) holds the originals. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston
- **Record types:** Customs passenger lists (arrival manifests); declarations of intention (first papers); naturalization petitions (second papers)
- **FamilySearch collections:**
  - 'Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891' (collection 1784312, approximately 1.2 million records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312) — indexed and searchable by name
  - Digitized volume 003345210 (389 images, 1840-1850, Port of Boston): 3% name-indexed, full-text searchable — this volume must be searched via full-text or browsed image by image; it is not reliably found through a name search alone
  - 'Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790-1906' (collection 1459213, approximately 346,000 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213)
- **Content note:** 1840s customs passenger lists record only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — not the town of origin, last residence, or US contact. Passenger lists for the entire manifest must be examined because infants and young children traveling with parents are listed alongside adults.
- **Also search:** Ancestry.com holds indexed passenger lists for this period and often catches names FamilySearch misses; NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for original microfilm

### Tax records
- **Types:** City of Boston ward tax books (property and poll tax); Suffolk County tax records
- **Where held:** City of Boston Archives; Massachusetts State Archives. Not substantially digitized; physical access required
- **Substitute value:** Ward tax books can locate an immigrant in a specific address and year, bridging gaps between census enumerations

### Other record types
- **City directories:** Boston city directories were published annually from the 1820s onward and list male heads of household and boarding-house residents by name and address — a key intercensal tool. Many are digitized at Archive.org and on Ancestry
- **Almshouse and poor-relief records:** Boston's Overseers of the Poor kept detailed records of relief recipients; many newly arrived Irish immigrants appear here. Held at Massachusetts State Archives
- **Hospital records:** Massachusetts General Hospital and Boston City Hospital served the immigrant population; admissions registers may survive

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts Passenger Lists 1820-1891 (coll. 1784312); Naturalization Records 1790-1906 (coll. 1459213); Church Records 1630-1920 (coll. 1921657); Town Vital Records 1620-1890 (coll. 2061550); Probate Records 1635-1991 (coll. 1678901) | Free |
| Ancestry | Passenger lists, federal census, city directories, newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Customs passenger lists RG 36; naturalization records | Free to access finding aids; some records fee-based |
| Newspapers.com | Boston-area historical newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service and pension records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records (partial) | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search for the 1840-1859 period at the Boston/Suffolk County level returned 1 digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 003345210, 389 images, 1840-1850, Port of Boston passenger lists). This is the complete result set for that query. The indexed collections in collections_search cover a broader swath.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Boston, Waltham, MA | Original customs passenger lists, naturalization records | In-person; some records reproduced on request |
| Massachusetts State Archives, Boston | Vital records, probate, court records, almshouse/poor relief | In-person; some finding aids online |
| Suffolk County Registry of Deeds, Boston | Deed books | In-person; some volumes online |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives | Catholic parish registers 1840s onward | Written request; not open-stack |
| Boston Public Library | Newspaper microfilm, city directories, local histories | In-person; some digitized |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS) | Manuscript collections, vital records, compiled genealogies | In-person and online (American Ancestors subscription) |

## Records NOT online
- City of Boston ward tax books (1840s) — held at City of Boston Archives; physical access only
- Most Catholic parish burial and baptismal registers from individual parishes (only a subset is in the FamilySearch church records collection)
- Almshouse and Overseers of the Poor records — Massachusetts State Archives; physical access
- Suffolk County Probate original files — partially digitized; older volumes may require in-person access
- Boston City Hospital and Massachusetts General Hospital admissions registers — institutional archives

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated destruction of a specific Boston record set for the 1840s. An empty search result represents a digitization gap, not confirmed loss. The fate of specific record sets not yet digitized is unknown from tool results; contact the repositories listed above.

## Research tips
- **Start with the passenger list, then work forward.** The 1840s customs passenger list gives country of origin but rarely a county or parish; use the date of arrival and ship name to locate the manifest, then use the 1850 census (which names all household members) to confirm family composition and ages, and naturalization records to firm up the timeline. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston
- **Search the Boston Pilot Missing Persons database** before concluding an Irish immigrant cannot be found. The database covers notices placed 1831-1921 by immigrants in North America seeking relatives, and it names townlands and parishes of origin not found in any passenger list.
- **Use the 1855 Massachusetts state census** to bridge the gap between the 1850 and 1860 federal censuses — it captures immigrants who may have died, moved, or changed spelling of their name between the two federal enumerations.
- **Check Catholic parish registers at the Archdiocese of Boston archives.** For Irish Catholics, baptismal and marriage registers from parishes like Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's can predate or substitute for civil records and may name godparents or witnesses who are kin. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston
- **Pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered.** A declaration of intention filed in Boston Municipal Court and a petition filed years later in Suffolk County Superior Court may each be in a different repository and collection — search all Massachusetts court series in collection 1459213 and at the National Archives at Boston.
- **Examine the full manifest, not just the target name.** 1840s manifests list all passengers on a voyage; family groups traveling together are listed sequentially and an entry for a 2-year-old child will appear alongside adult entries but may be the only record of that child's arrival.

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Boston, Massachusetts — Port of Entry (1840–1859)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Boston incorporated as a city in 1822 (town from 1630); Suffolk County formed 1643
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston is both city and county seat of Suffolk County
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Suffolk County, Massachusetts
- **Population during period:** Boston's population was approximately 93,000 in 1840 and 136,000 in 1850 (Wikipedia); by 1850 over a quarter of residents were Irish-born
- **Economy:** Maritime trade, textile finishing, manufacturing; the port was a commercial hub and a primary immigrant landing point
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Anglo-American in 1840; massive Irish influx 1845–1852 during the Great Famine; smaller German, Canadian, and British immigrant streams
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist, Unitarian, Episcopal, Roman Catholic (surging Irish arrivals drove rapid Catholic parish growth), Methodist, Baptist, Jewish congregation from 1840s
- **Key historical events:** Irish Great Famine (1845–1852) drove the largest single immigrant surge Boston had seen; the city and surrounding mill towns were transformed; Pilot newspaper began Missing Persons notices 1831

## Boundary changes
- Boston city and Suffolk County boundaries were stable throughout the 1840s and 1850s
- Charlestown, Roxbury, Dorchester, Brighton, and West Roxbury were still independent towns in the 1840s and were annexed only later (Charlestown 1874; Roxbury 1868; etc.); records for those communities during the target period are under their own town records, not Boston's

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Registration level and start:** Massachusetts required towns to register births, marriages, and deaths. The FamilySearch Wiki specific to Massachusetts vital records could not be reached with a specific page during this survey (all attempts returned a generic fallback); consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records directly for the precise statewide registration date and level.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch has the collection 'Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890' (collection 2061550, approximately 3.4 million records) covering births, marriages, and deaths registered at the town level. Boston registrations are within this collection.
- **Where held:** Town clerk records; digitized via FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550). The Massachusetts State Archives holds original registers.
- **Gaps:** Immigrant arrivals in the 1840s were often not registered for births occurring at sea or shortly after landing; the town-level system depended on voluntary compliance in the early years
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary alternative and often predate or substitute for civil records for Irish Catholic immigrants

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Cathedral of the Holy Cross, St. Patrick's Church, and other parishes founded during the famine wave); Congregationalist; Unitarian; Episcopal; Baptist; Methodist; Jewish congregation
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Catholic registers from the 1840s onward are held at the Archdiocese of Boston archives. FamilySearch has 'Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920' (collection 1921657, approximately 988,000 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657). Not all parishes are digitized — check whether the specific parish of interest has been microfilmed. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston
- **Language:** English for most denominations; early Irish Catholic records may include Latin sacramental entries

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1840 (lists head of household only; individuals not named) and 1850 (first census naming all household members, including birthplace and age — critical for 1840s arrivals). Both fall within the target window.
- **State census:** Massachusetts conducted a state census in 1855 and 1865; these can help locate immigrants who do not appear in the 1850 federal census or who moved between 1850 and 1860
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1850 mortality schedule records deaths in the year preceding enumeration (June 1849–June 1850) — useful for immigrants who died shortly after arrival
- **Access:** 1840 and 1850 federal censuses are indexed and free on FamilySearch; also on Ancestry (subscription)

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories
- **Where held:** Suffolk County Probate Court; FamilySearch has 'Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991' (collection 1678901, approximately 568,000 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901)
- **Value for immigrants:** Probate files can name relatives still in Ireland and confirm relationships not documented in passenger lists

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (colonial-era New England system)
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records
- **Where held:** Suffolk County Registry of Deeds. Not substantially digitized for the 1840s on FamilySearch; physical or in-person access required for deed books
- **Substitute value:** Tax records can place an immigrant in a specific ward or address between census years

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846-1848); some Massachusetts immigrants served
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA; Massachusetts adjutant general records at Massachusetts State Archives
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) and Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for federal records; Massachusetts State Archives for state-level service records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Catholic Cemetery Association of the Archdiocese of Boston (Holy Cross Cemetery, Cambridge Cemetery, others); Mount Auburn Cemetery (non-sectarian, Cambridge); Copp's Hill Burying Ground (older, non-Catholic)
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has partial coverage; not all 1840s burials are indexed
- **Physical records:** Sexton and burial registers held by individual cemeteries and the Archdiocese; many have not been digitized

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Boston Pilot (Irish Catholic, published 1838 onward) is the single most important newspaper for this immigrant group — it ran 'Missing Persons' notices from 1831 to 1921 placed by Irish immigrants seeking separated relatives, and published arrival notices. The Boston Daily Atlas, Boston Post, and Boston Herald were also in circulation.
- **Where held:** The Pilot Missing Persons database is searchable online; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and ProQuest Historical Newspapers hold digitized runs; the Boston Public Library holds microfilm
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (naturalization), arrival columns, and missing-persons advertisements are all genealogically critical for this population

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** The Port of Boston was one of five major US ports of entry in the 1840s; customs passenger lists for Boston cover 1820-1891 and are in NARA Record Group 36. The National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA) holds the originals. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston
- **Record types:** Customs passenger lists (arrival manifests); declarations of intention (first papers); naturalization petitions (second papers)
- **FamilySearch collections:**
  - 'Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891' (collection 1784312, approximately 1.2 million records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312) — indexed and searchable by name
  - Digitized volume 003345210 (389 images, 1840-1850, Port of Boston): 3% name-indexed, full-text searchable — this volume must be searched via full-text or browsed image by image; it is not reliably found through a name search alone
  - 'Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790-1906' (collection 1459213, approximately 346,000 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213)
- **Content note:** 1840s customs passenger lists record only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — not the town of origin, last residence, or US contact. Passenger lists for the entire manifest must be examined because infants and young children traveling with parents are listed alongside adults.
- **Also search:** Ancestry.com holds indexed passenger lists for this period and often catches names FamilySearch misses; NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for original microfilm

### Tax records
- **Types:** City of Boston ward tax books (property and poll tax); Suffolk County tax records
- **Where held:** City of Boston Archives; Massachusetts State Archives. Not substantially digitized; physical access required
- **Substitute value:** Ward tax books can locate an immigrant in a specific address and year, bridging gaps between census enumerations

### Other record types
- **City directories:** Boston city directories were published annually from the 1820s onward and list male heads of household and boarding-house residents by name and address — a key intercensal tool. Many are digitized at Archive.org and on Ancestry
- **Almshouse and poor-relief records:** Boston's Overseers of the Poor kept detailed records of relief recipients; many newly arrived Irish immigrants appear here. Held at Massachusetts State Archives
- **Hospital records:** Massachusetts General Hospital and Boston City Hospital served the immigrant population; admissions registers may survive

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts Passenger Lists 1820-1891 (coll. 1784312); Naturalization Records 1790-1906 (coll. 1459213); Church Records 1630-1920 (coll. 1921657); Town Vital Records 1620-1890 (coll. 2061550); Probate Records 1635-1991 (coll. 1678901) | Free |
| Ancestry | Passenger lists, federal census, city directories, newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Customs passenger lists RG 36; naturalization records | Free to access finding aids; some records fee-based |
| Newspapers.com | Boston-area historical newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service and pension records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records (partial) | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search for the 1840-1859 period at the Boston/Suffolk County level returned 1 digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 003345210, 389 images, 1840-1850, Port of Boston passenger lists). This is the complete result set for that query. The indexed collections in collections_search cover a broader swath.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Boston, Waltham, MA | Original customs passenger lists, naturalization records | In-person; some records reproduced on request |
| Massachusetts State Archives, Boston | Vital records, probate, court records, almshouse/poor relief | In-person; some finding aids online |
| Suffolk County Registry of Deeds, Boston | Deed books | In-person; some volumes online |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives | Catholic parish registers 1840s onward | Written request; not open-stack |
| Boston Public Library | Newspaper microfilm, city directories, local histories | In-person; some digitized |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS) | Manuscript collections, vital records, compiled genealogies | In-person and online (American Ancestors subscription) |

## Records NOT online
- City of Boston ward tax books (1840s) — held at City of Boston Archives; physical access only
- Most Catholic parish burial and baptismal registers from individual parishes (only a subset is in the FamilySearch church records collection)
- Almshouse and Overseers of the Poor records — Massachusetts State Archives; physical access
- Suffolk County Probate original files — partially digitized; older volumes may require in-person access
- Boston City Hospital and Massachusetts General Hospital admissions registers — institutional archives

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated destruction of a specific Boston record set for the 1840s. An empty search result represents a digitization gap, not confirmed loss. The fate of specific record sets not yet digitized is unknown from tool results; contact the repositories listed above.

## Research tips
- **Start with the passenger list, then work forward.** The 1840s customs passenger list gives country of origin but rarely a county or parish; use the date of arrival and ship name to locate the manifest, then use the 1850 census (which names all household members) to confirm family composition and ages, and naturalization records to firm up the timeline. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston
- **Search the Boston Pilot Missing Persons database** before concluding an Irish immigrant cannot be found. The database covers notices placed 1831-1921 by immigrants in North America seeking relatives, and it names townlands and parishes of origin not found in any passenger list.
- **Use the 1855 Massachusetts state census** to bridge the gap between the 1850 and 1860 federal censuses — it captures immigrants who may have died, moved, or changed spelling of their name between the two federal enumerations.
- **Check Catholic parish registers at the Archdiocese of Boston archives.** For Irish Catholics, baptismal and marriage registers from parishes like Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's can predate or substitute for civil records and may name godparents or witnesses who are kin. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston
- **Pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered.** A declaration of intention filed in Boston Municipal Court and a petition filed years later in Suffolk County Superior Court may each be in a different repository and collection — search all Massachusetts court series in collection 1459213 and at the National Archives at Boston.
- **Examine the full manifest, not just the target name.** 1840s manifests list all passengers on a voyage; family groups traveling together are listed sequentially and an entry for a 2-year-old child will appear alongside adult entries but may be the only record of that child's arrival.

Locality guide written as **loc_001**.

---

The records that matter most for this research sit in federal and tribal repositories, not state courthouses. Indian Territory in the mid-1800s was never a US state or organized territory in the usual sense — the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, and Seminole) governed themselves under federal treaty arrangements after being relocated from the eastern US under the 1830 Indian Removal Act. That means no county deed books, no county vital registers, and no standard census enumeration for this population during the target period. The primary records are at the National Archives in Fort Worth, Texas (Record Group 75, Bureau of Indian Affairs), supplemented by FamilySearch's "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (567,890 indexed records) and a digitized volume of Tribal Enrollment Cards from 1840–1870 that is fully name-indexed. The most practical starting point even for mid-1800s families is the Dawes Rolls (1898–1914), because each enrollment card traces backward to earlier rolls and records ages that pin birth years into the 1840s and 1860s. Annuity payment rolls (RG 75, M234, partially on Fold3 and FamilySearch) substitute for missing census years. One important warning: in 1890 the western half of Indian Territory became Oklahoma Territory with county-level civil records, while the eastern half kept the tribal system — which series to search depends on which side of that line a family lived on. Researchers tracing Freedmen ancestors need the separate Freedmen rolls track, not the blood-roll series. The FamilySearch Wiki's Oklahoma-specific pages did not load correctly during this survey and should be checked directly at familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records before treating this guide as complete.

The next step is to identify which tribe or tribes your ancestors were affiliated with, then search the Dawes Rolls and the Indian Censuses and Rolls collection as the foundation for a research plan.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Indian Territory (Present-Day Oklahoma) (1830–1890)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Designated as Indian Territory under the Indian Removal Act of 1830; the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, and Seminole) were relocated there through the 1830s–1840s via the Trail of Tears
- **Administrative center:** No single territorial capital; each of the Five Civilized Tribes maintained separate tribal governments, courts, and councils
- **Parent jurisdiction:** U.S. federal government (Bureau of Indian Affairs under the Department of War, later the Department of the Interior); Oklahoma did not achieve statehood until 1907
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the tools for this jurisdiction; tribal censuses from 1851 (see FamilySearch collection 1987432) document some population counts
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, ranching, and treaty-based annuity economies; each tribe operated under its own governance and trade structures
- **Ethnic composition:** Five Civilized Tribes; Freedmen (formerly enslaved persons of tribal members); mixed-blood families; intermarried white citizens admitted under tribal law

---

Pennsylvania in the late 1700s had no civil registration at all — statewide birth and death registration did not begin until 1906 — so Quaker meeting records effectively function as the vital records for that era. Monthly meetings (the local congregation level) kept registers of births, marriages, and deaths, plus two record types unique to the Society of Friends: **certificates of removal**, which document a family's move from one meeting to another, and **disownment proceedings**, which record members expelled for violations of Quaker discipline. Quaker marriage certificates were signed by every member present, making them especially rich for identifying relatives and neighbors. The densest Quaker populations in this period were in Philadelphia, Bucks, Chester, and Delaware counties.

The two main physical repositories are:
- **Friends Historical Library** at Swarthmore College
- **Quaker and Special Collections** at Haverford College

Both are in the Philadelphia area. FamilySearch has microfilmed many monthly meeting registers, but the one digitized volume it returned for this period — Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800 — covers governance proceedings, not individual family events, and must be browsed image by image with no name index.

For a published index, **William Wade Hinshaw's six-volume *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*** abstracts Pennsylvania monthly meeting records and is the standard starting point.

When you are ready, a research plan can be built using these findings to direct the search for specific Quaker ancestors.

The one digitized volume FamilySearch found for this period (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800, image group 001188322) covers governance, not family events.

Certificates of removal document Quaker family moves between meetings — when a family disappears from one meeting's records, search the certificate-of-removal receipt books of neighboring and distant monthly meetings.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania, United States — Late 1700s (Quaker Meeting Records Focus)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Pennsylvania was established as a proprietary colony in 1682 by William Penn and became a state in 1787.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia (colonial and state capital through 1799).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** British Crown (colony, pre-1776); Commonwealth of Pennsylvania (state, 1787–).
- **Population during period:** Population tool returned no data for this period. The 1790 federal census is the earliest available decennial enumeration.
- **Economy:** Farming, trade, crafts; Philadelphia was the largest city and primary Atlantic port of the new republic.
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quakers dominant in the southeastern counties (Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, Delaware); German settlers (Lutheran, Reformed) in the German-speaking belt; Scotch-Irish Presbyterians farther west.
- **Religious denominations:** Society of Friends (Quakers), Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Anglican/Episcopal, Mennonite, Moravian.
- **Key historical events:** American Revolution (1775–1783) disrupted some record-keeping and triggered Quaker disownment proceedings against members who took up arms.

## Boundary changes
- Chester County was divided in 1789 to create Delaware County. Families in that area before 1789 appear under Chester County records regardless of which side of the later county line they lived on — search Chester County first for pre-1789 events.
- New counties were created from existing ones as settlement expanded westward throughout this period; confirm which county a township fell in at the time of the event.
- Before 1787 (statehood), Pennsylvania operated under colonial administration. County names and structures were the same but records carried colonial authority.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki Pennsylvania Church Records page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records) states Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide civil registration until 1906. The Pennsylvania Vital Records wiki page was not specifically retrieved during this survey (returned generic content). No civil birth or death registration exists for the late 1700s.
- **What exists:** No civil vital registration for this period. Quaker meeting records and other church registers are the primary and often sole vital-event sources.
- **Where held:** Monthly meeting registers and minutes — see Church records below.
- **Gaps:** Absence is total for civil records in this period; the record gap is the norm, not an exception.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Society of Friends (Quakers) — the dominant research focus for this query; Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Anglican/Episcopal, Mennonite, Moravian also present.
- **Record types:**
  - **Quaker monthly meeting registers:** births, marriages, deaths, certificates of removal (family moves between meetings), and disownment proceedings.
  - **Quaker marriage certificates:** signed by all meeting members present — a witness list that names siblings, cousins, neighbors, and community members in a single document.
  - Other denominations kept separate baptism, marriage, and burial registers.
- **Where held:**
  - Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College, PA — the largest collection of American Quaker records, including Pennsylvania monthly meeting registers, minutes, certificates of removal, and disownment books. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records; Wikipedia: Quakers in Pennsylvania.)
  - Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College, PA — a second major repository for Pennsylvania Quaker manuscripts. (Wikipedia: Quakers in Pennsylvania.)
  - FamilySearch: 1 digitized volume found for the period — Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800, image group 001188322, 145 images, browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). This volume covers governance proceedings; individual births, marriages, and deaths appear in monthly meeting records, not here.
  - William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes) abstracts Pennsylvania monthly meeting records — the standard published index for Quaker genealogy in this era, available in major genealogical libraries and on FamilySearch microfilm. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts.)
- **Language:** English.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** 1790 is the first federal census; it enumerates Pennsylvania household heads by name with aggregate counts for other members. This is the earliest decennial record covering this period.
- **State/provincial census:** Pennsylvania conducted no state census in this period.
- **Other enumerations:** Colonial-era and early-statehood county tax and assessment lists (township level) predate the 1790 census and serve as the best population proxy for 1750–1789.
- **Access:** The 1790 census is indexed and fully available online at Ancestry.com and FamilySearch. Pre-1790 tax lists are partially digitized; many are transcribed in the published Pennsylvania Archives series.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianship records, orphans' court proceedings.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection 1999196) covers this period; 3,200,560 images available, browse-only (0 name-indexed records — must be browsed image by image).
- **Where held:** County orphans' court / register of wills (county level); Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (proprietary colony and Commonwealth grant system).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania Land Office (Penn proprietors in the colonial era; Commonwealth of Pennsylvania after 1781). The FamilySearch Wiki Pennsylvania Land and Property page was not specifically retrieved during this survey.
- **Types:** Warrants, surveys, patents, deeds, mortgage records.
- **Date range:** Records begin in the 1680s.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) holds original land warrants and patents; county recorder of deeds holds deed books. The Pennsylvania Land Records database at the State Archives is partially searchable online.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolution (1775–1783). Quakers as a body opposed military service; members who served were disowned — making disownment records a secondary tool for identifying who in a meeting took part in the war.
- **Record types:** Pennsylvania militia muster rolls, federal pension files, bounty land warrants. Published Pennsylvania Archives series transcribes many colonial and Revolutionary-era military records.
- **Where held:** National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/) for federal pension files; Pennsylvania State Archives for militia records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Quaker meetings maintained burial grounds attached to their meetinghouses; burial registers (where extant) are separate from civil death records.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) includes many Pennsylvania Quaker burial grounds with varying transcription coverage.
- **Physical records:** Original burial registers held by the surviving meeting or by the Friends Historical Library.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Pennsylvania Gazette (Philadelphia, 1728–1800) and other Philadelphia papers published marriage notices and death notices.
- **Where held:** Digitized through Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/); microfilm at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **Content value:** Marriage notices, death notices, estate notices — supplementary to meeting records.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was the primary colonial-era port of entry. By the late 1700s most Pennsylvania Quaker families had been in the colony for several generations; new immigration was less common.
- **Record types:** Colonial-era ship passenger lists, post-1789 naturalization records.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for federal-period records; Historical Society of Pennsylvania for colonial-era ship lists.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax lists and township assessment records.
- **Date range:** Available from the colonial period (1680s forward).
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives; county historical societies. Published in the Pennsylvania Archives series for several periods.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the critical substitute for census years before 1790 — they can place a household in a specific township in a specific year.

### Other record types
- **Certificates of removal:** When a Quaker family moved between monthly meetings, both the sending and receiving meetings recorded the transfer. These documents name the family and confirm their standing. They are the primary tool for tracing Quaker families who relocated between meetings or arrived from other colonies/states.
- **Disownment records:** Monthly meetings recorded disciplinary proceedings and disownments for violations of Quaker discipline (marrying a non-Quaker, military service, swearing oaths, business misconduct). These records name individuals who subsequently disappear from regular meeting registers and may appear in civil or other church records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196, 3.2M images, browse-only); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (collection 1571957, 312,045 records, indexed); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, 198,765 records, indexed); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (image group 001188322, 145 images, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census (including 1790 Pennsylvania) (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records including Quaker burial grounds (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Free |
| NARA | Federal records including pension files and naturalization records (https://www.archives.gov/) | Free / fee for copies |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including Philadelphia papers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume search filtered to religious record types (Religious, Baptism, Religious Marriage, Religious Death) returned 1 total digitized volume for Pennsylvania 1750–1810. This is the complete result set for those record-type groups. The broader collections search returned 6 collections for Pennsylvania overall (1 of which is a synthetic test fixture and should be disregarded).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College | Pennsylvania monthly meeting registers, minutes, certificates of removal, disownment records; largest US Quaker collection | In-person; contact for research inquiries |
| Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College | Quaker records and manuscripts | In-person; contact for research inquiries |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Land warrants, patents, militia records, probate, tax lists | In-person; some online |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia | Colonial-era records, newspapers, land records | In-person |
| County historical societies (Chester, Bucks, Philadelphia, Delaware) | Local records, deed books, cemetery records | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Monthly meeting registers for most Pennsylvania monthly meetings (outside Philadelphia Yearly Meeting) are held at the Friends Historical Library and Haverford College; many are on FamilySearch microfilm but are largely browse-only or physical-only.
- Certificates of removal and disownment proceedings: largely physical, held at the Friends Historical Library.
- Pre-1790 colonial tax and assessment lists: partially transcribed in the Pennsylvania Archives series but not fully digitized or name-indexed online.
- Land warrants and patents: Pennsylvania State Archives holds originals; partial online access only.

## Known record losses
No tool result returned during this survey stated that a specific Quaker meeting record set in Pennsylvania was destroyed or lost for the late 1700s. The fate of any specific monthly meeting's records should be confirmed with the Friends Historical Library before concluding absence.

## Research tips
- Search monthly meeting registers — not yearly meeting minutes — for individual births, marriages, deaths, and certificates of removal. The one digitized FamilySearch volume for this period covers Philadelphia Yearly Meeting governance; family events appear in the monthly meeting records. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)
- Start with William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes) as the published index for Pennsylvania Quaker records — it abstracts many monthly meeting registers and is available in major genealogical libraries. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts)
- When you find a Quaker marriage certificate, transcribe every witness name — the list can identify siblings, cousins, and neighbors not documented anywhere else for that family.
- Track certificates of removal across meetings: if a family vanishes from one meeting's records, search certificate-of-removal receipt books at neighboring monthly meetings and at the Swarthmore Friends Historical Library.
- Chester County divided in 1789 to create Delaware County — search Chester County records for all pre-1789 events involving families who later appear in Delaware County.
- For the pre-1790 period (before the first federal census), county tax lists — many transcribed in the Pennsylvania Archives series — are the best substitute enumeration for placing a household in a specific township.
- The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania returned only generic content during this survey; check https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records directly for current guidance on Pennsylvania church record holdings.

Certificates of removal document Quaker family moves between meetings — when a family disappears from one meeting's records, search the certificate-of-removal receipt books of neighboring and distant monthly meetings.

Disownment records name members removed from the meeting for violating Quaker discipline (military service, marrying a non-Quaker, oath-swearing); these individuals then appear in civil or other church records under a different denomination.
Chester County was divided in 1789 to create Delaware County — families in that area before 1789 appear under Chester County records regardless of which side of the later boundary they lived on.
Quaker marriage certificates were signed by all attendees; the witness list identifies siblings, cousins, neighbors, and community members and can name many individuals in a single document.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania, United States — Late 1700s (Quaker Meeting Records Focus)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Pennsylvania was established as a proprietary colony in 1682 by William Penn and became a state in 1787.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia (colonial and state capital through 1799).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** British Crown (colony, pre-1776); Commonwealth of Pennsylvania (state, 1787–).
- **Population during period:** Population tool returned no data for this period. The 1790 federal census is the earliest available decennial enumeration.
- **Economy:** Farming, trade, crafts; Philadelphia was the largest city and primary Atlantic port of the new republic.
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quakers dominant in the southeastern counties (Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, Delaware); German settlers (Lutheran, Reformed) in the German-speaking belt; Scotch-Irish Presbyterians farther west.
- **Religious denominations:** Society of Friends (Quakers), Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Anglican/Episcopal, Mennonite, Moravian.
- **Key historical events:** American Revolution (1775–1783) disrupted some record-keeping and triggered Quaker disownment proceedings against members who took up arms.

## Boundary changes
- Chester County was divided in 1789 to create Delaware County. Families in that area before 1789 appear under Chester County records regardless of which side of the later county line they lived on — search Chester County first for pre-1789 events.
- New counties were created from existing ones as settlement expanded westward throughout this period; confirm which county a township fell in at the time of the event.
- Before 1787 (statehood), Pennsylvania operated under colonial administration. County names and structures were the same but records carried colonial authority.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki Pennsylvania Church Records page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records) states Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide civil registration until 1906. The Pennsylvania Vital Records wiki page was not specifically retrieved during this survey (returned generic content). No civil birth or death registration exists for the late 1700s.
- **What exists:** No civil vital registration for this period. Quaker meeting records and other church registers are the primary and often sole vital-event sources.
- **Where held:** Monthly meeting registers and minutes — see Church records below.
- **Gaps:** Absence is total for civil records in this period; the record gap is the norm, not an exception.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Society of Friends (Quakers) — the dominant research focus for this query; Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Anglican/Episcopal, Mennonite, Moravian also present.
- **Record types:**
  - **Quaker monthly meeting registers:** births, marriages, deaths, certificates of removal (family moves between meetings), and disownment proceedings.
  - **Quaker marriage certificates:** signed by all meeting members present — a witness list that names siblings, cousins, neighbors, and community members in a single document.
  - Other denominations kept separate baptism, marriage, and burial registers.
- **Where held:**
  - Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College, PA — the largest collection of American Quaker records, including Pennsylvania monthly meeting registers, minutes, certificates of removal, and disownment books. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records; Wikipedia: Quakers in Pennsylvania.)
  - Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College, PA — a second major repository for Pennsylvania Quaker manuscripts. (Wikipedia: Quakers in Pennsylvania.)
  - FamilySearch: 1 digitized volume found for the period — Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800, image group 001188322, 145 images, browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). This volume covers governance proceedings; individual births, marriages, and deaths appear in monthly meeting records, not here.
  - William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes) abstracts Pennsylvania monthly meeting records — the standard published index for Quaker genealogy in this era, available in major genealogical libraries and on FamilySearch microfilm. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts.)
- **Language:** English.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** 1790 is the first federal census; it enumerates Pennsylvania household heads by name with aggregate counts for other members. This is the earliest decennial record covering this period.
- **State/provincial census:** Pennsylvania conducted no state census in this period.
- **Other enumerations:** Colonial-era and early-statehood county tax and assessment lists (township level) predate the 1790 census and serve as the best population proxy for 1750–1789.
- **Access:** The 1790 census is indexed and fully available online at Ancestry.com and FamilySearch. Pre-1790 tax lists are partially digitized; many are transcribed in the published Pennsylvania Archives series.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianship records, orphans' court proceedings.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection 1999196) covers this period; 3,200,560 images available, browse-only (0 name-indexed records — must be browsed image by image).
- **Where held:** County orphans' court / register of wills (county level); Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (proprietary colony and Commonwealth grant system).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania Land Office (Penn proprietors in the colonial era; Commonwealth of Pennsylvania after 1781). The FamilySearch Wiki Pennsylvania Land and Property page was not specifically retrieved during this survey.
- **Types:** Warrants, surveys, patents, deeds, mortgage records.
- **Date range:** Records begin in the 1680s.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) holds original land warrants and patents; county recorder of deeds holds deed books. The Pennsylvania Land Records database at the State Archives is partially searchable online.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolution (1775–1783). Quakers as a body opposed military service; members who served were disowned — making disownment records a secondary tool for identifying who in a meeting took part in the war.
- **Record types:** Pennsylvania militia muster rolls, federal pension files, bounty land warrants. Published Pennsylvania Archives series transcribes many colonial and Revolutionary-era military records.
- **Where held:** National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/) for federal pension files; Pennsylvania State Archives for militia records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Quaker meetings maintained burial grounds attached to their meetinghouses; burial registers (where extant) are separate from civil death records.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) includes many Pennsylvania Quaker burial grounds with varying transcription coverage.
- **Physical records:** Original burial registers held by the surviving meeting or by the Friends Historical Library.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Pennsylvania Gazette (Philadelphia, 1728–1800) and other Philadelphia papers published marriage notices and death notices.
- **Where held:** Digitized through Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/); microfilm at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **Content value:** Marriage notices, death notices, estate notices — supplementary to meeting records.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was the primary colonial-era port of entry. By the late 1700s most Pennsylvania Quaker families had been in the colony for several generations; new immigration was less common.
- **Record types:** Colonial-era ship passenger lists, post-1789 naturalization records.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for federal-period records; Historical Society of Pennsylvania for colonial-era ship lists.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax lists and township assessment records.
- **Date range:** Available from the colonial period (1680s forward).
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives; county historical societies. Published in the Pennsylvania Archives series for several periods.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the critical substitute for census years before 1790 — they can place a household in a specific township in a specific year.

### Other record types
- **Certificates of removal:** When a Quaker family moved between monthly meetings, both the sending and receiving meetings recorded the transfer. These documents name the family and confirm their standing. They are the primary tool for tracing Quaker families who relocated between meetings or arrived from other colonies/states.
- **Disownment records:** Monthly meetings recorded disciplinary proceedings and disownments for violations of Quaker discipline (marrying a non-Quaker, military service, swearing oaths, business misconduct). These records name individuals who subsequently disappear from regular meeting registers and may appear in civil or other church records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196, 3.2M images, browse-only); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (collection 1571957, 312,045 records, indexed); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, 198,765 records, indexed); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (image group 001188322, 145 images, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census (including 1790 Pennsylvania) (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records including Quaker burial grounds (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Free |
| NARA | Federal records including pension files and naturalization records (https://www.archives.gov/) | Free / fee for copies |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including Philadelphia papers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume search filtered to religious record types (Religious, Baptism, Religious Marriage, Religious Death) returned 1 total digitized volume for Pennsylvania 1750–1810. This is the complete result set for those record-type groups. The broader collections search returned 6 collections for Pennsylvania overall (1 of which is a synthetic test fixture and should be disregarded).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College | Pennsylvania monthly meeting registers, minutes, certificates of removal, disownment records; largest US Quaker collection | In-person; contact for research inquiries |
| Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College | Quaker records and manuscripts | In-person; contact for research inquiries |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Land warrants, patents, militia records, probate, tax lists | In-person; some online |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia | Colonial-era records, newspapers, land records | In-person |
| County historical societies (Chester, Bucks, Philadelphia, Delaware) | Local records, deed books, cemetery records | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Monthly meeting registers for most Pennsylvania monthly meetings (outside Philadelphia Yearly Meeting) are held at the Friends Historical Library and Haverford College; many are on FamilySearch microfilm but are largely browse-only or physical-only.
- Certificates of removal and disownment proceedings: largely physical, held at the Friends Historical Library.
- Pre-1790 colonial tax and assessment lists: partially transcribed in the Pennsylvania Archives series but not fully digitized or name-indexed online.
- Land warrants and patents: Pennsylvania State Archives holds originals; partial online access only.

## Known record losses
No tool result returned during this survey stated that a specific Quaker meeting record set in Pennsylvania was destroyed or lost for the late 1700s. The fate of any specific monthly meeting's records should be confirmed with the Friends Historical Library before concluding absence.

## Research tips
- Search monthly meeting registers — not yearly meeting minutes — for individual births, marriages, deaths, and certificates of removal. The one digitized FamilySearch volume for this period covers Philadelphia Yearly Meeting governance; family events appear in the monthly meeting records. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)
- Start with William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes) as the published index for Pennsylvania Quaker records — it abstracts many monthly meeting registers and is available in major genealogical libraries. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts)
- When you find a Quaker marriage certificate, transcribe every witness name — the list can identify siblings, cousins, and neighbors not documented anywhere else for that family.
- Track certificates of removal across meetings: if a family vanishes from one meeting's records, search certificate-of-removal receipt books at neighboring monthly meetings and at the Swarthmore Friends Historical Library.
- Chester County divided in 1789 to create Delaware County — search Chester County records for all pre-1789 events involving families who later appear in Delaware County.
- For the pre-1790 period (before the first federal census), county tax lists — many transcribed in the Pennsylvania Archives series — are the best substitute enumeration for placing a household in a specific township.
- The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania returned only generic content during this survey; check https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records directly for current guidance on Pennsylvania church record holdings.

---

You're researching Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania during the late 1800s steel boom — one of the most intensively documented industrial workforces in American history, though records are scattered across several physical repositories rather than concentrated online.

**Two critical context points before diving in:**

1. **No statewide civil registration until 1906.** For the entire 1870–1900 window, you're relying on church registers, city directories, newspaper notices, and census mortality schedules rather than birth/death certificates.

2. **Allegheny City ≠ Pittsburgh.** The City of Allegheny (now Pittsburgh's North Side) was a legally separate municipality throughout this period, not absorbed until 1907. Any ancestor north of the Ohio River will appear in records as "Allegheny City."

---

### Key Sources for Occupational/Industrial Research

| Source | What It Offers | Where Held |
|---|---|---|
| **Company employment records** | Worker names, hire dates, departments | Heinz History Center (Pittsburgh); Rivers of Steel archives (Homestead) — fragmentary survivals |
| **Union membership lists** | Names, possibly dues, local numbers | Rivers of Steel archives |
| **PA state factory inspector reports** | Names of workers at inspected plants | PA State Archives, Harrisburg |
| **Pittsburgh city directories** | Name, occupation, address, every year from 1810s | Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh — practical way to bridge the destroyed 1890 census gap |
| **Federal censuses (1870, 1880, 1900)** | Occupation, household, neighbors | Indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry |
| **Ethnic parish registers** | Births/deaths/marriages for Catholic immigrant communities | Still largely physical — contact parishes directly |

---

### Immigrant Communities
The Pittsburgh steel workforce drew heavy Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian immigration. For these groups, the ethnic Catholic parish register is often the **only surviving birth and death source**. Each community clustered in specific neighborhoods (e.g., Poles in the Strip District, Slovaks in Braddock), so knowing an ancestor's ethnicity and neighborhood narrows the parish quickly.

---

### Recommended Next Step
Build a research plan targeting your specific ancestor. With a name, approximate years, and nationality, I can help identify the right parish, the applicable city directory years, and which of the surviving company record collections is most likely to hold something.

# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (1870–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Allegheny County established 1788 from parts of Washington and Westmoreland Counties; Pittsburgh incorporated as a city 1816. Wikipedia dates Pittsburgh from 1758 (fort-era).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
