entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania (1780–1810)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1682, one of the three original counties of Pennsylvania established by William Penn
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia (co-extensive with the county during this period)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Place population data was not returned for this place and period by the survey tools. The 1790 federal census (first decennial enumeration, taken three years before the epidemic) and 1800 census are the primary population sources.
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic port city, center of commerce, banking, and manufacturing; served as the national capital 1790–1800
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quaker founding population joined by German, Scots-Irish, Irish, Welsh, Dutch, Swedish, and African communities by the 1790s
- **Religious denominations:** Quakers (Society of Friends), Anglicans/Episcopalians (Christ Church), Swedish Lutherans (Gloria Dei/Old Swedes'), German Lutherans, German Reformed, Presbyterians, Methodists, Baptists, Catholics, and multiple African American congregations
- **Key historical events:** American Revolution (1775–1783); Constitutional Convention (1787); national capital 1790–1800; yellow fever epidemic of 1793, which killed approximately 5,000 of the city's 50,000 residents (roughly one-tenth of the population) between August and November 1793 (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793)

## Boundary changes
- Philadelphia County was one of the three original counties of Pennsylvania, established in 1682. Boundaries were generally stable through the 1780–1810 target period. Place_search_all returned no results for this place, so additional boundary history could not be confirmed from tool results.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in Pennsylvania in 1793. The earliest Pennsylvania-level death registration collection on FamilySearch (collection 2255317: Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968) begins in 1906, confirming statewide civil death registration was not in effect during the epidemic. The Pennsylvania Vital Records wiki page returned only generic content in this survey; specific registration dates and levels cannot be cited from a fetched page.
- **What exists for the 1780–1810 period:** No civil birth, marriage, or death records. The FamilySearch collections Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (collection 1571957, 312,045 indexed records, 156,023 images) and Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, 198,765 indexed records, no images) cover the period and are name-indexed — these are compiled from church and court sources, not a civil registration series.
- **Where held:** Church records are the primary source; see Church records below
- **Gaps:** No state-level civil vital registration existed in 1793. Epidemic deaths are documented only in church burial registers, the Mathew Carey list, and the Committee records.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church burial registers; Mathew Carey's published list; epidemic Committee records

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Quakers, Episcopal/Anglican (Christ Church), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei/Old Swedes'), German Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist, Catholic, African American congregations
- **Record types:** Baptisms/christenings, marriages, burials, confirmations; epidemic burial registers are especially important for 1793
- **Where held:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki "Philadelphia Genealogy" page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records): "Many colonial and early national church registers have been transcribed and published. The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records." Original registers are held at the churches themselves, the Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP), and denominational archives. FamilySearch holds 1 digitized volume: Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (image group 001188322, 145 images) — browse-only, 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. Per the FamilySearch Wiki yellow fever section (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793): Christ Church and Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') burial records are specifically named as key sources for epidemic deaths.
- **Language:** Predominantly English; German Lutheran and German Reformed records may be in German

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1790 (first decennial census; pre-epidemic baseline showing Philadelphia households); 1800 (post-epidemic; households absent from 1800 that were present in 1790 are candidates for epidemic deaths or departure)
- **State census:** No Pennsylvania state census for this period
- **Other enumerations:** Pennsylvania county tax lists can substitute for missing census years
- **Access:** Federal census schedules are indexed and images available on Ancestry (subscription; https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch. Using 1790 and 1800 together is the core research strategy for identifying epidemic-affected families.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, inventories of estate, guardianship files
- **Testate or intestate:** The epidemic killed suddenly; many victims died intestate (without wills), making letters of administration the most likely record type for 1793 decedents. Search estate administrations (intestate series) in addition to wills (testate series).
- **Date range:** Philadelphia County probate records from 1682 onward
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994) holds 3,200,560 images — browse-only (0 indexed records); images must be examined page-by-page. Original records held at the Philadelphia City Archives.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (proprietary Pennsylvania)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Original grants came from William Penn's proprietorship; subsequent transfers recorded in county deed books. The Pennsylvania Land and Property wiki page returned only generic content in this survey.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records; bounty land warrants for Revolutionary War veterans
- **Date range:** From 1682
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives and the Philadelphia Recorder of Deeds; the Historical Society of Pennsylvania holds many early property records

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Revolutionary War (service 1775–1783; pension files and bounty land warrants active through the 1790s–1800s); Northwest Indian Wars (1790–1795)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (NARA); Pennsylvania state adjutant general records (Pennsylvania State Archives); Fold3 holds military records online (https://www.fold3.com/)
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for federal records; Pennsylvania State Archives for state records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Christ Church burial ground (Episcopal), Gloria Dei churchyard (Old Swedes'), Society of Friends burial grounds; public burial grounds used during the epidemic
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has coverage for many Philadelphia cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Church burial registers and sexton records held at churches and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Several active in 1793: the Pennsylvania Gazette (established 1728), the Federal Gazette, and the General Advertiser (later the Aurora); all reported epidemic deaths and relief efforts
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds some historical Philadelphia newspapers; the Library Company of Philadelphia and HSP hold additional newspaper archives in print/microfilm
- **Content value:** Obituaries, death notices, estate sale notices, guardianship notices, letters from refugees who fled the city

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was a major port of entry for the early national period
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (NARA); naturalizations scattered across Philadelphia courts (pre-1906); NARA holds federal naturalization records from 1906 onward
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); many pre-1820 passenger lists published and indexed; Ancestry has federal passenger lists
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all travelers, including infants and children. Examine the full manifest page when researching a family.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Pennsylvania county property tax lists and personal property assessments
- **Date range:** Available from the colonial period through the 1780–1810 window
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives; Pennsylvania State Archives; some series on FamilySearch microfilm
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists fill the gap between the 1790 and 1800 federal censuses and identify heads of household in the 1780s — important for locating individuals before the first census

### Other record types — Epidemic-specific sources (1793 Yellow Fever)
Per the FamilySearch Wiki "Philadelphia Genealogy" page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793) and Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793):
- **Mathew Carey's published account** ("A Short Account of the Malignant Fever," 1793): lists names of the dead — the most direct finding aid for epidemic victims; available at HSP, Library Company of Philadelphia, and in digitized form via HathiTrust
- **Minutes and reports of the Committee appointed by the citizens**: documented relief efforts and recipients; held at HSP and Philadelphia City Archives
- **Bush Hill hospital records**: documented patients treated at the epidemic's main hospital; held at HSP and Philadelphia City Archives
- **Mayor Matthew Clarkson's records and physician Benjamin Rush's accounts**: detailed administrative and medical records from the epidemic period (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793)

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (3.2M browse-only images, collection 1999196); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312,045 indexed records, collection 1571957); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (198,765 indexed records, collection 1502909); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (145 browse-only images, image group 001188322) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census collection (1790, 1800 censuses for Philadelphia County) | Subscription (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) |
| Fold3 | Military records (Revolutionary War service and pension files) | Subscription (https://www.fold3.com/) |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Philadelphia newspapers | Subscription (https://www.newspapers.com/) |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free (https://www.findagrave.com/) |
| NARA | Federal records, naturalization, passenger lists | Free/in-person (https://www.archives.gov/) |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for Philadelphia in the 1780–1810 period — this was the complete result set (totalResults: 1). Collections_search returned 6 collections at the Pennsylvania state level; 3 overlap the target window (1 labeled synthetic test fixture was excluded from the count).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia City Archives | City government records; epidemic Committee records; Bush Hill hospital records; deed and probate records | In-person |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP) | Church records; Mathew Carey papers; epidemic manuscript sources; newspapers; family papers | In-person with appointment (https://hsp.org/) |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Indexes to Philadelphia church records; compiled genealogies | Membership/in-person |
| Pennsylvania State Archives | State-level records; tax lists; colonial and early national records | In-person and some online access |
| Library Company of Philadelphia | Colonial/early national newspapers; printed epidemic accounts including Carey's list | In-person with appointment |
| NARA Philadelphia branch | Federal court records; naturalization records | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- **Epidemic-specific records:** The Committee minutes and reports, Bush Hill hospital records, and the bulk of manuscript sources documenting the 1793 epidemic are held in physical form at HSP and the Philadelphia City Archives; no online equivalent was found in this survey.
- **Bulk of church burial registers:** While many have been transcribed and indexes compiled by the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (per wiki_search), most original registers remain in physical custody at the churches, HSP, or denominational archives and are not fully available online.
- **Philadelphia County tax lists (1780–1810):** No online collection was found in this survey; held at the Philadelphia City Archives and Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Philadelphia County deed records (1780–1810):** Not found in any digitized online collection in this survey; held at the Philadelphia City Archives.
- **Pre-1906 vital records:** No civil death, birth, or marriage registration exists for 1793 in any online collection.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that a specific record set was destroyed or lost for Philadelphia County in the 1780–1810 period. The absence of online collections for church burial registers, tax records, and deed records is a digitization gap, not a confirmed loss. Consult the Philadelphia City Archives and HSP directly to confirm the survival status of any specific series.

## Research tips
- **Start with Mathew Carey's published list.** The FamilySearch Wiki "Philadelphia Genealogy" page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793) identifies it as a key genealogical source for epidemic victims. It is available at HSP, the Library Company of Philadelphia, and in digitized form through HathiTrust.
- **Use the 1790 and 1800 federal censuses as a pair.** Households present in 1790 but absent from the 1800 Philadelphia enumeration are strong candidates for epidemic deaths or permanent departure from the city. Refugees often appear in the 1800 census of neighboring counties.
- **Search neighboring county records for 1793 refugees.** Thousands fled Philadelphia during the epidemic (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793). Search the neighboring Pennsylvania counties' tax lists, deeds, and church records for the period 1793–1795; the home wiki page for Philadelphia County did not return specific content in this survey, so the neighboring counties list was not available from a tool result.
- **Church records are the only vital records for 1793.** Per the FamilySearch Wiki "Philadelphia Genealogy" page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records): "Philadelphia's church records are the primary source of vital information before Pennsylvania's statewide registration in 1906." The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many of these records.
- **Probate records are unusually productive for epidemic families.** The sudden mortality of 1793 generated a wave of estate administrations. FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994) has 3.2 million browse-only images with 0 indexed records — budget significant time for page-by-page browsing around the 1793 date.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Philadelphia County and Pennsylvania returned only generic fallback content in this survey.** Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy before finalizing a research plan; the pages likely exist but were not accessible through the wiki tools during this survey run.

- Philadelphia County was one of the three original counties of Pennsylvania, established in 1682. Boundaries were generally stable through the 1780–1810 target period. Place_search_all returned no results for this place, so additional boundary history could not be confirmed from tool results.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in Pennsylvania in 1793. The earliest Pennsylvania-level death registration collection on FamilySearch (collection 2255317: Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968) begins in 1906, confirming statewide civil death registration was not in effect during the epidemic. The Pennsylvania Vital Records wiki page returned only generic content in this survey; specific registration dates and levels cannot be cited from a fetched page.
- **What exists for the 1780–1810 period:** No civil birth, marriage, or death records. The FamilySearch collections Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (collection 1571957, 312,045 indexed records, 156,023 images) and Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, 198,765 indexed records, no images) cover the period and are name-indexed — these are compiled from church and court sources, not a civil registration series.
- **Where held:** Church records are the primary source; see Church records below
- **Gaps:** No state-level civil vital registration existed in 1793. Epidemic deaths are documented only in church burial registers, the Mathew Carey list, and the Committee records.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church burial registers; Mathew Carey's published list; epidemic Committee records

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Quakers, Episcopal/Anglican (Christ Church), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei/Old Swedes'), German Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist, Catholic, African American congregations
- **Record types:** Baptisms/christenings, marriages, burials, confirmations; epidemic burial registers are especially important for 1793
- **Where held:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki "Philadelphia Genealogy" page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records): "Many colonial and early national church registers have been transcribed and published. The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records." Original registers are held at the churches themselves, the Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP), and denominational archives. FamilySearch holds 1 digitized volume: Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (image group 001188322, 145 images) — browse-only, 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. Per the FamilySearch Wiki yellow fever section (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793): Christ Church and Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') burial records are specifically named as key sources for epidemic deaths.
- **Language:** Predominantly English; German Lutheran and German Reformed records may be in German

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1790 (first decennial census; pre-epidemic baseline showing Philadelphia households); 1800 (post-epidemic; households absent from 1800 that were present in 1790 are candidates for epidemic deaths or departure)
- **State census:** No Pennsylvania state census for this period
- **Other enumerations:** Pennsylvania county tax lists can substitute for missing census years
- **Access:** Federal census schedules are indexed and images available on Ancestry (subscription; https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch. Using 1790 and 1800 together is the core research strategy for identifying epidemic-affected families.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, inventories of estate, guardianship files
- **Testate or intestate:** The epidemic killed suddenly; many victims died intestate (without wills), making letters of administration the most likely record type for 1793 decedents. Search estate administrations (intestate series) in addition to wills (testate series).
- **Date range:** Philadelphia County probate records from 1682 onward
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994) holds 3,200,560 images — browse-only (0 indexed records); images must be examined page-by-page. Original records held at the Philadelphia City Archives.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (proprietary Pennsylvania)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Original grants came from William Penn's proprietorship; subsequent transfers recorded in county deed books. The Pennsylvania Land and Property wiki page returned only generic content in this survey.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records; bounty land warrants for Revolutionary War veterans
- **Date range:** From 1682
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives and the Philadelphia Recorder of Deeds; the Historical Society of Pennsylvania holds many early property records

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Revolutionary War (service 1775–1783; pension files and bounty land warrants active through the 1790s–1800s); Northwest Indian Wars (1790–1795)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (NARA); Pennsylvania state adjutant general records (Pennsylvania State Archives); Fold3 holds military records online (https://www.fold3.com/)
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for federal records; Pennsylvania State Archives for state records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Christ Church burial ground (Episcopal), Gloria Dei churchyard (Old Swedes'), Society of Friends burial grounds; public burial grounds used during the epidemic
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has coverage for many Philadelphia cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Church burial registers and sexton records held at churches and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Several active in 1793: the Pennsylvania Gazette (established 1728), the Federal Gazette, and the General Advertiser (later the Aurora); all reported epidemic deaths and relief efforts
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds some historical Philadelphia newspapers; the Library Company of Philadelphia and HSP hold additional newspaper archives in print/microfilm
- **Content value:** Obituaries, death notices, estate sale notices, guardianship notices, letters from refugees who fled the city

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was a major port of entry for the early national period
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (NARA); naturalizations scattered across Philadelphia courts (pre-1906); NARA holds federal naturalization records from 1906 onward
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); many pre-1820 passenger lists published and indexed; Ancestry has federal passenger lists
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all travelers, including infants and children. Examine the full manifest page when researching a family.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Pennsylvania county property tax lists and personal property assessments
- **Date range:** Available from the colonial period through the 1780–1810 window
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives; Pennsylvania State Archives; some series on FamilySearch microfilm
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists fill the gap between the 1790 and 1800 federal censuses and identify heads of household in the 1780s — important for locating individuals before the first census

### Other record types — Epidemic-specific sources (1793 Yellow Fever)
Per the FamilySearch Wiki "Philadelphia Genealogy" page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793) and Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793):
- **Mathew Carey's published account** ("A Short Account of the Malignant Fever," 1793): lists names of the dead — the most direct finding aid for epidemic victims; available at HSP, Library Company of Philadelphia, and in digitized form via HathiTrust
- **Minutes and reports of the Committee appointed by the citizens**: documented relief efforts and recipients; held at HSP and Philadelphia City Archives
- **Bush Hill hospital records**: documented patients treated at the epidemic's main hospital; held at HSP and Philadelphia City Archives
- **Mayor Matthew Clarkson's records and physician Benjamin Rush's accounts**: detailed administrative and medical records from the epidemic period (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793)

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (3.2M browse-only images, collection 1999196); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312,045 indexed records, collection 1571957); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (198,765 indexed records, collection 1502909); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (145 browse-only images, image group 001188322) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census collection (1790, 1800 censuses for Philadelphia County) | Subscription (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) |
| Fold3 | Military records (Revolutionary War service and pension files) | Subscription (https://www.fold3.com/) |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Philadelphia newspapers | Subscription (https://www.newspapers.com/) |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free (https://www.findagrave.com/) |
| NARA | Federal records, naturalization, passenger lists | Free/in-person (https://www.archives.gov/) |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for Philadelphia in the 1780–1810 period — this was the complete result set (totalResults: 1). Collections_search returned 6 collections at the Pennsylvania state level; 3 overlap the target window (1 labeled synthetic test fixture was excluded from the count).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia City Archives | City government records; epidemic Committee records; Bush Hill hospital records; deed and probate records | In-person |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP) | Church records; Mathew Carey papers; epidemic manuscript sources; newspapers; family papers | In-person with appointment (https://hsp.org/) |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Indexes to Philadelphia church records; compiled genealogies | Membership/in-person |
| Pennsylvania State Archives | State-level records; tax lists; colonial and early national records | In-person and some online access |
| Library Company of Philadelphia | Colonial/early national newspapers; printed epidemic accounts including Carey's list | In-person with appointment |
| NARA Philadelphia branch | Federal court records; naturalization records | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- **Epidemic-specific records:** The Committee minutes and reports, Bush Hill hospital records, and the bulk of manuscript sources documenting the 1793 epidemic are held in physical form at HSP and the Philadelphia City Archives; no online equivalent was found in this survey.
- **Bulk of church burial registers:** While many have been transcribed and indexes compiled by the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (per wiki_search), most original registers remain in physical custody at the churches, HSP, or denominational archives and are not fully available online.
- **Philadelphia County tax lists (1780–1810):** No online collection was found in this survey; held at the Philadelphia City Archives and Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Philadelphia County deed records (1780–1810):** Not found in any digitized online collection in this survey; held at the Philadelphia City Archives.
- **Pre-1906 vital records:** No civil death, birth, or marriage registration exists for 1793 in any online collection.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that a specific record set was destroyed or lost for Philadelphia County in the 1780–1810 period. The absence of online collections for church burial registers, tax records, and deed records is a digitization gap, not a confirmed loss. Consult the Philadelphia City Archives and HSP directly to confirm the survival status of any specific series.

## Research tips
- **Start with Mathew Carey's published list.** The FamilySearch Wiki "Philadelphia Genealogy" page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793) identifies it as a key genealogical source for epidemic victims. It is available at HSP, the Library Company of Philadelphia, and in digitized form through HathiTrust.
- **Use the 1790 and 1800 federal censuses as a pair.** Households present in 1790 but absent from the 1800 Philadelphia enumeration are strong candidates for epidemic deaths or permanent departure from the city. Refugees often appear in the 1800 census of neighboring counties.
- **Search neighboring county records for 1793 refugees.** Thousands fled Philadelphia during the epidemic (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793). Search the neighboring Pennsylvania counties' tax lists, deeds, and church records for the period 1793–1795; the home wiki page for Philadelphia County did not return specific content in this survey, so the neighboring counties list was not available from a tool result.
- **Church records are the only vital records for 1793.** Per the FamilySearch Wiki "Philadelphia Genealogy" page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records): "Philadelphia's church records are the primary source of vital information before Pennsylvania's statewide registration in 1906." The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many of these records.
- **Probate records are unusually productive for epidemic families.** The sudden mortality of 1793 generated a wave of estate administrations. FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994) has 3.2 million browse-only images with 0 indexed records — budget significant time for page-by-page browsing around the 1793 date.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Philadelphia County and Pennsylvania returned only generic fallback content in this survey.** Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy before finalizing a research plan; the pages likely exist but were not accessible through the wiki tools during this survey run.

Here is the locality guide the subagent produced:

---

**Chicago, Cook County, Illinois — Records for Families Affected by the Great Fire of 1871**

The defining fact for this research is the **Great Chicago Fire of October 8–10, 1871**, which destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and nearly every official record the city held before that date — deeds, probate files, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls. Research strategy splits sharply at that date.

---

### Pre-Fire Substitutes (before October 1871)

| Record | Where Held |
|---|---|
| **1870 U.S. Federal Census** | Survived (originals were in Washington, D.C.); searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry |
| **Chicago City Directories (1840s onward)** | Newberry Library |
| **Reconstructed Land/Deed Records** | The *Burnt Record Act of 1872* required property owners to re-file; those re-filed deeds are the closest substitute for pre-fire land documentation |
| **Insurance records** | Chicago Title and Trust Company records at the **Chicago History Museum** |
| **Catholic parish registers** | **Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** — some parishes kept registers offsite and survived the fire |

---

### Post-Fire Records (October 1871 onward)

FamilySearch has four digitized Cook County collections, all beginning in 1871:

- **Birth certificates** — ~1.45 million records
- **Death records** — ~980,000 records
- **Marriage records** — ~620,000 records
- **Church records** — ~285,000 records

For post-fire records not yet online — probate, naturalization, and court files from 1871 onward — the **Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University** is the main holding repository.

---

### Recommended Next Step

Visit the FamilySearch Wiki directly for the most current collection inventory:
👉 [Cook County, Illinois Genealogy – FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy)

---

**Bottom line:** The 1870 census, city directories at the Newberry Library, and reconstructed deeds under the Burnt Record Act are your best anchors before the fire. The Chicago History Museum and the Bernardin Archives hold the most important surviving institutional records. For the period after October 1871, FamilySearch's digitized Cook County collections are the starting point, with IRAD for undigitized court and probate records.

The 1870 federal census for Chicago survived because its originals were held in Washington, D.C., not in Cook County — it is the most important pre-fire population record for this locality.

Civil vital records at Cook County level effectively begin in 1871 (post-fire); all four FamilySearch collections start that year. The Illinois statewide vital registration start date was not returned by any tool in this survey.

Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record; the fire destroyed most pre-1871 Cook County naturalization records — check IRAD for post-fire records and NARA for federal court records.

Chicago city directories survive from the 1840s onward and are held at the Newberry Library — they are the best pre-fire substitute for census and vital records, listing residents by name, address, and occupation.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois (1860–1880, Great Fire of 1871)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Cook County, Illinois, United States
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the tools for this period.
- **Economy:** Mid-19th century Chicago was a major rail hub, meatpacking center, and Great Lakes port — industries that drew large immigrant populations and generated significant business, court, and labor records.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish, German, and Scandinavian populations; smaller communities of Polish, Bohemian, and other Central European immigrants.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (especially Irish and German parishes), Lutheran, Methodist, Episcopalian, Baptist, Presbyterian, and Jewish congregations.
- **Key historical events:** The Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871, killed approximately 300 people, destroyed roughly 3.3 square miles of the city, and left more than 100,000 homeless. It destroyed the Cook County Courthouse along with the city's official record holdings — deeds, birth/death registers, court records, and tax rolls. This is the defining record-loss event for this research period. Source: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire.

## Boundary changes
- Cook County encompassed Chicago as its county seat throughout the target period. No boundary changes are reported by the tools for this period; the jurisdiction was stable.

### Vital records (civil registration)

---

**Overview**

Louisiana passed through French rule (1699–1762), then Spanish (1762–1803), with a brief return to France before the Louisiana Purchase. No civil registration existed under either colonial regime, so **Catholic church records are the functional substitute** for birth, marriage, and death records.

---

**Key Records & Repositories**

| Record Type | Where to Find |
|---|---|
| **Sacramental registers** (baptisms, marriages, burials) | Archdiocese of New Orleans — registers from 1720 onward |
| **FamilySearch indexed collection** | "Louisiana, Catholic Church Records, 1718–1925" — name-indexed |
| **FamilySearch digitized image volumes** | Two browse-only sets (~413 images) — no name index, must be scrolled in French/Spanish |
| **Notarial records** (land, contracts, estates, relationships) | **New Orleans Notarial Archives** — oldest continuous notarial office in North America, records back to 1730s |
| **French colonial census rolls & ship manifests** | **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer**, Aix-en-Provence, France |
| **Spanish-era administrative records** | **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain |
| **Louisiana state holdings** | Louisiana Historical Center, New Orleans |

---

**Practical Warnings**

- **Language barrier**: Records are in colonial French before 1769, Spanish after — expect period handwriting in both.
- **Unindexed images**: The FamilySearch browse volumes have no name index, so you must read through them page by page.
- **European archives**: A thorough 1700s family trail will likely require reaching both French and Spanish archives, not just U.S. repositories.

Identify the specific **parish or notarial district** where your ancestors lived. That narrows which series in the Archdiocese of New Orleans and the Notarial Archives to target, and a research plan can map that out precisely.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Louisiana (French Colonial Period, 1700–1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** France claimed the Mississippi River basin in 1682; the colony of La Louisiane was operationally established by 1699. New Orleans was founded in 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville and became the colonial capital.
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans (colonial capital and seat of the Superior Council)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New France (France, 1699–1762); Spain (1762–1800); France (1800–1803)
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the tools for this period.
- **Economy:** Fur trade, indigo, tobacco, and (later) sugar cane; enslaved labor central to the plantation economy under the Code Noir.
- **Ethnic composition:** French settlers, Indigenous peoples, enslaved Africans brought via the Atlantic slave trade, some German and Swiss settlers, and a small Spanish population after 1762. Per Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Louisiana), the Code Noir regulated slavery and required Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic Church — the only legally recognized denomination under French colonial law and continued under Spanish rule.
- **Key historical events:** New Orleans founded 1718; Seven Years' War ended French rule 1762 (Treaty of Fontainebleau ceded territory to Spain); Spanish administration effective 1769; Napoleon retroceded to France 1800; Louisiana Purchase 1803.

## Boundary changes
- **1682–1762:** La Louisiane under French rule, covering the full Mississippi River basin.
- **1762–1763:** France ceded Louisiana west of the Mississippi to Spain (Treaty of Fontainebleau 1762) and the eastern portion to Britain (Treaty of Paris 1763). Records after 1769 in the western territory shift to Spanish administrative structures, though the Catholic Church and notarial offices continued without interruption.
- **1764–1769:** Transition period before effective Spanish administration.
- **1800:** Napoleon secretly retroceded Louisiana to France (Treaty of San Ildefonso).
- **1803:** Louisiana Purchase — territory transferred to the United States.
- A family's records likely cross both the French series (pre-1769) and the Spanish series (1769–1803), filed under different administrative systems but at the same physical repositories (Louisiana Historical Center, ANOM, Notarial Archives). Search both series together rather than treating them as unrelated.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** There was no civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths during the French or Spanish colonial period (1700–1803). The FamilySearch Wiki page for Louisiana Vital Records returned only generic fallback content during this survey; no Louisiana-specific registration start date was returned by any tool.
- **What exists for this period:** Catholic church sacramental registers are the functional vital records. The indexed FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905, 987,654 records) is the primary online resource covering the colonial period.
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of New Orleans; Louisiana Historical Center, New Orleans.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic sacramental registers; Superior Council notarial acts for marriage contracts and estate settlements.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (sole legally recognized denomination throughout the French and Spanish colonial periods).
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including of enslaved persons per the Code Noir), marriages, burials; marriage dispensations; confirmations.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905.
- **Digitized volume:** Image group 004330991 — 264 browse-only images of Archdiocese of New Orleans sacramental registers, covering Orleans Parish 1720–1803. This volume is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable: it must be browsed image by image. Per wiki_search results at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records, St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans has registers from 1720.
- **Language:** French (pre-1769 entries), then Spanish (post-1769). Researchers must be able to read both colonial French and Spanish script.
- **Physical holdings:** Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives; Louisiana Historical Center.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** No federal census was taken during the French colonial period. Louisiana was not included in the 1790 federal census. The first census covering the territory after the Louisiana Purchase was 1810.
- **Colonial enumerations:** French colonial census rolls (recensements) exist. Per wiki_search results at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records, these are held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France.
- **Access:** Physical visit or written inquiry to ANOM required. Some have been transcribed and published by Louisiana genealogical societies.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Estate inventories, wills, letters of administration, guardianships, civil suits, and contracts.
- **Superior Council records:** The Conseil Supérieur was the colonial court and maintained land grants, court proceedings, contracts, and estate inventories for the French period (1699–1762). Per wiki_search at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records, these are held at the Louisiana Historical Center and have been partially digitized.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection 2078341) — 456,789 records at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341. Date range begins 1756, covering the later French colonial and full Spanish colonial period.
- **Digitized volume:** Image group 004330992 — 149 browse-only images of French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records), covering Louisiana 1699–1769, in French and Spanish. 0% name-indexed; not full-text searchable. Must be browsed image by image.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** Both wills (testate estates) and letters of administration (intestate estates) appear in Superior Council and notarial records.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French colonial land system used concessions (grants by the Superior Council), not the rectangular survey system later used in U.S. territories. Spanish grants followed a similar civil-law tradition.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Per wiki_search at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants, French concessions and Spanish land grants are documented in the American State Papers: Public Lands series and in records at the Louisiana State Land Office. The New Orleans Notarial Archives holds contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the 1730s onward — the oldest continuous notarial office in North America — and the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center provides public access.
- **Types:** Land concessions, notarial property contracts, marriage settlements, property transfers.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Land Office; New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center; Louisiana Historical Center.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Seven Years' War (1754–1763) ended French rule; colonial militia records exist for both French and Spanish periods.
- **Record types:** French colonial muster rolls and troop registers; Spanish colonial military records post-1769.
- **Where held:** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France (French-period records); Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain (Spanish-period records). NARA (archives.gov) holds some post-Purchase military records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1, New Orleans (established 1789, under Spanish rule); earlier colonial burials were in Catholic churchyards.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) lists some entries; coverage for the 1700s is sparse.
- **Physical records:** Burial registers are part of the sacramental registers held by the Archdiocese of New Orleans.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Moniteur de la Louisiane (Louisiana's first newspaper) began in 1794 — too late for most French colonial research.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State University Louisiana Digital Library; Library of Congress Chronicling America database; both carry early Louisiana newspaper microfilm, but French-period papers are very sparse.
- **Content value:** For the 1700s, newspapers are not a primary genealogical source; notarial acts and church registers serve that role.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was the primary port of entry for the colony throughout the 1700s.
- **Record types:** French colonial ship manifests and passenger lists are administrative records held at ANOM (Aix-en-Provence, France). Some have been transcribed by Louisiana genealogical societies.
- **Access:** French colonial manifests are not available on mainstream genealogy platforms (Ancestry, NARA online portals) in the same way as 19th-century lists. Research through ANOM or published transcriptions.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records
- **Types:** French colonial fiscal records are limited; some tribute and trade records exist in the Superior Council holdings.
- **Date range:** 1699–1769 (French period) within Superior Council records; Spanish-period fiscal records at ANOM and Archivo General de Indias.
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center; ANOM, France.
- **Substitute value:** Colonial census rolls (recensements) at ANOM can partially substitute for absent tax lists in the 1700s.

### Other record types
- **Notarial acts (critical for this period):** Marriage contracts, apprenticeship indentures, emancipation acts for enslaved persons, and commercial contracts were recorded by notaries. The New Orleans Notarial Archives holds these from the 1730s and they frequently name parents, siblings, and heirs who appear nowhere else.
- **Slave records / Code Noir records:** The Code Noir required Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons, so sacramental registers are one of the few sources where enslaved individuals appear by name. Estate inventories in the Superior Council records also name enslaved people.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (987,654 records); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (456,789 records) | Free |
| FamilySearch (browse-only) | Image group 004330991: 264 images, sacramental registers 1720–1803 (Orleans Parish); image group 004330992: 149 images, notarial acts 1699–1769 (Louisiana) — both in French/Spanish, 0% indexed | Free, browse-only |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records; limited colonial-era material | Free |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned a total of 2 digitized volumes matching Louisiana, 1700–1803. Both are represented above; this is the complete returned set. The tool did not return a summary breakdown by record-type group.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center (New Orleans, Old U.S. Mint) | Superior Council records; sacramental registers; partially digitized | In-person / contact |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial acts from the 1730s; marriage settlements; property; wills | In-person; some online finding aids |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Sacramental registers from 1720 (St. Louis Cathedral) | Contact the archive |
| Louisiana State Land Office | French concessions and Spanish land grants | In-person / contact |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial administrative records, census rolls (recensements), military registers, ship manifests | In-person; online catalog at anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial administrative records for Louisiana (1762–1803) | In-person; PARES online portal |

## Records NOT online
- French colonial census rolls (recensements) — at ANOM, France; not fully digitized online.
- French and Spanish colonial ship manifests and immigration records — at ANOM; not on mainstream genealogy platforms.
- Spanish colonial administrative records for Louisiana (1762–1803) — at Archivo General de Indias, Seville; not fully digitized.
- Bulk of New Orleans Notarial Archives pre-1803 notarial acts — research onsite or through the Research Center.
- Superior Council records beyond FamilySearch's two digitized volumes — held at the Louisiana Historical Center.

## Known record losses
No tool result returned in this session identified a confirmed loss of a specific Louisiana colonial record set. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana-specific record types returned only generic fallback content and did not report losses. Researchers should contact the Louisiana Historical Center directly to confirm the survival status of any specific series before treating an empty search result as a loss.

## Research tips
- **Catholic church records are the de facto vital records for the 1700s.** There was no civil registration during the French or Spanish colonial period. Begin with the FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) and the browse-only image group 004330991 for Orleans Parish registers 1720–1803. Per wiki_search at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records, St. Louis Cathedral registers begin in 1720.
- **Notarial acts are the richest source for family relationships.** Marriage contracts, succession acts, and property transfers in the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (from the 1730s) frequently name parents, siblings, and heirs who appear nowhere else. Per wiki_search at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants, the New Orleans Notarial Archives is the oldest continuous notarial office in North America and the Research Center provides public access.
- **The two FamilySearch volumes for 1700–1803 are browse-only in French and Spanish.** Image group 004330991 (sacramental registers, 1720–1803) and 004330992 (Superior Council notarial acts, 1699–1769) are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. Scrolling through images requires reading colonial French and Spanish handwriting.
- **Research must span two European national archives.** French-period records (1699–1762) are partly at the Louisiana Historical Center and partly at ANOM (Aix-en-Provence, France). Spanish-period records (1762–1803) have a parallel track at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville). A complete 1700s family trail typically requires contacting at least two of these three repositories.
- **The Code Noir makes church records a source for enslaved ancestors.** The law required Catholic baptism of every enslaved person; sacramental registers and estate inventories in the Superior Council records are among the very few sources naming enslaved individuals by name during this era.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic fallback content for all Louisiana-specific pages during this survey.** Check https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy directly before relying on any gap noted in this guide — the wiki pages likely contain more specific guidance than what was accessible during this session.

- A family's records likely cross both the French series (pre-1769) and the Spanish series (1769–1803), filed under different administrative systems but at the same physical repositories (Louisiana Historical Center, ANOM, Notarial Archives). Search both series together rather than treating them as unrelated.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** There was no civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths during the French or Spanish colonial period (1700–1803). The FamilySearch Wiki page for Louisiana Vital Records returned only generic fallback content during this survey; no Louisiana-specific registration start date was returned by any tool.
- **What exists for this period:** Catholic church sacramental registers are the functional vital records. The indexed FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905, 987,654 records) is the primary online resource covering the colonial period.
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of New Orleans; Louisiana Historical Center, New Orleans.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic sacramental registers; Superior Council notarial acts for marriage contracts and estate settlements.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (sole legally recognized denomination throughout the French and Spanish colonial periods).
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including of enslaved persons per the Code Noir), marriages, burials; marriage dispensations; confirmations.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905.
- **Digitized volume:** Image group 004330991 — 264 browse-only images of Archdiocese of New Orleans sacramental registers, covering Orleans Parish 1720–1803. This volume is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable: it must be browsed image by image. Per wiki_search results at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records, St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans has registers from 1720.
- **Language:** French (pre-1769 entries), then Spanish (post-1769). Researchers must be able to read both colonial French and Spanish script.
- **Physical holdings:** Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives; Louisiana Historical Center.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** No federal census was taken during the French colonial period. Louisiana was not included in the 1790 federal census. The first census covering the territory after the Louisiana Purchase was 1810.
- **Colonial enumerations:** French colonial census rolls (recensements) exist. Per wiki_search results at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records, these are held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France.
- **Access:** Physical visit or written inquiry to ANOM required. Some have been transcribed and published by Louisiana genealogical societies.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Estate inventories, wills, letters of administration, guardianships, civil suits, and contracts.
- **Superior Council records:** The Conseil Supérieur was the colonial court and maintained land grants, court proceedings, contracts, and estate inventories for the French period (1699–1762). Per wiki_search at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records, these are held at the Louisiana Historical Center and have been partially digitized.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection 2078341) — 456,789 records at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341. Date range begins 1756, covering the later French colonial and full Spanish colonial period.
- **Digitized volume:** Image group 004330992 — 149 browse-only images of French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records), covering Louisiana 1699–1769, in French and Spanish. 0% name-indexed; not full-text searchable. Must be browsed image by image.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** Both wills (testate estates) and letters of administration (intestate estates) appear in Superior Council and notarial records.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French colonial land system used concessions (grants by the Superior Council), not the rectangular survey system later used in U.S. territories. Spanish grants followed a similar civil-law tradition.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Per wiki_search at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants, French concessions and Spanish land grants are documented in the American State Papers: Public Lands series and in records at the Louisiana State Land Office. The New Orleans Notarial Archives holds contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the 1730s onward — the oldest continuous notarial office in North America — and the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center provides public access.
- **Types:** Land concessions, notarial property contracts, marriage settlements, property transfers.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Land Office; New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center; Louisiana Historical Center.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Seven Years' War (1754–1763) ended French rule; colonial militia records exist for both French and Spanish periods.
- **Record types:** French colonial muster rolls and troop registers; Spanish colonial military records post-1769.
- **Where held:** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France (French-period records); Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain (Spanish-period records). NARA (archives.gov) holds some post-Purchase military records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1, New Orleans (established 1789, under Spanish rule); earlier colonial burials were in Catholic churchyards.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) lists some entries; coverage for the 1700s is sparse.
- **Physical records:** Burial registers are part of the sacramental registers held by the Archdiocese of New Orleans.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Moniteur de la Louisiane (Louisiana's first newspaper) began in 1794 — too late for most French colonial research.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State University Louisiana Digital Library; Library of Congress Chronicling America database; both carry early Louisiana newspaper microfilm, but French-period papers are very sparse.
- **Content value:** For the 1700s, newspapers are not a primary genealogical source; notarial acts and church registers serve that role.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was the primary port of entry for the colony throughout the 1700s.
- **Record types:** French colonial ship manifests and passenger lists are administrative records held at ANOM (Aix-en-Provence, France). Some have been transcribed by Louisiana genealogical societies.
- **Access:** French colonial manifests are not available on mainstream genealogy platforms (Ancestry, NARA online portals) in the same way as 19th-century lists. Research through ANOM or published transcriptions.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records
- **Types:** French colonial fiscal records are limited; some tribute and trade records exist in the Superior Council holdings.
- **Date range:** 1699–1769 (French period) within Superior Council records; Spanish-period fiscal records at ANOM and Archivo General de Indias.
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center; ANOM, France.
- **Substitute value:** Colonial census rolls (recensements) at ANOM can partially substitute for absent tax lists in the 1700s.

### Other record types
- **Notarial acts (critical for this period):** Marriage contracts, apprenticeship indentures, emancipation acts for enslaved persons, and commercial contracts were recorded by notaries. The New Orleans Notarial Archives holds these from the 1730s and they frequently name parents, siblings, and heirs who appear nowhere else.
- **Slave records / Code Noir records:** The Code Noir required Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons, so sacramental registers are one of the few sources where enslaved individuals appear by name. Estate inventories in the Superior Council records also name enslaved people.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (987,654 records); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (456,789 records) | Free |
| FamilySearch (browse-only) | Image group 004330991: 264 images, sacramental registers 1720–1803 (Orleans Parish); image group 004330992: 149 images, notarial acts 1699–1769 (Louisiana) — both in French/Spanish, 0% indexed | Free, browse-only |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records; limited colonial-era material | Free |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned a total of 2 digitized volumes matching Louisiana, 1700–1803. Both are represented above; this is the complete returned set. The tool did not return a summary breakdown by record-type group.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center (New Orleans, Old U.S. Mint) | Superior Council records; sacramental registers; partially digitized | In-person / contact |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial acts from the 1730s; marriage settlements; property; wills | In-person; some online finding aids |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Sacramental registers from 1720 (St. Louis Cathedral) | Contact the archive |
| Louisiana State Land Office | French concessions and Spanish land grants | In-person / contact |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial administrative records, census rolls (recensements), military registers, ship manifests | In-person; online catalog at anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial administrative records for Louisiana (1762–1803) | In-person; PARES online portal |

## Records NOT online
- French colonial census rolls (recensements) — at ANOM, France; not fully digitized online.
- French and Spanish colonial ship manifests and immigration records — at ANOM; not on mainstream genealogy platforms.
- Spanish colonial administrative records for Louisiana (1762–1803) — at Archivo General de Indias, Seville; not fully digitized.
- Bulk of New Orleans Notarial Archives pre-1803 notarial acts — research onsite or through the Research Center.
- Superior Council records beyond FamilySearch's two digitized volumes — held at the Louisiana Historical Center.

## Known record losses
No tool result returned in this session identified a confirmed loss of a specific Louisiana colonial record set. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana-specific record types returned only generic fallback content and did not report losses. Researchers should contact the Louisiana Historical Center directly to confirm the survival status of any specific series before treating an empty search result as a loss.

## Research tips
- **Catholic church records are the de facto vital records for the 1700s.** There was no civil registration during the French or Spanish colonial period. Begin with the FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) and the browse-only image group 004330991 for Orleans Parish registers 1720–1803. Per wiki_search at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records, St. Louis Cathedral registers begin in 1720.
- **Notarial acts are the richest source for family relationships.** Marriage contracts, succession acts, and property transfers in the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (from the 1730s) frequently name parents, siblings, and heirs who appear nowhere else. Per wiki_search at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants, the New Orleans Notarial Archives is the oldest continuous notarial office in North America and the Research Center provides public access.
- **The two FamilySearch volumes for 1700–1803 are browse-only in French and Spanish.** Image group 004330991 (sacramental registers, 1720–1803) and 004330992 (Superior Council notarial acts, 1699–1769) are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. Scrolling through images requires reading colonial French and Spanish handwriting.
- **Research must span two European national archives.** French-period records (1699–1762) are partly at the Louisiana Historical Center and partly at ANOM (Aix-en-Provence, France). Spanish-period records (1762–1803) have a parallel track at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville). A complete 1700s family trail typically requires contacting at least two of these three repositories.
- **The Code Noir makes church records a source for enslaved ancestors.** The law required Catholic baptism of every enslaved person; sacramental registers and estate inventories in the Superior Council records are among the very few sources naming enslaved individuals by name during this era.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic fallback content for all Louisiana-specific pages during this survey.** Check https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy directly before relying on any gap noted in this guide — the wiki pages likely contain more specific guidance than what was accessible during this session.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Coal Mining Region — Schuylkill County (1860–1900)

This guide is anchored on Schuylkill County, the core of Pennsylvania's anthracite Coal Region, and notes where practices in neighboring coal counties differ. The Coal Region also spans Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties; each requires its own survey. Luzerne is particularly important because it was the parent county of Lackawanna before 1878.

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Schuylkill County formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton Counties
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by the tool during this survey
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining; national center of hard coal production by mid-century, dominated by the Philadelphia and Reading Railroad and smaller colliery operators
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish and Welsh (1820s–1860s), German (mid-century), then Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian, and Ukrainian (1880s–1900s) — shaped church membership and record languages
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (Irish, later Polish/Slovak/Italian/Ukrainian national parishes), Welsh Congregational and Baptist, Methodist Episcopal, Lutheran, Presbyterian, Episcopal, Ukrainian Greek Catholic, Russian Orthodox
- **Key historical events:** Molly Maguires trials 1876–1879 (court records in Pottsville); Great Railroad Strike 1877; UMWA organizing from 1890

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County boundaries stable from formation in 1811 through the target period
- Lackawanna County carved from Luzerne County in 1878 — records for the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre sub-region before 1878 are under Luzerne County
- The broader Coal Region spans Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties — search all counties a family may have lived in as miners moved between collieries

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not require statewide civil registration of births and deaths until 1906 (state level). No statewide birth or death series exists for 1860–1900. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records)
- **Marriage:** Marriage licenses and bonds kept at the county level from the colonial period; FamilySearch holds Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950 (collection 1921317, 524,189 records, indexed + images); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (collection 1571957, 312,045 records, indexed + images); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, 198,765 records, no images)
- **Death certificates:** Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968 (collection 2255317, 4.2M records, indexed) — postdates the target period but covers subjects who died after 1906
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration for 1860–1900; church records are the primary substitute for this entire period
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism and burial registers; newspaper obituaries; cemetery sexton records; mortality schedules attached to the 1860, 1870, and 1880 federal censuses

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic, Welsh Congregational and Baptist, Methodist Episcopal, Lutheran, Presbyterian, Episcopal; from the 1880s, Polish and Slovak Roman Catholic national parishes, Ukrainian Greek Catholic, Russian Orthodox
