# Locality Guide: Massachusetts (Early Puritan Settlements, 1620–1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Plymouth Colony established 1620 (Pilgrim settlers); Massachusetts Bay Colony chartered 1628, settled during the Great Migration of approximately 20,000 Puritans, 1630–1640. The two colonies merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691 under a new royal charter. (Wikipedia: Massachusetts Bay Colony)
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay Colony); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Crown of England (colonial period)
- **Population during period:** The population tool returned no data for this period. The Great Migration (1630–1640) brought approximately 20,000 settlers to the Bay Colony. (Wikipedia)
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fishing, fur trading, timber — shaped early land grants, proprietors' records, and probate inventories
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers; small numbers of non-Puritan English, servants, and Indigenous peoples
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) was the established colonial church; small Baptist, Quaker, and Anglican congregations also existed
- **Key historical events:** Great Migration 1630–1640; King Philip's War 1675–1676 (disrupted several towns); Plymouth Colony merger 1691

## Boundary changes
- Plymouth Colony (1620–1691) and Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628–1691) operated as entirely separate jurisdictions with distinct record systems throughout the target period.
- In 1691, a new royal charter merged both colonies into the Province of Massachusetts Bay.
- Records before 1691 must be searched in each colony's record series separately — they do not form a unified collection.
- The FamilySearch wiki notes that Plymouth Colony records (1620–1691) are published and indexed separately from Massachusetts Bay Colony records. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Town-level registration of births, marriages, and deaths was mandated by the Massachusetts Bay Colony beginning in **1639** (town level). Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records, confirmed by Wikipedia. The specific Massachusetts Vital Records wiki page returned only generic content during this survey and could not add to this date.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch holds "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (collection id: 2061550, 3,456,789 records) covering births, marriages, and deaths recorded at the town level. The "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" multi-volume Tanner–Corbin series abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns and is an important compiled resource. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records
- **Where held:** Original records at individual town halls; Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds colonial-era copies. FamilySearch: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550
- **Gaps:** No civil registration before 1639 — events 1620–1638 require church records or other substitutes. King Philip's War (1675–1676) disrupted some towns.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Congregational church baptismal and marriage registers; the Tanner–Corbin published series

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (Puritan) as the established church kept the most complete records; small Baptist, Quaker, and Anglican congregations also present
- **Record types:** Membership admissions, baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations, and disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments). Church records are the primary source for births before 1639. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational
- **Where held:** Many early records published in the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series and local historical society publications (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational). FamilySearch holds "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (collection id: 1921657, 987,654 records: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657). FamilySearch also holds one digitized volume of Suffolk County Congregational church admissions and baptisms, 1630–1700 (image group 007612045, 121 images) — this volume is **full-text searchable but 0% name-indexed**: use FamilySearch's full-text search interface, not the standard record search. NEHGS (Boston) holds significant manuscript church record collections.
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census was 1790 — no federal census records exist for 1620–1700.
- **State/provincial census:** No colonial-era census returns appear in the FamilySearch collections for this period. Some local enumerations were made under colonial authority but survive sporadically.
- **Other enumerations:** Town meeting and proprietors' records sometimes list townsmen and proprietors, acting as partial substitutes. FamilySearch holds one browse-only digitized volume: town meeting and proprietors' records, 1620–1698 (image group 007612044, 188 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image with no search capability).
- **Access:** No name-indexed census records exist for this period.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions, court minutes
- **Date range:** Probate records begin in the 1630s at county probate courts. FamilySearch holds "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (collection id: 1678901, 567,890 records: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901). Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records
- **Testate or intestate:** Wills (testate) and administrations (intestate) form separate series — identify which applies before searching.
- **Where held:** County probate courts; Massachusetts Archives holds colonial court records and governor's correspondence from the 1620s onward.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (colonial New England)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Land grants were made by the General Court; county registries of deeds recorded transfers from the 1630s. The wiki_search result notes deed books "survive in remarkably complete runs at county registries of deeds." Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records
- **Types:** Deeds, land grants, patents, proprietors' records
- **Date range:** From the 1630s at the county level
- **Where held:** County registries of deeds (physical; some digitized on county sites); Massachusetts Archives. No FamilySearch indexed land record collection appeared in results for 1620–1700. The browse-only town meeting and proprietors' records volume (image group 007612044) may include early land grants.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** King Philip's War, 1675–1676; various earlier colonial skirmishes
- **Record types:** Colonial militia muster rolls and service records. Federal NARA records begin with conflicts after 1775 and do not cover colonial-era militia.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (colonial court and governor's records include militia documentation); published transcriptions in town and county histories. No FamilySearch indexed collection for Massachusetts colonial military records was returned in this survey.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Congregational meetinghouse burial grounds in every colonial town; King's Chapel Burying Ground, Granary Burying Ground, and Copp's Hill in Boston are notable early examples.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) holds transcriptions of many colonial gravestone inscriptions.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for the 1600s are fragmentary; gravestone inscriptions often provide the most direct evidence of death dates for this period.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No Massachusetts newspapers existed in the 1600s. The first regular colonial newspaper (Boston News-Letter) was not established until 1704.
- **Where held:** Not applicable for 1620–1700.
- **Content value:** Town records, church discipline records, and court minutes serve the function newspapers would later fill.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Boston; Plymouth
- **Record types:** Passenger lists for the Great Migration period (1620–1643) are not available in the FamilySearch Passenger Lists collection (id: 1784312), which begins in 1820. The NEHGS "Great Migration" study series (published volumes by Robert Charles Anderson) documents every known settler arriving 1620–1643 with sourced biographical sketches. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records
- **Where held:** Great Migration series at NEHGS (Boston) and AmericanAncestors.org; scattered original ship passenger lists in English and colonial archives, not available as a unified indexed online series.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children. When researching a family's colonial arrival, examine the Great Migration study series for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Colonial rate lists and town tax assessments
- **Date range:** Variable by town; some survive from the 1640s
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives; individual town archives. Not represented in any FamilySearch indexed collection returned for this period.
- **Substitute value:** Colonial rate lists can place an individual in a specific town at a specific date, substituting for the absent census record.

### Other record types
- **Town meeting records:** Each Massachusetts town kept town meeting minutes recording land grants, appointments, and community business. FamilySearch holds one browse-only volume: town meeting and proprietors' records, 1620–1698 (image group 007612044, 188 images; must be browsed image by image — 0% indexed and not full-text searchable).
- **Published genealogies and county histories:** 19th-century county and town histories reprint early records and often contain the only surviving transcription of records since lost. NEHGS holds extensive published genealogies for New England families.
- **Great Migration study series:** Robert Charles Anderson's multi-volume work documents every known settler to Massachusetts 1620–1643 with sourced biographical sketches and is the essential starting point for Great Migration research.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Town Vital Records 1620–1890 (3,456,789 records, id: 2061550); Church Records 1630–1920 (987,654 records, id: 1921657); Probate Records 1635–1991 (567,890 records, id: 1678901) | Free |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery and gravestone records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | National Archives; colonial-era militia records not held federally | Free/in-person |

The FamilySearch Passenger Lists collection (id: 1784312) begins in 1820 and does not cover the 1620–1700 target period. The Naturalization Records collection (id: 1459213) begins in 1790 and also falls outside this period.

**Coverage of this survey:** 2 digitized volumes match this place and period in the FamilySearch volume catalog; both are detailed above. The returned set was complete (no additional pages).

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | Colony records, governor's correspondence, court records from 1620s; tax and legislative records | In-person; some records digitized |
| NEHGS, Boston | Great Migration study series, manuscript church records, published genealogies, town histories | In-person / AmericanAncestors.org (membership) |
| County Registries of Deeds | Deed and land grant books from the 1630s in complete runs | In-person / some county sites online |
| County Probate Courts | Probate records from the 1630s | In-person / FamilySearch collection 1678901 |
| Individual Town Halls | Original town vital records and meeting minutes | In-person / mail request |
| Plymouth County Archives | Plymouth Colony records (separate series, 1620–1691) | In-person |

## Records NOT online

- Colonial militia records (King Philip's War and earlier): not in any online indexed database; held at the Massachusetts Archives and in published town/county histories
- Town tax and rate lists: not in any FamilySearch indexed collection for this period
- County deed and land grant books: the county registries hold remarkably complete runs but these are not in FamilySearch's indexed collections for 1620–1700; the town meeting and proprietors' records volume (image group 007612044) is browse-only
- Pre-1700 passenger and ship records from the Great Migration: not in any FamilySearch indexed collection; the Great Migration study series at NEHGS is the primary compiled source

## Known record losses

No tool result returned in this survey names a specific destroyed record set for Massachusetts 1620–1700. King Philip's War (1675–1676) is documented by Wikipedia as having disrupted colonial settlements; whether specific town records were destroyed in that conflict was not stated by any tool result in this survey. Contact the Massachusetts Archives for holdings confirmation before concluding any specific series is absent.

## Research tips

- **Start with the Great Migration study series.** For any ancestor arriving in Massachusetts before 1643, Robert Charles Anderson's multi-volume series at NEHGS is the most thorough compiled source, with sourced biographical sketches for every known settler. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records
- **Search Plymouth Colony separately.** Plymouth Colony (1620–1691) records are published and indexed independently from Massachusetts Bay Colony records — searching only the Bay Colony series will miss Plymouth families. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records
- **Use the "Vital Records to 1850" published series.** The Tanner–Corbin series abstracts town clerk records for more than 200 Massachusetts towns and is often more accessible than original volumes. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records
- **Congregational church records are essential for pre-1639 events.** Before the 1639 town-recording mandate, only church records document births, marriages, and deaths — search baptismal and membership registers first for the 1620–1638 window. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational
- **Handle the two FamilySearch digitized volumes appropriately.** The town meeting and proprietors' records (image group 007612044, 1620–1698) must be browsed image by image — no name or text search is possible. The Suffolk County church admissions and baptisms (image group 007612045, 1630–1700) is full-text searchable via FamilySearch's full-text search, but is not reachable through the standard record search.
- **Probate and deed records survive from the 1630s** in remarkably complete runs and are among the best sources for confirming family relationships, property transfers, and community standing in this period. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records

- **Denominations present:** Congregational (Puritan) as the established church kept the most complete records; small Baptist, Quaker, and Anglican congregations also present
- **Record types:** Membership admissions, baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations, and disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments). Church records are the primary source for births before 1639. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational
- **Where held:** Many early records published in the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series and local historical society publications (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational). FamilySearch holds "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (collection id: 1921657, 987,654 records: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657). FamilySearch also holds one digitized volume of Suffolk County Congregational church admissions and baptisms, 1630–1700 (image group 007612045, 121 images) — this volume is **full-text searchable but 0% name-indexed**: use FamilySearch's full-text search interface, not the standard record search. NEHGS (Boston) holds significant manuscript church record collections.
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census was 1790 — no federal census records exist for 1620–1700.
- **State/provincial census:** No colonial-era census returns appear in the FamilySearch collections for this period. Some local enumerations were made under colonial authority but survive sporadically.
- **Other enumerations:** Town meeting and proprietors' records sometimes list townsmen and proprietors, acting as partial substitutes. FamilySearch holds one browse-only digitized volume: town meeting and proprietors' records, 1620–1698 (image group 007612044, 188 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image with no search capability).
- **Access:** No name-indexed census records exist for this period.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions, court minutes
- **Date range:** Probate records begin in the 1630s at county probate courts. FamilySearch holds "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (collection id: 1678901, 567,890 records: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901). Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records
- **Testate or intestate:** Wills (testate) and administrations (intestate) form separate series — identify which applies before searching.
- **Where held:** County probate courts; Massachusetts Archives holds colonial court records and governor's correspondence from the 1620s onward.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (colonial New England)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Land grants were made by the General Court; county registries of deeds recorded transfers from the 1630s. The wiki_search result notes deed books "survive in remarkably complete runs at county registries of deeds." Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records
- **Types:** Deeds, land grants, patents, proprietors' records
- **Date range:** From the 1630s at the county level
- **Where held:** County registries of deeds (physical; some digitized on county sites); Massachusetts Archives. No FamilySearch indexed land record collection appeared in results for 1620–1700. The browse-only town meeting and proprietors' records volume (image group 007612044) may include early land grants.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** King Philip's War, 1675–1676; various earlier colonial skirmishes
- **Record types:** Colonial militia muster rolls and service records. Federal NARA records begin with conflicts after 1775 and do not cover colonial-era militia.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (colonial court and governor's records include militia documentation); published transcriptions in town and county histories. No FamilySearch indexed collection for Massachusetts colonial military records was returned in this survey.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Congregational meetinghouse burial grounds in every colonial town; King's Chapel Burying Ground, Granary Burying Ground, and Copp's Hill in Boston are notable early examples.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) holds transcriptions of many colonial gravestone inscriptions.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for the 1600s are fragmentary; gravestone inscriptions often provide the most direct evidence of death dates for this period.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No Massachusetts newspapers existed in the 1600s. The first regular colonial newspaper (Boston News-Letter) was not established until 1704.
- **Where held:** Not applicable for 1620–1700.
- **Content value:** Town records, church discipline records, and court minutes serve the function newspapers would later fill.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Boston; Plymouth
- **Record types:** Passenger lists for the Great Migration period (1620–1643) are not available in the FamilySearch Passenger Lists collection (id: 1784312), which begins in 1820. The NEHGS "Great Migration" study series (published volumes by Robert Charles Anderson) documents every known settler arriving 1620–1643 with sourced biographical sketches. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records
- **Where held:** Great Migration series at NEHGS (Boston) and AmericanAncestors.org; scattered original ship passenger lists in English and colonial archives, not available as a unified indexed online series.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children. When researching a family's colonial arrival, examine the Great Migration study series for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Colonial rate lists and town tax assessments
- **Date range:** Variable by town; some survive from the 1640s
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives; individual town archives. Not represented in any FamilySearch indexed collection returned for this period.
- **Substitute value:** Colonial rate lists can place an individual in a specific town at a specific date, substituting for the absent census record.

### Other record types
- **Town meeting records:** Each Massachusetts town kept town meeting minutes recording land grants, appointments, and community business. FamilySearch holds one browse-only volume: town meeting and proprietors' records, 1620–1698 (image group 007612044, 188 images; must be browsed image by image — 0% indexed and not full-text searchable).
- **Published genealogies and county histories:** 19th-century county and town histories reprint early records and often contain the only surviving transcription of records since lost. NEHGS holds extensive published genealogies for New England families.
- **Great Migration study series:** Robert Charles Anderson's multi-volume work documents every known settler to Massachusetts 1620–1643 with sourced biographical sketches and is the essential starting point for Great Migration research.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Town Vital Records 1620–1890 (3,456,789 records, id: 2061550); Church Records 1630–1920 (987,654 records, id: 1921657); Probate Records 1635–1991 (567,890 records, id: 1678901) | Free |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery and gravestone records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | National Archives; colonial-era militia records not held federally | Free/in-person |

The FamilySearch Passenger Lists collection (id: 1784312) begins in 1820 and does not cover the 1620–1700 target period. The Naturalization Records collection (id: 1459213) begins in 1790 and also falls outside this period.

**Coverage of this survey:** 2 digitized volumes match this place and period in the FamilySearch volume catalog; both are detailed above. The returned set was complete (no additional pages).

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | Colony records, governor's correspondence, court records from 1620s; tax and legislative records | In-person; some records digitized |
| NEHGS, Boston | Great Migration study series, manuscript church records, published genealogies, town histories | In-person / AmericanAncestors.org (membership) |
| County Registries of Deeds | Deed and land grant books from the 1630s in complete runs | In-person / some county sites online |
| County Probate Courts | Probate records from the 1630s | In-person / FamilySearch collection 1678901 |
| Individual Town Halls | Original town vital records and meeting minutes | In-person / mail request |
| Plymouth County Archives | Plymouth Colony records (separate series, 1620–1691) | In-person |

## Records NOT online

- Colonial militia records (King Philip's War and earlier): not in any online indexed database; held at the Massachusetts Archives and in published town/county histories
- Town tax and rate lists: not in any FamilySearch indexed collection for this period
- County deed and land grant books: the county registries hold remarkably complete runs but these are not in FamilySearch's indexed collections for 1620–1700; the town meeting and proprietors' records volume (image group 007612044) is browse-only
- Pre-1700 passenger and ship records from the Great Migration: not in any FamilySearch indexed collection; the Great Migration study series at NEHGS is the primary compiled source

## Known record losses

No tool result returned in this survey names a specific destroyed record set for Massachusetts 1620–1700. King Philip's War (1675–1676) is documented by Wikipedia as having disrupted colonial settlements; whether specific town records were destroyed in that conflict was not stated by any tool result in this survey. Contact the Massachusetts Archives for holdings confirmation before concluding any specific series is absent.

## Research tips

- **Start with the Great Migration study series.** For any ancestor arriving in Massachusetts before 1643, Robert Charles Anderson's multi-volume series at NEHGS is the most thorough compiled source, with sourced biographical sketches for every known settler. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records
- **Search Plymouth Colony separately.** Plymouth Colony (1620–1691) records are published and indexed independently from Massachusetts Bay Colony records — searching only the Bay Colony series will miss Plymouth families. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records
- **Use the "Vital Records to 1850" published series.** The Tanner–Corbin series abstracts town clerk records for more than 200 Massachusetts towns and is often more accessible than original volumes. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records
- **Congregational church records are essential for pre-1639 events.** Before the 1639 town-recording mandate, only church records document births, marriages, and deaths — search baptismal and membership registers first for the 1620–1638 window. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational
- **Handle the two FamilySearch digitized volumes appropriately.** The town meeting and proprietors' records (image group 007612044, 1620–1698) must be browsed image by image — no name or text search is possible. The Suffolk County church admissions and baptisms (image group 007612045, 1630–1700) is full-text searchable via FamilySearch's full-text search, but is not reachable through the standard record search.
- **Probate and deed records survive from the 1630s** in remarkably complete runs and are among the best sources for confirming family relationships, property transfers, and community standing in this period. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records

Here is the locality guide the subagent produced:

---

**Oklahoma — Land Run Era (c. 1880–1910)**
*(Three overlapping jurisdictions: Unassigned Lands → Oklahoma Territory (est. May 2, 1890) + adjacent Indian Territory, both merging at statehood in 1907)*

---

### Key Records & Repositories

**Federal Homestead / Land Records — #1 priority**
Every Land Run claimant filed with the General Land Office. The final proof affidavit names the settler, witnesses (often neighbors and relatives), and years of residence. Two access points:
- FamilySearch: *"Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907"* (indexed)
- BLM GLO Records: [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)

**1890 Oklahoma Territorial Census**
The national 1890 federal census was largely destroyed. Oklahoma's territorial census survives at the **Oklahoma Historical Society** and is the primary enumeration for the first generation of settlers.

**County Vital Records (Marriage, 1890+)**
FamilySearch holds indexed collections of territorial-era county marriages.

**Indian Censuses & Rolls**
If a family may have had Native ancestry, or lived near Indian Territory:
- Dawes Rolls (Five Civilized Tribes) on FamilySearch
- Indian Territory agency census rolls

**Territorial Court & Naturalization Records**
Pre-1906 naturalizations were done by territorial courts — records are physical-only:
- **National Archives at Fort Worth** (covers Oklahoma and Indian Territory)
- **Oklahoma State Archives** (Oklahoma City)

**Church / Mission Records**
FamilySearch holds some mission and church record collections for the region.

---

### Critical Warnings

1. **Oklahoma Territory ≠ Indian Territory, 1890–1907.** A family near the boundary may have records under either jurisdiction — search both.
2. **Most settlers came from Kansas, Texas, or Missouri.** Tracing origins in departure-state records is usually the necessary first step before Oklahoma sources make sense.
3. The FamilySearch Wiki returned limited detail for Oklahoma-specific pages during this survey. Visit [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Genealogy) directly before treating any gap as final.

---

This guide is saved to the project as **loc_001**. When you're ready to move forward, a research plan can be built from it.

Indian Territory (Five Civilized Tribes area) remained a separate legal entity from Oklahoma Territory from 1890 through 1907. A family could have records filed under either territory depending on exactly which side of the line they lived on — search both unless the township or county is already established.

Most Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and other states. Identifying origins usually requires tracing the family backward through departure-state records before searching Oklahoma sources. See https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts

The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed nationwide, but Oklahoma Territory has a surviving 1890 territorial/special census held by the Oklahoma Historical Society — one of very few 1890 enumerations in the country. See https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run

Naturalization records before 1906 may appear in any court of record, not just federal courts — territorial district court files at the National Archives at Fort Worth and the Oklahoma State Archives are the primary search targets.

FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for all Oklahoma-specific pages (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips, and topic pages) during this survey. Visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Genealogy directly before relying on absences noted here.

Land-entry case files and homestead final proofs (FamilySearch volume 005221388, 1889-1907) are 74% name-indexed and searchable; Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (volume 005221389, 1898-1910) are 0% indexed and must be browsed image-by-image.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Oklahoma (Land Run Era, 1880–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Oklahoma Territory created May 2, 1890 by the Organic Act, from the Unassigned Lands of Indian Territory. The state of Oklahoma was admitted November 16, 1907, merging Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory.
- **Administrative center:** Guthrie was the capital of Oklahoma Territory (1890–1907). Oklahoma City became the state capital.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Before 1890 the Unassigned Lands were part of Indian Territory (federal domain); adjacent Five Civilized Tribes area remained Indian Territory until statehood.
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 settlers entered on April 22, 1889 (Land Run). The 1890 territorial census enumerated the new population; the 1900 federal census recorded about 392,000 in Oklahoma Territory and 392,000 in Indian Territory separately.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, homesteading, cattle ranching; later wheat agriculture and early oil discovery.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Anglo-American settlers from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and the Midwest; significant African-American 'Exoduster' communities; Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Seminole) in adjacent Indian Territory; freedmen (formerly enslaved people of tribal members).
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, and Catholic denominations established congregations beginning sporadically in 1889 per [Oklahoma Land Records wiki search result](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).
- **Key historical events:** Land Run of April 22, 1889 (Unassigned Lands); subsequent runs in 1891, 1892, 1893, 1895; creation of Oklahoma Territory 1890; Dawes Act allotment of tribal lands 1887–1906; statehood 1907.

## Boundary changes
- Before April 22, 1889: The Unassigned Lands were unsettled federal domain within Indian Territory with no settler civil government.
- May 2, 1890: Oklahoma Territory created from the Unassigned Lands and the No Man's Land (Panhandle). Indian Territory (Five Civilized Tribes) remained a separate jurisdiction immediately to the east.
- 1890–1907: Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory coexisted as distinct legal entities. Records generated west of the territorial boundary are Oklahoma Territory records; records east of it are Indian Territory records. Which side a given family lived on determines which record set to search.
- November 16, 1907: Both territories merged into the state of Oklahoma. County government was extended across the former Indian Territory.
- Researchers must identify which territory their ancestor was in; searching only one will miss half the population.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Oklahoma Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey and did not provide a specific statewide registration start year. The FamilySearch Wiki should be consulted directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records for current information.
- **What exists:** No statewide civil registration during the territorial period (1889–1907) is documented in the tool results for this survey. County-level marriage records begin 1890 per FamilySearch collection 2134789.
- **Where held:** Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995 (FamilySearch collection 2134789, 456,789 records / 913,578 persons, indexed + images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134789. County courthouses hold original registers.
- **Gaps:** No birth or death registration series for the territorial period appears in tool results. Church records and family Bibles are the primary substitute for births and deaths before statehood.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism/burial registers; mission records; homestead final proof affidavits (which record family members by name); probate files; newspaper notices.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, and Catholic missions active from 1889 onward per [Oklahoma Land Records wiki search result](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run). Mission churches in Indian Territory predate the Land Run by decades.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, membership rolls, mission school records.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1654321, Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965 (123,456 records / images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321. Denominational archives and the Oklahoma Historical Society hold originals.
- **Language:** Records are in English for settler congregations; some tribal mission records may include Cherokee or other Native languages.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Oklahoma and Indian Territory appear in the 1900 and 1910 federal censuses. The 1880 federal census covers the states and territories that existed then — families in pre-run Oklahoma were not yet there.
- **1890 surviving census:** The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed nationwide. # Locality Guide: Oklahoma (Land Run Era, 1880–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Oklahoma Territory created May 2, 1890 by the Organic Act, from the Unassigned Lands of Indian Territory. The state of Oklahoma was admitted November 16, 1907, merging Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory.

- **Parent jurisdiction:** Before 1890 the Unassigned Lands were part of Indian Territory (federal domain); adjacent Five Civilized Tribes area remained Indian Territory until statehood.
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 settlers entered on April 22, 1889 (Land Run). The 1890 territorial census enumerated the new population; the 1900 federal census recorded about 392,000 in Oklahoma Territory and 392,000 in Indian Territory separately.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, homesteading, cattle ranching; later wheat agriculture and early oil discovery.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Anglo-American settlers from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and the Midwest; significant African-American 'Exoduster' communities; Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Seminole) in adjacent Indian Territory; freedmen (formerly enslaved people of tribal members).
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, and Catholic denominations established congregations beginning sporadically in 1889 per [Oklahoma Land Records wiki search result](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).
- **Key historical events:** Land Run of April 22, 1889 (Unassigned Lands); subsequent runs in 1891, 1892, 1893, 1895; creation of Oklahoma Territory 1890; Dawes Act allotment of tribal lands 1887–1906; statehood 1907.

- May 2, 1890: Oklahoma Territory created from the Unassigned Lands and the No Man's Land (Panhandle). Indian Territory (Five Civilized Tribes) remained a separate jurisdiction immediately to the east.
- 1890–1907: Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory coexisted as distinct legal entities. Records generated west of the territorial boundary are Oklahoma Territory records; records east of it are Indian Territory records. Which side a given family lived on determines which record set to search.
- November 16, 1907: Both territories merged into the state of Oklahoma. County government was extended across the former Indian Territory.
- Researchers must identify which territory their ancestor was in; searching only one will miss half the population.

Here is the locality guide the research agent produced:

---

**Alabama Region, circa 1800 — Locality Research Guide**

The land that would become Alabama was not yet a separate jurisdiction in 1800 — it was part of the **Mississippi Territory**, organized in 1798. That shapes everything about what records survive and where they are held.

---

### Key Record Sources

**Mississippi Territory records (the right jurisdiction for Alabama circa 1800)**
- **Territorial censuses**: 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 — primary name sources. Physically held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)** in Montgomery.
- **FamilySearch Mississippi-scope collections** begin: land records (1798), court records (1799), church records (1800), and a census-substitute index (from 1792).

**Alabama-labeled FamilySearch collections** (church, marriages, probate) do not begin until 1803 at the earliest, so they miss 1800 entirely.

---

### Special Complication: Spanish Administration

The **Mobile area** was under Spanish rule through 1813. Church registers, land grants, and census returns for southern Alabama families are therefore in the **Archivo General de Indias** in Seville, Spain, with copies at the **Library of Congress** — not in any U.S. online repository.

---

### Digitized, Browsable Volumes

Unfortunately, a volume search returned **zero results** for both Alabama and Mississippi Territory in the 1780–1820 window within FamilySearch's digitized-volume system. This is a **digitization gap**, not a records loss — physical microfilm and paper records exist, particularly at ADAH and in the Spanish archives.

---

### Recommended Next Steps

1. Search the **Mississippi Territory collections on FamilySearch** (land, court, church records from 1798–1810).
2. Contact or visit **ADAH** for the territorial census holdings.
3. For southern Alabama families, look to the **Library of Congress** copies of the Spanish colonial records.
4. Consult [FamilySearch Alabama Genealogy Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy) for additional guidance.

When you're ready, the agent can build a full research plan routing searches through these Mississippi Territory collections.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood (ca. 1780–1819)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama Territory organized 1817 from the Mississippi Territory; Alabama achieved statehood December 14, 1819
- **Parent jurisdiction at 1800:** Mississippi Territory (organized April 7, 1798); the Mobile area remained under Spanish administration until 1813
- **County seat / administrative center:** Territorial capital was St. Stephens (Washington County); Mobile was the dominant southern settlement
- **Population during period:** No specific census figures returned from tools. European-American settlement was sparse and concentrated along river corridors and the Mobile Bay area. Creek and Cherokee nations inhabited much of the interior.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fur trade, and early cotton cultivation near river bottoms; Mobile was a regional trading port
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations in the interior; French Creole, Spanish, and Anglo-American settlers around Mobile and river corridors; enslaved persons present throughout settled areas
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic mission churches in the Mobile area (dating from French colonial period); Methodist and Baptist circuit riders arrived in the interior during the territorial period
- **Key historical events:** Creek War of 1813–1814 displaced much of the interior Creek population and opened new territory to Anglo-American settlement; Mobile came under U.S. control in 1813

## Boundary changes
- Before 1798: The Mobile area was administered successively by France (1702–1763), Britain (1763–1780), and Spain (1780–1813). The interior had no colonial civil administration.
- 1798–1817: The eastern part of present-day Alabama was part of the Mississippi Territory. The Mobile District remained under Spanish authority until 1813.
- 1817: Alabama Territory was carved out of the Mississippi Territory.
- 1819: Alabama achieved statehood.
- **Consequence for records:** Any records generated in present-day Alabama before 1817 are filed under Mississippi Territory jurisdiction. Searching under "Alabama" will miss these entirely. This is a temporal split — before 1817, look under Mississippi Territory; after 1817, look under Alabama Territory / Alabama.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Alabama Vital Records page was not successfully retrieved during this survey (all wiki_read calls returned generic content). No civil vital registration start date can be confirmed from this survey's tool results. No civil registration system existed in 1800.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch's Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950 (id 1598408, 612,345 records, 306,172 images) is the earliest indexed vital-events collection, beginning in 1809 — nine years after the target date. No civil birth or death registration collections appear for this period.
- **Where held:** County-level marriage registers at county courthouses; Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (see below); estate inventories naming heirs; territorial census enumerations

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile area, from French colonial period); Methodist and Baptist circuit riders (interior, territorial period)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials from Catholic missions; limited circuit records from interior Protestant congregations
- **Where held:** FamilySearch, Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950 (id 1986396, 156,789 records, 78,394 images — indexed + images). For the Mobile District: Spanish-era Catholic church registers are in the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress. French colonial records are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, with microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives (per [Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)).
- **Language:** French and Spanish church records are in those languages, not English

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1800 federal census covered the Mississippi Territory in principle, but coverage for the present-day Alabama portion is fragmentary. The 1810 census is more complete.
- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory was enumerated in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 — these are the prime sources for families present in 1800. Physical holdings are at ADAH, Montgomery (per [Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)).
- **FamilySearch index (index only, no images):** Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890 (id 2016756, 287,634 records). Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890 (id 1927171, 198,340 records) covers the territorial period beginning in 1792.
- **Spanish colonial:** The Spanish authorities enumerated the Mobile District; these census returns are in the Archivo General de Indias, Seville.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories — testate (will present) and intestate (administration)
- **Alabama collection:** Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985 (id 1537764, 438,210 records, 219,105 images — indexed + images) begins in 1809
- **Mississippi territorial court records:** Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920 (id 1855293, 245,670 records, 122,835 images — indexed + images) begins in 1799 and covers territorial-period court records. This is the primary online source for 1800.
- **Where held:** ADAH; county courthouses (later period); territorial-era records at ADAH and NARA Atlanta

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal public-domain land state (rectangular survey) for American-era grants; metes and bounds for Spanish and British colonial grants
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** U.S. General Land Office for American grants; Spanish Crown for pre-1813 Mobile District grants
- **Types:** Federal land patents and grants; Spanish colonial land grants; deeds; tax records
- **Earliest online source:** Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907 (id 1919694, 312,450 records, 156,225 images — indexed + images). Spanish and British colonial grants predate this and are in the Archivo General de Indias, with copies at the Library of Congress (per [Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)).
- **Where held:** ADAH; BLM General Land Office for federal patents; Archivo General de Indias for Spanish grants; Library of Congress for copies

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813–1814); War of 1812 (Mobile area); territorial militia muster rolls
- **Record types:** Militia rolls (part of the territorial record set at ADAH); federal pension files and bounty land warrants at NARA; service records at NARA
- **Where held:** ADAH for territorial militia rolls (per [Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)); NARA and Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for federal military records

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes some early Alabama cemeteries, but coverage for pre-1820 burials is sparse
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers (where they exist) are at local churches or ADAH

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Newspapers were rare in the Alabama region before 1819. Among the earliest are the Mobile Centinel (est. 1811) and the Madison Gazette (Huntsville, est. 1812).
- **Access:** Some early Alabama newspapers are on microfilm at ADAH; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for later digitized issues

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile was the region's primary port. New Orleans was the broader regional entry point.
- **Record types:** No formal American immigration passenger lists exist for Mobile specifically in 1800; Spanish colonial port records for Mobile are in the Archivo General de Indias.
- **Inland records:** Declarations of intention and naturalizations filed in territorial courts are included in the court records set; search Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920 (id 1855293) for these.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial tax lists; Spanish colonial capitation tax records for the Mobile District
- **Date range:** Territorial tax lists are part of the broader record set at ADAH, per [Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are a primary substitute for the fragmentary 1800 federal census, establishing presence in the territory in a specific year

### Other record types
- **Indigenous records:** Creek and Cherokee agency records, removal records, and treaty records are held at NARA; Dawes Rolls cover those who survived to the later enrollment period
- **Spanish colonial records:** Census returns, land grants, and church registers for the Mobile District, all in the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907 (id 1919694); Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920 (id 1855293); Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890 (id 1927171); Mississippi, Church Records, 1800–1950 (id 2034891); Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950 (id 1986396); Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950 (id 1598408); Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985 (id 1537764); Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890 (id 2016756) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census collections (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military Records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Subscription |
| NARA | Federal land patents, pension files, military records (https://www.archives.gov/) | In-person / online |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume_search returned 0 digitized image volumes catalogued under Alabama or Mississippi Territory for 1780–1820. This is the direct answer to the question about browsable record volumes: none are present in FamilySearch's volume system under these place labels for this period. The eight FamilySearch collections listed above do include images, but the earliest (Mississippi Church Records, Mississippi Territorial Land Records) begin in 1798–1800, while the Alabama-specific collections start in 1803–1809. The 0-volume result does not mean no physical microfilm or paper records exist; it means nothing is catalogued in the FamilySearch digitized-volume system under these place labels for this window.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Dept. of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery | Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810); territorial court records; militia rolls; tax lists; early land records | In-person; some via ADAH website |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial land grants, church registers, census returns for Mobile District | In-person; copies at Library of Congress |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records (1702–1763) | In-person |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | Microfilm copies of French colonial records | In-person or contact |
| Library of Congress | Copies of Spanish colonial records for Mobile District | In-person; online catalogue |
| NARA (Atlanta and Washington DC) | Federal land records, pension files, military service records | In-person / online finding aids |

## Records NOT online

- Mississippi Territory censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 (physical only at ADAH; 1810 partially in FamilySearch's census substitute index)
- Spanish colonial church registers for the Mobile District (Archivo General de Indias; Library of Congress copies — physical access)
- French colonial records (Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer and Mobile Municipal Archives microfilm — physical access)
- Territorial militia rolls and tax lists (ADAH — physical)
- Early territorial court records not yet digitized beyond the Mississippi, County Court Records collection

## Known record losses

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood (ca. 1780–1819)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama Territory organized 1817 from the Mississippi Territory; Alabama achieved statehood December 14, 1819
- **Parent jurisdiction at 1800:** Mississippi Territory (organized April 7, 1798); the Mobile area remained under Spanish administration until 1813
- **County seat / administrative center:** Territorial capital was St. Stephens (Washington County); Mobile was the dominant southern settlement
- **Population during period:** No specific census figures returned from tools. European-American settlement was sparse and concentrated along river corridors and the Mobile Bay area. Creek and Cherokee nations inhabited much of the interior.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fur trade, and early cotton cultivation near river bottoms; Mobile was a regional trading port
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations in the interior; French Creole, Spanish, and Anglo-American settlers around Mobile and river corridors; enslaved persons present throughout settled areas
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic mission churches in the Mobile area (dating from French colonial period); Methodist and Baptist circuit riders arrived in the interior during the territorial period
- **Key historical events:** Creek War of 1813–1814 displaced much of the interior Creek population and opened new territory to Anglo-American settlement; Mobile came under U.S. control in 1813

## Boundary changes
- Before 1798: The Mobile area was administered successively by France (1702–1763), Britain (1763–1780), and Spain (1780–1813). The interior had no colonial civil administration.
- 1798–1817: The eastern part of present-day Alabama was part of the Mississippi Territory. The Mobile District remained under Spanish authority until 1813.
- 1817: Alabama Territory was carved out of the Mississippi Territory.
- 1819: Alabama achieved statehood.
- **Consequence for records:** Any records generated in present-day Alabama before 1817 are filed under Mississippi Territory jurisdiction. Searching under "Alabama" will miss these entirely. This is a temporal split — before 1817, look under Mississippi Territory; after 1817, look under Alabama Territory / Alabama.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Alabama Vital Records page was not successfully retrieved during this survey (all wiki_read calls returned generic content). No civil vital registration start date can be confirmed from this survey's tool results. No civil registration system existed in 1800.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch's Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950 (id 1598408, 612,345 records, 306,172 images) is the earliest indexed vital-events collection, beginning in 1809 — nine years after the target date. No civil birth or death registration collections appear for this period.
- **Where held:** County-level marriage registers at county courthouses; Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (see below); estate inventories naming heirs; territorial census enumerations

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile area, from French colonial period); Methodist and Baptist circuit riders (interior, territorial period)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials from Catholic missions; limited circuit records from interior Protestant congregations
- **Where held:** FamilySearch, Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950 (id 1986396, 156,789 records, 78,394 images — indexed + images). For the Mobile District: Spanish-era Catholic church registers are in the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress. French colonial records are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, with microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives (per [Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)).
- **Language:** French and Spanish church records are in those languages, not English

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1800 federal census covered the Mississippi Territory in principle, but coverage for the present-day Alabama portion is fragmentary. The 1810 census is more complete.
- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory was enumerated in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 — these are the prime sources for families present in 1800. Physical holdings are at ADAH, Montgomery (per [Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)).
- **FamilySearch index (index only, no images):** Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890 (id 2016756, 287,634 records). Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890 (id 1927171, 198,340 records) covers the territorial period beginning in 1792.
- **Spanish colonial:** The Spanish authorities enumerated the Mobile District; these census returns are in the Archivo General de Indias, Seville.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories — testate (will present) and intestate (administration)
- **Alabama collection:** Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985 (id 1537764, 438,210 records, 219,105 images — indexed + images) begins in 1809
- **Mississippi territorial court records:** Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920 (id 1855293, 245,670 records, 122,835 images — indexed + images) begins in 1799 and covers territorial-period court records. This is the primary online source for 1800.
- **Where held:** ADAH; county courthouses (later period); territorial-era records at ADAH and NARA Atlanta

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal public-domain land state (rectangular survey) for American-era grants; metes and bounds for Spanish and British colonial grants
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** U.S. General Land Office for American grants; Spanish Crown for pre-1813 Mobile District grants
- **Types:** Federal land patents and grants; Spanish colonial land grants; deeds; tax records
- **Earliest online source:** Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907 (id 1919694, 312,450 records, 156,225 images — indexed + images). Spanish and British colonial grants predate this and are in the Archivo General de Indias, with copies at the Library of Congress (per [Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)).
- **Where held:** ADAH; BLM General Land Office for federal patents; Archivo General de Indias for Spanish grants; Library of Congress for copies

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813–1814); War of 1812 (Mobile area); territorial militia muster rolls
- **Record types:** Militia rolls (part of the territorial record set at ADAH); federal pension files and bounty land warrants at NARA; service records at NARA
- **Where held:** ADAH for territorial militia rolls (per [Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)); NARA and Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for federal military records

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes some early Alabama cemeteries, but coverage for pre-1820 burials is sparse
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers (where they exist) are at local churches or ADAH

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Newspapers were rare in the Alabama region before 1819. Among the earliest are the Mobile Centinel (est. 1811) and the Madison Gazette (Huntsville, est. 1812).
- **Access:** Some early Alabama newspapers are on microfilm at ADAH; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for later digitized issues

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile was the region's primary port. New Orleans was the broader regional entry point.
- **Record types:** No formal American immigration passenger lists exist for Mobile specifically in 1800; Spanish colonial port records for Mobile are in the Archivo General de Indias.
- **Inland records:** Declarations of intention and naturalizations filed in territorial courts are included in the court records set; search Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920 (id 1855293) for these.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial tax lists; Spanish colonial capitation tax records for the Mobile District
- **Date range:** Territorial tax lists are part of the broader record set at ADAH, per [Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are a primary substitute for the fragmentary 1800 federal census, establishing presence in the territory in a specific year

### Other record types
- **Indigenous records:** Creek and Cherokee agency records, removal records, and treaty records are held at NARA; Dawes Rolls cover those who survived to the later enrollment period
- **Spanish colonial records:** Census returns, land grants, and church registers for the Mobile District, all in the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907 (id 1919694); Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920 (id 1855293); Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890 (id 1927171); Mississippi, Church Records, 1800–1950 (id 2034891); Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950 (id 1986396); Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950 (id 1598408); Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985 (id 1537764); Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890 (id 2016756) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census collections (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military Records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Subscription |
| NARA | Federal land patents, pension files, military records (https://www.archives.gov/) | In-person / online |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume_search returned 0 digitized image volumes catalogued under Alabama or Mississippi Territory for 1780–1820. This is the direct answer to the question about browsable record volumes: none are present in FamilySearch's volume system under these place labels for this period. The eight FamilySearch collections listed above do include images, but the earliest (Mississippi Church Records, Mississippi Territorial Land Records) begin in 1798–1800, while the Alabama-specific collections start in 1803–1809. The 0-volume result does not mean no physical microfilm or paper records exist; it means nothing is catalogued in the FamilySearch digitized-volume system under these place labels for this window.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |

| Alabama Dept. of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery | Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810); territorial court records; militia rolls; tax lists; early land records | In-person; some via ADAH website |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial land grants, church registers, census returns for Mobile District | In-person; copies at Library of Congress |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records (1702–1763) | In-person |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | Microfilm copies of French colonial records | In-person or contact |
| Library of Congress | Copies of Spanish colonial records for Mobile District | In-person; online catalogue |
| NARA (Atlanta and Washington DC) | Federal land records, pension files, military service records | In-person / online finding aids |

- Spanish colonial church registers for the Mobile District (Archivo General de Indias; Library of Congress copies — physical access)

## Locality Guide — Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1900)

**Guide written as loc_001**, centered on **Schuylkill County** — the historic heart of the anthracite region and the county your Irish ancestors most likely inhabited if working the mines in this era.

---

### Summary of Findings

The county's population nearly doubled between 1860 and 1900, driven overwhelmingly by Irish and later Welsh, German, and Slavic immigration into the mining towns. Here is what you need to know to research Irish coal-miner families there:

---

### Key Record Sets

**1. Catholic Parish Registers**
- The most important starting point for Irish families.
- Schuylkill County parishes fall under the **Archdiocese of Philadelphia** (and later the Diocese of Allentown) — *not* the Diocese of Scranton as many researchers assume.
- Registers are held locally and through diocesan archives; not broadly digitized.

**2. Anthracite Coal Industry Records**
- The **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index** covers roughly 41,000 colliery workers drawn from company payroll books — an excellent finding tool for named miners.
- Company records for Schuylkill County operators survive in varying degrees through the Hagley Museum and state archives.

**3. Molly Maguires Records**
- Trial transcripts and Pinkerton detective reports name **hundreds of Irish-born miners and their families**, making them a surprisingly rich genealogical source for the 1870s–1880s.

**4. FamilySearch Digitized Collections**
Five digitized volumes exist for Schuylkill County — naturalization records, church registers, probate, marriage, and deeds — but:
  - **Four of the five must be browsed image-by-image** (no name index).
  - The **deeds collection is only 22% indexed** — the rest requires browsing.

**5. Naturalization Records**
- Pre-1906, naturalizations could be filed in *any court of record*, so you must check multiple courts (common pleas, quarter sessions, orphans' court) rather than assuming a single source.

---

| Pitfall | What to do instead |
|---|---|
| Assuming Schuylkill County parishes are in the Scranton diocese | Check Philadelphia/Allentown diocesan archives |
| Searching only indexed FamilySearch records | Budget time for image browsing — most county records are unindexed |
| Checking only one naturalization court | Search all courts of record for the county |
| Treating Schuylkill County in isolation | Irish families near county lines likely have records in Luzerne, Carbon, Lackawanna, or Northumberland too |

---

### Neighboring Coal Counties — Each Needs Its Own Survey

The full anthracite region spans five counties. A miner's family could straddle any county line, and records will follow:

- **Lackawanna County** (formed from Luzerne in 1878; Scranton center)
- **Carbon County** (Mauch Chunk / Jim Thorpe area)
- **Northumberland County** (southern fields)
